q: What flight deck emergency equipment must you check?
a: Fire extinguisher, crash axe, overhead door, plus smoke and escape gear
qOrig: What flight deck emergency items are required to be checked?
detail: Nine items, all on the Preliminary Preflight. Then emergency descent devices, protective breathing equipment, gloves, AVSAX, life vest and flashlights, each stowed.
ref: FCOM NP.21.1 Preliminary Preflight Procedure - Captain or First Officer
note: The overhead door is checked closed and latched, not just present. It is your escape route out the top of the flight deck.

q: Where is the aircraft Sanitation Certificate?
a: Not named in our manuals; check Comply365 international documents
qOrig: Where is the aircraft Sanitation Certificate located? (inspected during Japanese JCAB Ramp Checks)
detail: The FOM names only the Airworthiness Certificate, Aircraft Registration and radio license as always required on board. Country-specific operating documents are added for international flights. Those are electronic, on the electronic flight bag in Comply365. No sanitation certificate appears anywhere in the FOM, FCOM or QRH.
quote: These documents are electronic and located on the EFB in Comply365.
note: The closest named item is the Certificate of Residual Disinsection, filed in Comply365 under Flying, Regulatory and Operating Docs, International Documents. Confirm the Japan ramp check list with the check airman.

q: Is HA approved for the NADP 1 departure?
a: Yes. Normal takeoff procedures satisfy it
qOrig: Is HA allowed to perform the NADP 1 Departure Procedure? (Japanese JCAB Ramp Check question; they...
detail: FOM 5.4.7 carries the noise abatement departure procedure under Ops Spec C068. Compliance with published noise abatement procedures is required at noise-sensitive airports. Because normal takeoff procedures already satisfy both the close-in (NADP 1) and distant (NADP 2) profiles, No separate NADP profile to fly.
ref: FOM 5.4.7 Noise Abatement Departure Procedure (NADP), Ops Spec C068
quote: (AS) Normal takeoff procedures satisfy either close-in or distant NADP profile requirements.
note: The FOM tags this (AS), and post-merger it is the governing procedure. Specific gradients and configuration-change altitudes come from the fleet manuals, the 10-7, or the Jeppesen Airway Manual noise abatement pages.

q: Where is the Jumpseat and Rest Facility Briefing Card?
a: Carried on the electronic flight bag; not required for flight
qOrig: Where is the Cockpit Jumpseat and/or Rest Facility Briefing Card located?
detail: The FOM lists the Jumpseat Card on the electronic flight bag and marks it not required for dispatch. The Captain still owes the occupant a briefing: seat and harness, communication gear, exits, emergency equipment, sterile flight deck, and flight deck door security. The card only helps you cover it.
ref: FOM 5.1.22.1.2.3 Flight Deck Jumpseat - Occupant Briefing
quote:
The Jumpseat Briefing
Card is not required for flight, but it may be used to assist this briefing:
note: On the 787, if two Overhead Flight Attendant Rest bunks are used as alternate pilot bunks, a separate laminated briefing card is supplied to the Cabin Crew.

q: How do you escape through the 787 overhead door?
a: Remove the cover, rotate the lock handle, then use descent devices
qOrig: How would you operate/escape through the 787 Flight Deck Overhead Door?
detail: The door is hinged to fall inward and hang from the ceiling, so stay clear as it drops. It only opens on the ground with the airplane depressurized. Slide the descent device compartment latch open, pull a device out, and hold its handle through every step until you are on the ground.
quote:
The flight deck overhead door is used for emergency egress using the installed
descent devices.
note: Climb out using the first observer seat, the observer console, the fold-down step in the bulkhead, and the hinged area of the door.

q: Where are the crew rest requirements?
a: Flight Operations Manual chapter 5, Crew Rest Facility
qOrig: Where can the Crew Rest procedures/requirements be found?
detail: Use is limited to Flight Crew on the Hawaiian seniority list, one occupant per bunk, no food or drink except bottled water. It cannot be occupied from pushback to 10,000 ft above field elevation, or from 45 minutes before landing to block in.
quote:
The purpose
of the crew rest facility is to provide a quiet place for the crew to rest. It is not a lounge, a meal
area, or a place to stow personal carry-on items.
note: The 787 primary facility is the Overhead Flight Crew Rest, maximum two occupants. The Overhead Flight Attendant Rest is the backup, limited to two labeled alternate pilot bunks for one segment.

q: What is the OFCR/OFAR door lock combination?
a: Not recorded. Security sensitive
qOrig: 787 - What is the OFCR/OFAR Door lock combination?
detail: FCOM 1.46 (OFCR) and FCOM 1.47 (OFAR) describe the entrance enclosure keyless lock: a door handle, a button keypad and a reset button. To unlock you enter the airline-programmed code and rotate the handle either direction; releasing the handle re-latches the bolt so the door can be closed without retracting it.
ref: FCOM 1.46 Overhead Flight Crew Rest - Door Lock Operation (also FCOM 1.47 OFAR)
quote:
To unlock the door, enter the airline-programmed code and rotate the door handle
in either direction to retract the door bolt. When the door handle is released, the
bolt automatically returns to the latched position allowing the door to be closed
without retracting the bolt.
note: The FCOM only describes the keyless lock as taking an 'airline-programmed code' and never prints the digits. Actual combinations are Sensitive Security Information under FOM 15.1 Security Policy and are not in the FCOM, FOM or QRH.

q: How many may use the OFCR?
a: 2 occupants
detail: The primary 787 crew rest facility is the Overhead Flight Crew Rest (OFCR); the backup is the Overhead Flight Attendant Rest (OFAR). If flight time or FDP requires it the Company may provide up to two bunks in the OFAR, labeled alternate pilot bunks, with a laminated briefing card supplied to the Cabin Crew.
quote: No more than 2 occupants are authorized to use the OFCR at any time.
note: The OFCR seat, bunks and common area may not be occupied during taxi, takeoff or landing. 787s departing a domicile or outstation with an Augmented, Double Augmented or Double Crew must carry at least 4 prepackaged bedding packets (sheet, blanket, pillow and case).

q: What is the flight deck door entry code?
a: Not recorded. Security sensitive
qOrig: What is the Flight Deck Door entry code?
detail: FOM 15.2.6.3 states the keypad control device shall not be used for normal entry and that entry attempts using the keypad shall be denied by the Flight Crew. FOM 15.2.6.3 also warns that an unexpected keypad activation signal must be treated as a Level 4 hijack or attempted hijack in progress until the Flight Attendants say otherwise.
quote:
The keypad control device shall not be used for normal entry. Entry attempts using the keypad
shall be denied by the Flight Crew. For A330F exception, see 15.2.6.10 – Flight Deck Access without
Functioning Service Interphone.
note: The code is not published in FOM, FCOM or QRH; it is SSI (FOM 15.1.1.1 lists security access codes as SSI). Note the policy point: the keypad is not for normal entry and keypad attempts must be denied.

ELTs are installed in the passenger cabin, as shown in the Emergency Equipment

note: It is a graphic, so text search will not find individual items. The flight deck companion diagram is FCOM 1.45.7 and the symbol legend is FCOM 1.45.6. Crew rest equipment is separate: OFCR at FCOM 1.46.17, OFAR at FCOM 1.47.13.

q: Where is the 787 overhead door described?
a: FCOM Doors systems description, Flight Deck Overhead Door
qOrig: Where can you find the 787 forward overhead door description, operation, components and egress procedures?

ref: FCOM 1.40.19 Flight Deck Overhead Door (controls at FCOM 1.30.30)
quote:
Flight Deck Overhead Door
The flight deck overhead door is used for emergency egress using the installed
descent devices. The door can only be opened on the ground with the airplane
depressurized.
note: Two places: FCOM 1.30.30 Flight Deck Overhead Door and Vent for the cover, handle and components, and FCOM 1.40.19-1.40.21 for description, operation and the egress route. FCOM NP.21.1 requires it closed and latched at preflight.

q: Where is preflight planning and the international release?
a: FOM Dispatch chapter, Flight Information and Redispatch section
qOrig: FOM Preflight Planning and International Dispatch Release...
detail: FOM Chapter 8 (Dispatch) holds the planning material: 8.1 authorized operations and airports, 8.2 alternates, 8.3 navigation, 8.4 weather, and 8.5 flight information documents and redispatch. FOM 8.5.1 defines the Flight Information Packet/Dispatch Release Package and makes the PIC responsible for having it prior to departure from an originating station.
ref: FOM 8.5 Flight Information - Documents and Redispatch (8.5.1 Flight Information Packet/Dispatch Release Package)
quote:
Dispatch produces the Flight Information Packet/Dispatch Release Package containing required and
supplemental data for flight release. The PIC shall review and ensure the following information (as
applicable) is in their possession prior to departure from an originating station:
note: The HA international release example and its legend are FOM 8.5.7 and 8.5.7.1. Preflight duties themselves are FOM 5.2; theater-specific international items are FOM chapters 19-24.

q: Named vs unnamed waypoint?
a: Named is in the database. Unnamed is lat/long or hand entered
qOrig: What is the difference between a named vs non-defined/unnamed waypoint?
detail: Non-defined or user-named waypoints are waypoints that are either not in the aircraft database, unnamed such as a latitude/longitude like 26N170W, or manually entered by the crew. These may require specific verification procedures, and the FOM sends you to fleet-specific manuals for the route verification procedure.
quote: waypoints that are either not in the aircraft database, unnamed (a latitude/longitude, such as “26N170W” or “26N70”), or a waypoint that the Fight Crew manually enters.
note: Oceanic tie-in: FOM 22.3.4 Unnamed Waypoint Verification carries the NAT-specific check.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.2.7: "independently verify the full latitude and longitude coordinates of “unnamed” (Lat/Long) waypoints" ICAO draws the same line, calling lat/long waypoints unnamed and requiring both pilots to verify their full coordinates.

q: What is in the dispatch release package?
a: Dispatch release, flight plan, weather package, and NOTAMs
qOrig: What documents are included in the Dispatch/Release package? (“Lucky 7”; in order or printing)
detail: Seven items: the dispatch release including the minimum equipment list, the flight plan, the aerodrome forecast, the routine weather report, special weather and significant meteorological reports with turbulence, Class D notices, and flight data center notices. The load closeout is also required before departure.
ref: FOM 8.5.1 Flight Information Packet/Dispatch Release Package
quote:
Dispatch produces the Flight Information Packet/Dispatch Release Package containing required and
supplemental data for flight release.
note: Your signature on the dispatch release says you reviewed all of it. Before pushback also confirm tail number, equipage and maintenance status match the release.

q: B043 vs B044 flight plan?
a: B043 international fuel reserve, B044 planned redispatch
qOrig: What is the difference between a BO44 vs B043 flight plan?
detail: B043 is the Ops Spec authorizing special fuel reserves in international operations, where the 10 percent applies only to planned oceanic/remote continental time and the final reserve is 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption.
quote: Ops Spec B043
note: Both reduce carried fuel but by different mechanisms: B043 narrows the window the 10 percent applies to; redispatch (B044) shortens the leg the 10 percent is computed against. 8.5.9 lists Ops Specs A002, A004, A008, B044 and B050.

q: Standard release vs redispatch?
a: Redispatch runs two plans, so you carry less fuel
qOrig: Discuss the differences between a standard dispatch release vs a Re-Dispatch/Re-Release...
detail: A standard release dispatches you to the destination on one plan. Planned redispatch is an FAA-authorized flag procedure that minimizes the fuel needed to meet the 10 percent requirement. You operate with two plans: the original dispatch to the intermediate destination, and a second plan from a planned redispatch waypoint to the intended destination.
quote: The terms of original Dispatch Release must be adhered to until the Captain and the Dispatcher concur on the terms of the redispatch.
note: Terminology to have cold: Intended Destination is the ultimate destination from the redispatch waypoint; Intermediate Destination is the one on the original release; the Redispatch Point is the common point on both flight plans where the continue decision is made.

q: Where is country-specific guidance?
a: FOM theater chapters plus Jeppesen State Rules and Procedures
qOrig: International Planning: Where can you find country-specific guidance?
detail: FOM chapters 19 through 24 are organized by theater and carry country-specific airspace, navigation, communication and procedural rules.
ref: FOM chapters 19-24 Theater chapters; example FOM 19.3.1.2 Holding Airspeeds
quote:
For holding procedures and airspeeds, see Jeppesen FD Pro app at the following location: Pubs
> North America > North America Airway Manual > State Rules and Procedures – Canada >
Instrument Flight Rules – Holding Procedures.
note: The six theater chapters are 19 North America, 20 Pacific, 21 Caribbean, 22 Atlantic, 23 Europe, 24 Asia. They repeatedly hand off to Jeppesen FD Pro State Rules and Procedures, and airport-specific items live in the Jeppesen 10-7 pages.
icao: NAT Doc 007 Foreword: "This Document is for guidance only. Regulatory material relating to North Atlantic aircraft operations" For the NAT theater this manual sits behind the FOM chapter; the regulatory material lives in ICAO Annexes, State AIPs and NOTAMs.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Destination alternate weather required to depart?
a: At or above alternate minimums for the ETA
qOrig: Weather required to be at our destination/destination alternate (Flag) to depart?
detail: A flight may not be dispatched unless the weather at the destination alternate is forecast at or above the alternate minimums for the time the aircraft would arrive there. Those minimums come from the Derived Alternate Airport IFR Weather Minimums table in 8.2.2.1 under Ops Spec C055.
ref: FOM 8.2.2.1 Destination Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: A flight may not be dispatched to the destination airport unless the weather conditions at a destination alternate airport are forecast to be at or above the alternate minimums
note: Second alternate rules live in 8.2.2.2 and Exemption 20108 in 8.2.2.3.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: ETOPS alternate weather before departure?
a: C055 minima, earliest to latest landing time
qOrig: Weather required for ETOPS alternate airport(s) prior to departure?
detail: The Dispatcher will not list an airport as an ETOPS alternate unless reports or forecasts indicate weather will be at or above the ETOPS alternate minima in Ops Spec C055 (see 8.2.2) for the whole window it might be used, earliest to latest possible landing time, and field condition reports indicate a safe landing can be made.
quote: Field condition reports indicate that a safe landing can be made.
note: Each designated ETOPS alternate must have RFFS equivalent to ICAO Category 4 or higher, with a 30-minute response time, which means equipment available on arrival of the diverting airplane, not equipment parked there in advance.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: ETOPS alternate weather in flight?
a: Crew operating minima
qOrig: Weather required for ETOPS alternate airport(s) in flight?
detail: From after takeoff until approaching the EEP, alternate weather must be at or above the crew's operating minima, that is what the operating crew needs to fly the approach given their minima and any applicable MEL, and the alternate must remain suitable to conduct an IAP. A turnback is required if an ETOPS alternate is no longer available.
ref: FOM 6.3.5 In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: Note that these weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning.
note: This is a favourite oral question because the answer changes at the EEP. If a METAR for an ETOPS alternate cannot be obtained after the EEP, a new ETOPS alternate must be designated.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Destination alternate weather in flight?
a: Crew operating minima
qOrig: Weather required at destination alternate airport in flight.
detail: Dispatch planning uses the derived alternate minimums table at 8.2.2.1. In flight the standard shifts to the crew's operating minima, meaning what the operating crew needs to conduct the approach given their minima and any applicable MEL. FOM 6.3.5 states plainly that the in-flight weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning.
quote: Note that these weather requirements are less restrictive than the criteria used by Dispatch in planning.
note: The dispatch-versus-inflight distinction is the whole question. Do not apply the 400-and-1 derived alternate minimums to an in-flight divert decision.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Takeoff weather minimums at the departure airport?
a: 1 sm or RVR 5000; lower than standard per table
qOrig: Weather required at departure airport for takeoff.
detail: Standard takeoff minimums are 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000 for aircraft of two engines or less (FOM 5.4.1.1).
quote: Defined as 1 sm visibility or RVR 5000 for aircraft having 2 engines or less.
note: FOM 5.4.4 authorizes lower than standard down to 500 RVR with the required lighting, and below 500 RVR (787) via the HGS/HUD Takeoff Briefing Card in the PRC. Charted SID/obstacle minimums may be more restrictive than the 10-9A.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Who can fly a low visibility takeoff?
a: Below 500 RVR, work off the PRC low visibility card
qOrig: Any limitations on who can perform a low visibility takeoff?
detail: Ops Spec C078 authorizes lower than standard takeoff minimums wherever a procedure allows standard minimums. For the 787, takeoffs below 500 RVR (150 m) require the Takeoff Low Visibility Card in the PRC. At foreign airports published 10-9A minimums may not conform to Ops Specs, and crews are restricted to the higher of the 10-9A or Ops Specs.
ref: FOM 5.4.4 IFR Lower than Standard Takeoff Minimum Requirements
quote: For takeoffs less than 500 RVR (150 m), see Takeoff Low Visibility Card in PRC.
note: NEW in Rev 125: 5.4.4 added 787 bannering and the HGS/HUD Takeoff Briefing Card, which is why this now applies to your fleet.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Visibility drops on approach. Can you continue?
a: Yes, once the final approach segment has begun
qOrig: If the visibility drops while on the approach, can we continue the approach?
detail: Do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums. However, if a weather report is obtained AFTER the final approach segment has been initiated and it indicates below minimum conditions, the pilot may continue the approach to DA/DH or MDA.
quote: the pilot may continue the approach to DA/DH or MDA.
note: The trigger is the start of the FINAL APPROACH SEGMENT, not the FAF crossing or the clearance. For non-precision and CAT I: TDZ RVR is controlling, Mid and Rollout are advisory, and Mid may substitute if TDZ is unavailable. RVR above 6000 is advisory only.

secTitle: Know Weather Minima & Limitations for Dispatch, Takeoff, Approach, and Landing
q: Different visibility rules at international airports?
a: Yes. Some ICAO states allow Converted Meteorological Visibility
qOrig: Are there different requirements at some international airports?
detail: Some ICAO countries allow use of Converted Meteorological Visibility (CMV) when RVR is not reported, for approaches that are not low-visibility. The FOM directs you to the Aerodrome Operating Minimums and Converted Meteorological Visibility references in the Jeppesen Publications for further guidance.
quote: Some ICAO countries allow for use of Converted Meteorological Visibility (CMV) when RVR is not reported for non low-vis approaches.
note: Separately, at foreign airports the published 10-9A takeoff minimums may not conform to Ops Specs, and crews are restricted to the HIGHER of the 10-9A or Ops Specs (FOM 5.4.4). Theatre chapters 19 through 24 carry the country-specific items.

q: Who has operational control of a flight?
a: The PIC and the Dispatcher, jointly
qOrig: Who has operational control of a flight?
detail: The PIC and the Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for preflight planning, delay, and the Dispatch Release, and jointly determine the suitability of weather, field and traffic conditions, airway facilities, and the filed route. Neither can dispatch alone; both must agree.
quote: jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight
note: Regulatory basis 14 CFR 121.533/.535/.537/.551/.557/.627 and Ops Spec A008. Captain-side point: joint responsibility is not shared authority in flight. Once airborne the PIC retains final authority under 2.1.2.

q: What requires Dispatch notification in flight?
a: Any abnormality or irregularity
qOrig: What items require Dispatch notification during a flight?
detail: Flights experiencing abnormalities or irregularities, including but not limited to those listed in 7.2.3 Pilot Reports Quick Reference, shall contact Dispatch and report the details. Notification is mandatory; the timing flexes to safety of flight. If time does not permit contact in flight, contact shall be made after gate arrival.
quote: “Contact Dispatch” implies that while notification is mandatory, such communications should take place as safety of flight considerations permit.
note: Rev 125.1 revised 7.2.3 to state the table is not all-inclusive and that the Company may request safety reports for items not listed when additional information is needed. Separately 11.1.3 covers Cabin notification, and 11.2.11 gives the NTSB briefing format for the Flight Attendants.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: Where are the FMS/ACARS uplink and setup procedures?
a: FCOM Communications chapter, Supplementary Procedures, and Performance Inflight AeroData
qOrig: Where are the FMS/ACARS/Uplink and Setup Procedures located?
detail: FCOM SP.5 gives the verification procedures for messages uplinked in COMPANY format: pre-departure clearance and oceanic clearance must be manually compared against the filed flight plan with voice contact if anything disagrees, D-ATIS altimeter numeric and alpha values must match, and weight and balance and takeoff data are verified per the FOM.
ref: FCOM SP.5 Communications - Flight Deck Communications System (Datalink)
quote:
The following procedures are one means which may be used to verify
Pre-Departure Clearance, Digital-Automatic Terminal Information
Service (D-ATIS), Oceanic Clearances, Weight and Balance and Takeoff
Data messages transmitted via the COMPANY format.
note: Three places to know: FCOM SP.5 for uplink verification policy, FCOM 5.40 MFD Communications Functions for the datalink/ACARS pages and managers, and FCOM PI.19 AeroData for the ACARS takeoff and landing performance requests. FMS setup itself is FCOM NP.21.2 CDU Preflight Procedure.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you know the nav database is current?
a: Check the ACTIVE date range on the FMS IDENT page
qOrig: How can you tell if the Nav database is current?
detail: The identification page shows the effective date range of the active navigation database, with the inactive cycle on the line below. Preflight has you cycle the active database to erase old pilot entries, then confirm the ACTIVE range covers today.
quote: Verify that the navigation database ACTIVE date range is current.
note: If a database expires in flight, keep using it. The date can only be changed on the ground, after landing.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: Can you change the nav database?
a: Yes. Swap in the inactive cycle on the IDENT page
qOrig: Can you change the Nav database? How?
detail: Select the inactive date range to copy it into the scratchpad, then select the ACTIVE line to move it up. The old active date drops to the inactive line. Ground only, and it erases all previously entered route data, so reload the route afterward.
quote:
If the active navigation database is out of date, it can be changed to the inactive
navigation database.
note: The REF NAV DATA page only displays waypoint, navaid, airport and runway data. It does not change the database.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you know the AMM database is current?
a: CrossCheck app lists required versions; sync all apps before the trip
qOrig: 787 – How can you tell the AMM database is current?
detail: Our manuals give no moving map specific expiry display. Within 24 hours of starting a trip every app on the electronic flight bag must meet minimum currency and be synchronized so all charts and databases are current. CrossCheck and the Manual Currency page show which versions are required.
quote:
all apps on the EFB must meet minimum
  currency requirements, all flight-related apps must be synchronized to ensure all charts and
  databases are current, and all required operational memos, manual revisions/bulletins, and
  safety flashes must be read and acknowledged or signed as applicable.
note: The airport moving map rides inside Jeppesen FD Pro. If that app will not run, the Jeppesen Trip Kit is the approved backup.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
q: How do you verify the correct ECL is loaded?
a: Database revision must match the QRH front page
qOrig: 787 – How do you verify the correct ECL is loaded?
detail: During the preflight flow you push the CHECKLIST display switch, select RESETS, then Verify/Set AIRLINE DATABASE. Select the AIRLINE DATABASE that has a REVISION matching the ECL Revision listed on the front page of the current approved QRH, then select RESET ALL.
quote: Select the AIRLINE DATABASE that has a REVISION that matches the “ECL Revision” listed on the front page of the current approved QRH.
note: The QRH is the authority here, not the airplane. If the airplane database revision does not match the QRH front page, the ECL is not the approved checklist. RESET ALL after setting it clears any prior crew state.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: Who reads the closeout data?
a: The First Officer reads the count and jumpseat numbers
qOrig: Who reads the closeout data?
detail: Passenger count verification is part of the load closeout procedure. The Captain checks them against the Flight Deck Report. Any discrepancy goes to Load Planning before you go.
quote: The First Officer reads the passenger count and jumpseat numbers from the Load Closeout.
note: The closeout passenger count drives performance. The Flight Deck Report count is what the agents and flight attendants work from, so the two must agree.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: Who verifies the closeout, and when?
a: The Captain, before pushback
qOrig: Who verifies it? When?
detail: The Captain verifies the numbers match the Flight Deck Report, and as Pilot in Command must receive and review the closeout prior to pushback. If a delay or a return to the gate changes passengers or loading, get a revised closeout before takeoff.
ref: FOM 5.2.19 Load Closeout/SABLE Weight and Balance Loadsheet
quote:
The Flight Crew will normally receive the Load
Closeout via ACARS and the Pilot-In-Command (PIC) must receive and review it prior to pushback.
note: On the 787 the closeout normally arrives by ACARS, and the final takeoff performance request uplinks zero fuel weight and takeoff data with it.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: What closeout items must be verified?
a: Takeoff weight, weight and balance, passenger count, dangerous goods notice
qOrig: List several items that are required to be verified.
detail: Compare the planned takeoff weight on the dispatch release against the actual takeoff weight on the closeout. Crosscheck the weight and balance and performance numbers, including the flight management system entries, for reasonableness. Verify the passenger and jumpseat count, and confirm the dangerous goods entry is accurate.
ref: FOM 5.2.19 Load Closeout/SABLE Weight and Balance Loadsheet
quote:
The crosscheck includes comparing the
planned Takeoff Weight on the Dispatch Release against the Actual Takeoff Weight indicated on the
Load Closeout or SABLE Weight and Balance Loadsheet.
note: If the release and closeout takeoff weights differ, apply the dispatch release weight tolerance rules before accepting the numbers.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: No TPR. How do you get takeoff performance?
a: Use the release Takeoff and Landing Report, or call Dispatch
qOrig: How do you obtain takeoff performance if a TPR is unavailable?
detail: The Takeoff and Landing Report comes on the dispatch release and flight plan. It is the third choice, behind the final and then the preliminary takeoff performance request. Dispatch can also compute an updated report and send it to the printer, by email, or read it to you.
quote:
Dispatcher: An updated TLR can be calculated and sent to the aircraft
     printer, email, or relayed verbally to the flight crew.
note: Do not build takeoff data with the onboard performance tool. The FCOM prohibits it. The FOM allows new data by ACARS or from Dispatch.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: Can you use the TLR for takeoff data?
a: Yes. It is the takeoff data on the Dispatch Release
qOrig: Can we use the TLR for takeoff information? When would we use it?
detail: FOM 5.4.5 requires takeoff data be available and checked for each takeoff, and names where it comes from: the Flight Information Packet carries the TPR, the Dispatch Release carries the TLR. So the TLR is a legitimate source of takeoff data, not a workaround. Validation criteria live in the fleet manuals, and invalid data is replaced by ACARS or Dispatch.
quote: Flight Information Packet (TPR)/Dispatch Release (TLR)
note: Takeoff data must be available and checked for every takeoff. If the data is invalid against the fleet validation criteria, get new data by ACARS or from Dispatch, who has the online performance tool.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: TLR concerns with temp and altimeter?
a: Dispatch's assumed temperature and altimeter, not actual conditions
qOrig: Any concerns when using TLR for takeoff information? Temp and altimeter.
detail: The Takeoff and Landing Report is built on the conditions the dispatcher expected at dispatch and the weight the dispatcher planned. If the actual temperature or altimeter setting has moved, those numbers no longer match the day. Send a fresh takeoff performance request or get updated data from Dispatch.
ref: FCOM PI.18.2 Hierarchy Of Takeoff Performance
quote:
The TLR is considered the tertiary data source for takeoff
     performance. The TLR includes the environmental conditions
     the dispatcher considered at dispatch, and the takeoff weight
     planned by the dispatcher.
note: Numeric validation tolerances are not in the FOM or FCOM. They sit in the AeroData Performance Handbook on the electronic flight bag. Get the exact temperature and altimeter limits from the check airman.

secTitle: Perform ACARS and FMS Initialization and Verification
group: Load Closeout/TPR Update and review procedure
q: Dangerous goods on board. What governs?
a: Review and acknowledge the eNOTOC, then retain it
qOrig: Describe the Dangerous goods procedures if you have any on your flight...
detail: Dangerous goods on board means the PIC must receive a NOTOC (FOM 14.1.1).
quote:
• Acknowledging the eNOTOC by selecting either “ACCEPT*” on the MCDU or “ACKNOWLEDGE
  NOTOC” on the Comm page (depending on fleet type).
note: HA rules differ from AS: hand edits to the eNOTOC are not permissible (AS allows Ramp Lead edits to tail number and DG location on the paper NOTOC, FOM 14.1.5). eNOTOC arrives at departure minus 30 min international, minus 15 min interisland (FOM 14.1.4).

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Where are the standard customer service PAs?
a: Flight Operations Manual chapter 7, Standard Customer Service Announcements
qOrig: What section of the FOM are the Standard Customer Service Announcements (PA’s) located?
detail: Identify yourself as the Captain or First Officer. Keep it plain: no aviation abbreviations, no jargon, no knots, broken clouds, chop or abort. Limit announcements while passengers are asleep. Drop the choice of airlines line on Southeast Alaska flights.
quote:
Pilots can use the PA system as a customer service tool to enhance safety and leave a positive
impression with our customers.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Which PAs must the flight crew make?
a: The required PAs, starting with the seat belt sign
qOrig: Which announcements are required to be made by the Flight Crew?
detail: Flight Crews are required to make the PAs in 7.1.19 during each flight with passengers or persons on board, acknowledging that flight conditions and priorities may occasionally preclude timely execution in the interest of safety.
quote: Flight Crew may use judgment to vary the wording of these announcements except where the announcement is noted as verbatim.
note: Workload permitting, pilots announce any change in Seat Belt Sign condition, and the F/As must also announce it regardless of whether the pilots do. The FOM encourages Aloha from the Flight Deck and Mahalo on Hawaii flights.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Pushing back late. When is a PA required?
a: At scheduled departure time, then every 15 minutes
qOrig: When should you need to make a PA if you are pushing off the gate late? Minutes?
detail: FOM 7.1.21.1 states that at the departure time the Captain will either authorize pushback/engine start or notify Operations and the passengers of the delay, giving the reason if known.
ref: FOM 7.1.21.1 General - Departure Time Delay Announcement ('push or talk')
quote:
• Departure Time Delay Announcement (“push or talk”) – At the departure time, the Captain will
  either authorize pushback/starting engines procedures or notify Operations and the passengers
  of the delay.
note: The 'push or talk' rule is the trigger: at departure time you either authorize pushback or you tell Operations and the passengers.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Demonstrate a late pushback, go-around and engine failure PA
a: Use FOM sample PAs: delay, go-around, emergency equipment
qOrig: Demonstrate a late pushback PA, a go around PA, and engine failure PA...
detail: Late pushback: at departure time either push or talk, give the reason and an approximate length, then update every 15 minutes (FOM 7.1.21.1). Go-around: FOM 7.1.21 says a short PA should be made when workload and ATC coordination permit, and below 10,000 ft, on an extended downwind or in holding, you may state the reason and your intentions.
ref: FOM 7.1.21 Standard Customer Service Announcements and FOM 7.1.22 Emergency Vehicles Requested Sample PA
quote:
• Missed Approach/Go-Around – Should a go-around be necessary, a short PA announcement
  should be made when workload and ATC coordination permits.
note: No verbatim engine failure PA in the FOM. The closest scripted text is FOM 7.1.22 (emergency equipment standing by) and the NTSB brief examples at FOM 11.2.11, one of which is an engine shutdown and return.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: How do you make a PA on the headset?
a: Push and hold the ACP PA mic switch
qOrig: How do you make a PA using a headset (which button/transmit switches)?
detail: With a headset or boom mic, the PA is keyed from the audio control panel: push and hold the PA mic switch, which extinguishes the MIC light for any other transmitter and keys the announcement from that station to all PA areas (FCOM 5.10.2).
ref: FCOM 5.10.2 Audio Control Panel (ACP) - PA Mic Switch
quote:
6      PA Mic Switch
Push and hold –
  • the MIC light for any other transmitter extinguishes
  • keys passenger address announcement from this station to all PA areas

  7      Receiver Lights
Illuminated (green) – indicates the respective receiver volume control is manually
selected on.
note: The ACP PA mic switch is direct access to ALL PA areas and takes top cabin PA priority, above priority all-area announcements and above handset announcements (FCOM 5.30.2). Monitor the PA by pushing the PA receiver volume control on the ACP.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: PA PRIO vs PA ALL?
a: PRIO is priority. ALL includes crew rest
qOrig: What is the difference between PA PRIO and PA ALL selections?
detail: The 787 audio control panel provides selectable PA transmit options. PA ALL keys the passenger address announcement from that station to all PA areas, which includes the crew rest facilities. The priority selection is used when the announcement must override lower-priority audio.
quote:
keys passenger address announcement from this station to all PA areas

  7      Receiver Lights
Illuminated (green) – indicates the respective receiver volume control is manually
selected on.
note: Confirm the exact PRIO versus ALL behaviour and the crew-rest exclusion selection against FCOM 5.30.2 in the PDF.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: How do you make a PA on the flight deck handset?
a: Select the PA dial code, push handset PA push-to-talk
qOrig: How do you make a PA using the flight deck handset?
detail: Take the handset off the cradle, select the PA area with the numeric keys, the step up/step down switches, or the dial code select switch, then push and hold the handset PA push-to-talk switch, which connects the handset microphone to the selected PA area and is only used in PA mode (FCOM 5.10.19).
quote:
2   Handset PA Push-To-Talk Switch
Push –
  • connects the handset microphone to the selected PA area
  • only used in the PA mode

January 31, 2023 787 FCOM - HAWAIIAN AIRLINES                                            5.
note: Select PA CALL from the TCP speed dial list or enter/step to the PA area dial code on the handset, then key the handset PA push-to-talk.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Which PA reaches the cabin but not crew rest?
a: Individual passenger address areas on the cabin interphone directory page
qOrig: What selection should you use to make a PA throughout the cabin, but NOT to the crew rest facilities?
detail: The passenger address mic switch on the audio control panel keys every area at once, crew rest included. To leave the bunks out, go through the cabin interphone directory or the flight deck handset and pick only the cabin areas you want.
quote:
Pushing a PA mic switch on an audio control panel provides
direct access to all PA areas.
note: The directory carries CREW REST as its own entry, separate from the passenger address areas. That is the one you avoid selecting when the off duty pilot is asleep.

secTitle: Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the flight deck
q: Where is the list of cabin communication codes?
a: Printed on the flight deck handset, the two digit station codes
qOrig: (787) Where can you find a list of Cabin Communication Codes?
detail: The two digit station codes are printed right on the flight deck handset. You can also step through them on the cabin interphone directory and subdirectory pages, or type a code into the scratchpad and select MAKE CALL. An invalid code returns INVALID ENTRY.
quote:
A list of the two digit station codes is located on the
handset.
note: Hawaiian builds the directory, so it is not reproduced in the manual. Speed dial covers the common ones: passenger address, all call, purser, forward galley, ground crew.

secTitle: Perform FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start
q: What check is called to the flight deck before start?
a: Walkaround Check complete, verbally from the Ground Crew
qOrig: What “check” must be communicated to the Flt Deck prior to engine start?
detail: FOM 5.2.20 requires, before movement, that the Flight Crew check all door indications to confirm closed and receive a verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the Walkaround Check is complete.
ref: FOM 5.2.20 Cabin Safety Check Prior to Taxi or Pushback
quote:
to confirm they are closed and receive a verbal confirmation from the Ground Crew that the
  Walkaround Check is complete. If installed, the Installed Physical Secondary Barrier (IPSB) must
  be verified stowed and latched.
note: Two separate confirmations happen here: the A Flight Attendant/FFA says 'Cabin Secure' and closes the flight deck door, and the Ground Crew verbally confirms the Walkaround Check. The crew must also check all door indications and verify the IPSB stowed and latched if installed.

secTitle: Perform FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start
q: Review the engine failure procedure
a: In the FCOM and the FCTM
qOrig: Review Engine failure procedure...
detail: Engine failure procedure review, RTO PM callouts, max angle climb speed and minimum autopilot engagement altitude are FCOM NP.21 and L.10 plus FCTM. Verify each figure against the PDF; do not carry them from memory into a Procedures Validation.

secTitle: Perform FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start
q: Where do you find the EFP for a runway?
a: Takeoff performance report item 28; also AeroData special engine out procedures
qOrig: Where can you find the EFP for a specific runway? Anywhere else?
detail: Item 28 of the takeoff performance report gives the engine failure procedure for that runway, and item 27 gives the engine out flap retraction altitude. The printed AeroData special engine out procedures for departure and destination are your backup copy. Brief both against the runway and intersection you are actually using.
quote:
27. Engine out flap retraction altitude
28. Engine failure procedure




November 1.
note: The engine out procedure is runway specific and can change when the intersection or thrust mode changes. Re-read item 28 on every new performance report, not just the first one.

secTitle: Perform FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start
q: Where is the departure briefing guidance?
a: Yes. FOM Threat-Based Departure Briefing/TPC
qOrig: Do we have any guidance regarding the Departure briefing? Where can it be found?
detail: FOM 5.2.7 says the PF initiates the departure briefing prior to pushback and that it should be interactive, concise and big picture, with the PM identifying relevant threats first, using the Crew Briefing Reference Card threat list and 10-7 airport threats as needed, and the PF adding any others.
quote:
Prior to pushback, the PF initiates the departure briefing. The departure briefing should be
interactive, concise, and focused on the big picture. Pilots jointly identify any relevant threats,
followed by the PF presenting the departure plan and any other considerations.
note: TPC = Threats (PM and PF), Plan (PF), Considerations (PF). The threat list is on the Crew Briefing Reference Card plus airport threats in the 10-7. The arrival mirror image is FOM 5.5.16 Threat-Based Approach Briefing/TPC.

q: How do you talk to the ground crew before pushback?
a: Flight interphone headset, nose gear jack, standard phraseology
qOrig: How do you communicate with your ground crew prior to pushback? (Cockpit/Ground Communications)
detail: Normal means is the flight interphone. The ground crew plugs into the flight interphone jack on the nose landing gear (FCOM 5.30.1) and the flight deck keys INT on the ACP or control wheel. FOM 5.2.24 scripts the exact phraseology for brake release, cleared to start, and cleared to disconnect.
quote:
Interphone communication between Flight Deck and pushback crew is normally required. Standard
phraseology shall be used.
note: FCOM NP.21.30 Pushback or Towing Procedure makes it a Captain item: establish communications with ground handling personnel. The jack itself is described in FCOM 5.30.1.

q: How do you alert the ground crew?
a: Flight interphone; CONNECT INTERPHONE hand signal if unavailable
qOrig: How do you alert/call the ground crew?
detail: Ground-to-flight-deck alerting is well documented: a ground crew call gives an aural chime, the GROUND CALL EICAS communications message, and a CALL light on the ACP transmitter select switch (FCOM 5.30.1).
quote:
CONNECT INTERPHONE; indicates the need for direct contact
                between the Flight Crew and ground personnel.
note: The 787 FCOM shows no flight deck switch dedicated to calling the ground crew. The FLIGHT DECK CALL SW on the nose wheel well panel (FCOM 8.10.5) runs ground-to-flight-deck only.

q: No interphone for pushback. What are the hand signals?
a: Set brakes, release brakes, emergency stop, all clear
qOrig: If pushing back without an interphone, what are the hand signals?
detail: No interphone means you brief it before anyone moves. Cover the pushback plan and the signals you will use, and be specific about how the ground crew tells you to stop. The signal set itself is the standard marshalling one: set brakes, release brakes, emergency stop, all clear.
quote:
In the event that interphone communication is not available, the Captain will brief the Ground
Crew on expected pushback procedures and review hand signals.
note: Start engines doubles as the walkaround complete signal when headset communication is not available.

q: Can you be pulled forward with two engines running?
a: No. Prohibited with both engines running
qOrig: Can you have the aircraft pulled forward with two engines running?
detail: FOM 5.2.23 states the ground crew policy currently prohibits forward tow operations with both engines running. Shut one down first, or use a single engine taxi procedure if the tow is really a repositioning.
quote:
The Ground Crew policy currently prohibits forward tow operations with both engines
running.
note: This is a ground crew policy limit, not an aircraft limitation. Expect the crew chief to refuse the pull rather than the airplane to stop you.

secTitle: Complete Normal engine Start FCOM Procedure
q: Which quick action items apply during engine start?
a: Aborted Engine Start, ENG AUTOSTART, Fire Eng on Ground/Tailpipe
qOrig: Which Quick Action Items (787) may be required during ENG START, e.g. Aborted Engine Start, Hot Start, Hung Start?
detail: Quick Action Index items that can bite during ENG START are Aborted Engine Start L, R (7.1), ENG AUTOSTART L, R (7.3), ENG LIMIT EXCEED L, R (7.4), Fire Eng Tailpipe L, R (8.5), FIRE ENG L, R (8.2), and Fire Eng on Ground L, R (Back Cover.2).
quote:
*Aborted Engine Start L, R ........................... 7.1
*AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE.
note: No separate 787 hot start or hung start checklist. Autostart manages start faults, and ENG AUTOSTART L, R (QRH 7.3) is the annunciated failure when autostart cannot start the engine.

secTitle: Complete Normal engine Start FCOM Procedure
q: Is there a QRH procedure for a tailpipe fire?
a: Yes. Fire Eng Tailpipe L, R, ground only, no fire warning
qOrig: Is there a QRH procedure for a TAILPIPE FIRE?
detail: It is a ground checklist for a tailpipe fire with no engine fire warning. Fuel control switch cutoff, verify the engine fire switch is in, advise the cabin, then run the start selector to START to motor the engine. Advise air traffic control, and return the selector to NORM once the fire is out.
ref: QRH 8.5 Fire Eng Tailpipe L, R
quote:
Condition:   An engine tailpipe fire occurs on the ground
             with no engine fire warning.
note: Motoring only works with the auxiliary power unit running or two external power sources on. Losing that power source is what turns this into an evacuation decision.

secTitle: Complete Normal engine Start FCOM Procedure
q: What is the hand signal for a tailpipe fire?
a: Horizontal figure eight; other hand points to fire
qOrig: What is the hand signal for Tailpipe Fire?
detail: FOM 5.3.12 defines FIRE as a horizontal figure 8 made by hand or wand, with the other hand or wand pointing at the location of the fire.
quote:
FIRE; signifies a fire and it’s location to the Flight Crew by indicating a horizontal
figure 8, by hand or wand.
note: Same FIRE signal is used for any fire location, not just a tailpipe fire. Pair it with QRH 8.5 Fire Eng Tailpipe L, R.

secTitle: Complete Normal engine Start FCOM Procedure
q: Is there a QRH procedure for a ground engine fire?
a: Yes. Fire Eng on Ground L, R
qOrig: Is there a QRH procedure for an ENG FIRE on the ground?
detail: Fire Eng on Ground L, R applies when fire is observed or detected in the affected engine on the ground.
ref: QRH Back Cover.2 Fire Eng on Ground L, R
quote: Condition:   One or more of these occur on the ground:
note: It lives on the back cover of the QRH, not in the Fire chapter, and it is cross-referenced from QRH 8.4 and from the Quick Action Index.

secTitle: Perform FCOM Procedures Following Engine Start/Before Taxi
q: What must you consider before pushback and taxi?
a: NOTAMs, ATIS, closures or construction, and the taxi route
qOrig: What items must be considered prior to pushback/taxi?
detail: Two things before you move. Review NOTAMs and current ATIS for taxiway or runway closures, construction, or any other airport risk that touches your taxi route. Then confirm both pilots understand the expected route. If either of you is unsure, stop and ask the controller.
quote:
• Review NOTAMs and current ATIS for any taxiway or runway closures, construction activity, or
  other airport risks that could affect the taxi route.
note: Complex taxi instructions have to be written down. Dual acknowledgment is required for runway crossing, hold short, line up and wait, cleared for takeoff and cleared to land.

secTitle: Perform FOM Takeoff and Departure Briefing Including Identification of Operational Threats
q: What is the main concept of the TPC briefing?
a: Threats jointly, then the PF plan, then considerations
qOrig: Discuss the main concept of the TPC briefing...
detail: TPC replaces a read-the-plate monologue with a threat-led, interactive exchange. The PM opens by naming relevant threats, the PF adds any others, then the PF briefs the plan and the considerations. It should be interactive, concise and focused on the big picture, with management strategies discussed as threats surface.
quote: The approach briefing should be interactive, concise, and focused on the big picture.
note: Captain-side: an interactive briefing is where you set flight-deck tone. If the FO never speaks during your brief, the T was skipped and you have lost the main safety value of the format.

secTitle: Perform FOM Takeoff and Departure Briefing Including Identification of Operational Threats
q: Who starts the briefing?
a: The PF, but the PM speaks first on threats
qOrig: Who starts the briefing?
detail: Within the format the PM identifies relevant threats first, then the PF briefs any additional threats followed by the plan and considerations.
quote: Prior to beginning the descent, the PF initiates the approach briefing.

secTitle: Perform FOM Takeoff and Departure Briefing Including Identification of Operational Threats
q: Where is the briefing guidance?
a: Yes. Threats, Plan, Considerations departure briefing before pushback
qOrig: Do we have any guidance regarding this briefing? Where can it be found?
detail: The pilot flying starts it before pushback, and it runs Threats, Plan, Considerations. The pilot monitoring names the relevant threats first, using the Crew Briefing Reference Card and the airport 10-7 page. Then the pilot flying briefs taxi and departure runway, performance and configuration, route, and the return plan.
quote:
Prior to pushback, the PF initiates the departure briefing. The departure briefing should be
interactive, concise, and focused on the big picture.
note: Considerations is where you assign specific pilot monitoring duties tied to the threats you just named. Recap the critical threats at the end.

q: Where is taxi guidance in the FOM?
a: Flight Operations chapter, Taxi section, right after pushback and engine start
qOrig: Where in the FOM can you find information on taxiing?
detail: Taxi sits in the Flight Operations chapter between pushback and takeoff. It covers when taxi is prohibited, taxi thrust, taxi guidance and speeds, runway incursion prevention, low visibility taxi, hand signals and tarmac delays. It then points you to the fleet manuals for airplane specific technique.
quote:
While taxiing in the ramp/gate area, any congested area, where taxi instructions are complex, or
during periods of reduced visibility, the Flight Crew shall devote their full attention to taxiing the
aircraft.
note: Taxi is prohibited when braking action is reported NIL by the airport or another aircraft. That is a company rule, not a technique.

q: Must both pilots have the FD Pro taxi chart out?
a: Not stated in our manuals. FD Pro procedure
qOrig: Do both crewmembers must have the FD Pro TAXI chart out and available during surface movements?
detail: This is a Jeppesen FD Pro X or EFB workflow step, not FOM/FCOM content. Verify against the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365 and demonstrate on the actual device during OE. FOM 5.7.3.15 does require the ENTIRE cleared route be loaded into the approved charting app for ORCN segments.

q: Can the ND airport map be used for navigation?
a: Not stated in our manuals
qOrig: (787) Can the Airport map displayed on the ND be used for navigation?
detail: The airport map on the ND is a situational awareness aid and is not approved as a primary navigation source; confirm the exact FCOM wording before stating it. Recommended speed prior to a 90 degree turn is FCTM Ground Operations. FOM 5.3.3 caps taxi speed at 30 kts straight and smooth, approximately 10 kts in congested areas.

q: Max breakaway thrust N1?
a: 40% N1 maximum for breakaway
qOrig: Thrust Use – Max breakaway thrust, N1?
detail: FCOM NP.21.33 lists three engine warm up requirements before takeoff: run the engines at least 3 minutes, use no more than 40% N1 for breakaway, and engine oil temperature above the bottom of the temperature scale. FOM 5.3.2 Taxi Thrust only warns to stay aware of equipment, structures, and aircraft behind you when engines are above idle.
ref: FCOM NP.21.33 Before Takeoff Procedure - Engine warm up requirements
quote:
Use no more than 40% N1 for breakaway
 • Engine oil temperature must be above the bottom of the temperature
   scale
                Pilot Flying                         Pilot Monitoring
                                         Set the TAXI light switch ON and the
                                         RUNWAY TURNOFF light switches
                                         as needed.
note: Same 40% N1 number appears in FCOM SP sand and dust guidance, paired with a 10 knot ground speed cap. FOM 5.3.2 Taxi Thrust carries no number, so the pointer to FOM is wrong.

q: Max taxi speed?
a: 30 kts straight and smooth, 10 kts congested
qOrig: Max Taxi Speed/s, and Braking technique?
detail: While taxiing in the ramp or gate area, any congested area, where taxi instructions are complex, or during reduced visibility, the Flight Crew shall devote full attention to taxiing the aircraft.
quote: Speed shall be limited to not more than 30 kts, achieved only on straight, smooth taxiways, and approximately 10 kts in congested areas.
note: Note shall, and 30 kts is conditional on straight and smooth, not a blanket allowance. When operationally feasible, single-engine taxi is the standard procedure for fuel efficiency.

q: Why keep groundspeed in your scan?
a: To hold 30 kts max, about 10 kts congested
qOrig: Emphasize importance of keeping groundspeed in scan...
detail: FOM 5.3.3 caps taxi speed at 30 kts, only on straight smooth taxiways, and approximately 10 kts in congested areas, and requires full crew attention while taxiing in the ramp, congested areas, complex taxi instructions, or reduced visibility.
quote:
Speed shall be limited to not more than 30 kts, achieved only on straight, smooth taxiways, and
approximately 10 kts in congested areas.
note: There is no taxi speed readout on the PFD. Ground speed on the ND is the reference, so keep it in the scan. Turn speed matters more than straight line speed for tire scrub and passenger comfort.

q: Recommended speed before a 90 degree turn?
a: No turn number published; about 10 knots in congested areas
qOrig: Review recommended speed prior to entering a 90n turn...
detail: Our manuals do not give a speed tied to a 90 degree turn. What they do give is a taxi limit: no more than 30 knots, and only on straight smooth taxiways, with roughly 10 knots in congested areas. Turns happen in the congested areas, so 10 knots is the working number.
quote:
Speed shall be limited to not more than 30 kts, achieved only on straight, smooth taxiways, and
approximately 10 kts in congested areas.
note: The turn specific technique lives in the FCTM ground operations chapter, which is not one of the three manuals above. Confirm the number there before you quote it.

q: When do you use differential braking for hot brakes?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Demonstrate use of differential braking if brake temperature on one side is significantly hotter than the...
detail: No differential braking technique for uneven brake temperatures appears in the FOM, FCOM or QRH. What is published is the hot brake response: minimize taxiing, leave the parking brake off unless you need it, and expect wheel fuse plugs can melt. Cooling time comes from the brake cooling schedule.
quote:
2 Minimize taxiing.
3 Unless needed, do not set the parking brake.
4 Wheel fuse plugs can melt.
note: Brake temperatures per wheel are on the gear synoptic. BRAKE TEMP shows at 5.0 or higher and clears below 3.0. The braking technique itself is FCTM ground operations material.

q: Gear location and turning radius?
a: Wing tip swings the widest arc, 144 feet radius
qOrig: Location of gear/turning Radius...
detail: The wing tip sets your obstruction clearance because it swings the largest arc and everything else stays inside it. Wing tip radius is 144 feet, nose radius 110 feet, tail radius 126 feet, at the maximum steering angle of 70 degrees. Gear positions are on the principal dimensions page just ahead of it.
quote:
The wing tip swings the largest arc while turning and determines the minimum
obstruction clearance path. All other portions of the airplane structure remain
within this arc.
note: Never turn away from an obstacle within 15 feet of the wing tip or 55 feet of the nose. Turning away is what swings the tail and the far wing into it.

q: Where is the guidance on oversteering in turns?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Where can you find taxi guidance/technique regarding oversteering in turns?
detail: Oversteering technique is not written in the FOM, FCOM or QRH. The system facts are: the tiller turns the nosewheels up to 70 degrees either way, the rudder pedals up to 8 degrees, and the two inputs sum. The FOM simply says devote full attention to taxiing and see the fleet manuals.
quote:
Limited steering control is available through the rudder pedals. The tillers can turn
the nosewheels up to 70º in either direction.
note: The oversteer discussion is in the FCTM ground operations chapter. Judge it against the wing tip arc, since the wing tip is what actually hits something.

q: Normal 180 degree turning radius?
a: 144 feet wing tip radius; 154 feet pavement needed
qOrig: What is the normal 180 degree turning radius?
detail: A normal 180 degree turn is a slow continuous turn with minimum thrust on all engines and no differential braking. That gives a 144 foot wing tip radius and needs 154 feet of pavement width. Anything narrower is no longer the normal turn.
quote:
Note: Minimum pavement width for 180o turn: 154 Feet 0 Inches
          (47.0 Meters).
note: Most runways are 150 feet wide, so the normal no brakes turn does not quite fit. Know that before you accept a back taxi and turn.

q: Pivot 180 degree turning radius?
a: 150 foot runway with light differential braking and thrust
qOrig: What is the non-normal (pivot) 180 degree turning radius?
detail: On a 150 foot wide runway the airplane will not make the 180 with a clean continuous turn. It takes light differential braking and differential thrust to tighten it. Keep it light and keep it slow, and watch the wing tip, not the nose.
quote:
Caution: Requires light differential braking/thrust for 180o turns on a
             150 foot (45 meter) wide runway.
note: The FCOM publishes no separate pivot turn radius, only this caution. Same 15 foot wing tip and 55 foot nose obstacle rule applies. If the shoulder is soft, ask for a tug.

q: When do SMGCS procedures apply?
a: At airports with a published low visibility taxi plan
qOrig: When do SMGCS procedures go into effect?
detail: Airports may develop a low visibility taxi plan such as SMGCS and may publish low visibility taxi procedures. Canadian airports with low visibility taxi plans may produce SMGCS charts in Jeppesen format.
quote: If an airport is equipped with Surface Movement Guidance and Control System (SMGCS), see the AMM Low Vis feature in Jeppesen FD Pro or Jeppesen Low Visibility Taxi Route charts
note: The specific RVR trigger value at which SMGCS becomes active is airport-published on the 10-9 series, not a single FOM number. Canada-specific low visibility taxi plans are at FOM 19.3.1.5.

q: Can you depart at night with runway edge lights out?
a: Only at 1/4 sm or RVR 1600, with FODO permission
qOrig: Can we depart at night from a runway where the edge lights are inoperative?
detail: If ALL runway lights are inoperative, takeoff is not authorized during darkness unless both conditions are met: reported visibility greater than or equal to 1/4 sm or RVR 1600, and permission of the Flight Operations Duty Officer.
quote: Permission of the Flight Operations Duty Officer (FODO)
note: Two different tests depending on all versus partial. The FODO call is only required for ALL lights inoperative. This is a Captain decision item that people commonly get wrong by assuming any light outage grounds the departure.

q: Runway change during taxi. What do you do?
a: New takeoff data, reload FMC departure, re-brief
qOrig: If given a change of departure runway during the taxi, how is this accomplished prior to takeoff and what...
detail: FOM 5.4.5 requires runway analysis data to be available and checked for each takeoff; data comes from the Flight Information Packet (TPR) or Dispatch Release (TLR), and if invalid, new takeoff data can be obtained via ACARS or from Dispatch.
quote:
new takeoff data can be obtained via ACARS or from Dispatch
(who has access to the online performance tool).
note: On the 787, if the HUD TAKEOFF runway changes, FCOM NP.21.3 requires both flight director switches OFF, then back ON after the new runway is executed on the CDU.

q: Must you stop taxiing if a guest stands up?
a: No
qOrig: Are we required to stop the aircraft during taxi if a guest stands up?
detail: Depending on the circumstances, it may be safer to continue to taxi.
quote: There is no regulatory requirement that the aircraft stop if a passenger gets out of their seat.
note: Captain judgment call. Stopping on an active taxiway can create a bigger hazard than the standing passenger. Coordinate with the Cabin Crew rather than reflexively braking.

q: SureWx with active precipitation or a contaminated surface?
a: In the SureWx guide and the FOM
qOrig: While using SureWx app, if/when there is active precipitation or during contaminated surface operations,...
detail: SureWx holdover-time workflow is vendor material. The governing policy is the pretakeoff contamination check requirement. Verify the app steps in the SureWx guide and the de-icing policy in FOM Chapter 9 and the fleet cold weather supplement.

q: SureWx holdover time expired. What check is required?
a: In the SureWx guide and the FOM
qOrig: While using SureWx app and the holdover time has expired, what check is required prior to takeoff?
detail: SureWx holdover-time workflow is vendor material. The governing policy is the pretakeoff contamination check requirement. Verify the app steps in the SureWx guide and the de-icing policy in FOM Chapter 9 and the fleet cold weather supplement.

q: Which manual holds the cold weather and de-icing material?
a: The FODM, plus fleet-specific manuals
qOrig: In which manual is most of the cold weather/de-icing information found?
detail: FOM 9.3.1 sends you to the fleet-specific manuals and the FODM for cold weather procedures, and FOM 9.3.1.1 sends you to the FODM again for Liquid Water Equivalent holdover times. FOM 16.2.9 names the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual alongside the FODM.
quote: Comply with the cold weather procedures in the fleet-specific manuals and FODM.
note: FOM does not spell out the FODM acronym in text. Aircraft-side cold weather procedures are in FCOM SP.16 Cold Weather Operations; FOM 9.3 is the policy layer only.

q: What are your cold weather ops resources?
a: Deicing manual (FODM), holdover times app, and fleet-specific manuals
qOrig: What are your cold weather ops resources? (Manuals, cards etc.)
detail: Three sources. The deicing manual, FODM, carries the deice and anti-ice procedures and the printed holdover tables. The holdover times app on the electronic flight bag gives the live numbers. The FCOM adverse weather supplementary procedures carry the airplane specific cold weather steps.
quote: Comply with the cold weather procedures in the fleet-specific manuals and FODM.
note: Holdover times built on liquid water equivalent data are FAA authorized and shall be used over METAR or ATIS derived times unless you can see the data is wrong.

q: Wet vs contaminated runway?
a: Wet is a water film. Contaminated is beyond that
qOrig: What is the difference between a wet vs contaminated runway?
detail: The FOM carries the operational consequence rather than a bare definition: for a Landing Distance Available of less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data. The wet versus contaminated distinction drives which performance table you are allowed to use, which is why the LDA threshold matters more on the line than the textbook definition.
quote: For LDA less than 7000 ft, do not use WET data.
note: The full wet/contaminated definitions and the RCAM/Runway Condition Code tables sit in FCTM and the TALPA material, which are not in our manuals. Verify the definition wording there. Related: FOM 9.1.13 Degraded Braking uses the Can U StoP mnemonic.

q: Braking action report vs RCAM?
a: PIREP is pilot-reported deceleration; RCAM is an assessment tool
qOrig: What is the difference between a braking action report vs RCAM?
detail: A braking action report is a pilot qualitative PIREP (GOOD, GOOD to MEDIUM, MEDIUM, MEDIUM to POOR, POOR, NIL) and airport personnel cannot issue one. The RCAM is a published FAA or ICAO matrix used primarily by airports to assess conditions and generate a Runway Condition Code, 0 (NIL) through 6 (dry), and correlate it with those same descriptive terms.
ref: FOM 9.1.2 Braking Action Report / FOM 9.1.6 Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM)
quote:
A braking action report (PIREP) is a qualitative description of deceleration by pilots such as GOOD,
GOOD to MEDIUM, MEDIUM, MEDIUM to POOR, POOR, and NIL.
note: Key operational rule in FOM 9.1.2: a PIREP may downgrade expected braking action from the RCAM or FICON, but must never be used to upgrade it.

q: What is a FICON NOTAM?
a: NOTAM giving runway condition codes by runway third
qOrig: What is a FICON (Field Condition) NOTAM?
detail: A FICON reports condition for touchdown, midpoint, and rollout in the direction of takeoff and landing, listed as runway thirds such as 3/4/2, with an expected braking action expressed as a Runway Condition Code. Where a single report gives multiple conditions along the runway, assume the most restrictive for the whole runway.
quote:
A FICON is a specifically formatted NOTAM reporting runway condition for each third of the
runway, and giving an expected braking action as a Runway Condition Code (RWYCC).
note: Absence of a FICON does not assure the runway is dry; airports are encouraged but not required to issue one for a wet runway.

q: What is a Runway Condition Code?
a: The TALPA number, 0 through 6
qOrig: What is a runway CC (Runway Condition Code)?
detail: The Runway Condition Code is the TALPA output used to assess a contaminated runway. On the 787 it drives the landing crosswind limitation directly: RwyCC 6 gives 40 kts, 5 (Good) 40, 4 (Good to Medium) 35, 3 (Medium) 25, 2 (Medium to Poor) 17, 1 (Poor) 15, and 0 (Nil) is no operation.
ref: FCOM L.10 Landing Crosswind Limitations TALPA
quote: The crosswind limitation is determined by entering the table below with Runway Condition Code or Control/Braking Action.
note: A FICON NOTAM is how the runway condition code reaches you. Reduce the crosswind limit by 5 knots on wet or contaminated runways whenever asymmetric reverse thrust is used.

q: Max takeoff crosswind?
a: Off the takeoff table, less 5 kts above 40 percent N1
qOrig: Max takeoff crosswind limitations?
detail: Takeoff crosswind limits come from the FCOM L.10 takeoff table, entered using the columns labeled 25 percent MAC and 30 percent MAC, which is why the takeoff table is CG and weight sensitive while the landing TALPA table is not.
quote: Reduce all takeoff crosswind guidelines by 5 knots if thrust is above 40% N1 (GE engines) at brake release for takeoff roll.
note: Demonstrated crosswinds are for certification only and do not represent operational limitations; the tables are the limits. Do not interchange the takeoff and landing tables, they serve different functions. read the exact takeoff table values off the FCOM L.10 PDF rather than quoting from memory.

q: What is TALPA?
a: Takeoff and Landing Performance Assessment
qOrig: (787) TALPA; What is TALPA?
detail: TALPA is the framework that translates reported runway surface condition into a Runway Condition Code and a braking action, which then drive performance and limits.
ref: FCOM L.10 Landing Crosswind Limitations TALPA
quote: The crosswind limitation is determined by entering the table below with Runway Condition Code or Control/Braking Action.
note: Reduce the crosswind limitation by 5 knots on wet or contaminated runways whenever asymmetric reverse thrust is used. Winds are measured at 33 ft (10 m) tower height and apply to runways 148 ft (45 m) or greater in width.

q: Max crosswind for a HUD takeoff?
a: 20 knots crosswind
qOrig: (787) Max Crosswind for a HUD takeoff?
detail: FCOM L.10.9 gives HUD takeoff wind component limits of 25 knots headwind, 15 knots tailwind, and 20 knots crosswind, and restricts low weather minima takeoff to ILS guidance on U.S. Type II or Type III ILS facilities. Compare with the autoland limits on the same page: 25 headwind, 15 tailwind, 25 crosswind but only 15 knots for CAT II/III.
ref: FCOM L.10.9 Autoflight - AFM Limitations - Low Visibility (HUD) Takeoff
quote:
on HUD takeoff operations:
# Headwind                                           25 knots
# Tailwind                                           15 knots
# Crosswind                                          20 knots
note: This limit applies only when takeoff weather minima are predicated on HUD takeoff operations. It is not the general takeoff crosswind limit, which comes from the TALPA and non-TALPA tables at FCOM L.10.4 through L.10.7.

q: Max altitude with flaps extended?
qOrig: Max altitude with flaps extended.
detail: The maximum altitude with flaps extended is 20,000 feet.
ref: FCOM L.10 Limitations, Non-AFM Operational Information
quote: The maximum altitude with flaps extended is 20,000 feet.
note: Adjacent limits worth carrying from the same page: prior to takeoff the maximum allowable difference between the Captain's or First Officer's altitude display and field elevation is 75 feet, and takeoff is permitted only in the normal flight control mode.

q: Normal rotation rate?
a: Not published as a number in our manuals.
qOrig: Normal rotation rate? (degrees/sec)
detail: Our manuals never give a rotation rate in degrees per second. The FCOM only tells you to use the normal takeoff rotation rate, and to rotate at that normal rate to the all engine initial climb pitch attitude. Do not guess a number in the sim.
quote:
know the all-engine initial climb pitch attitude. Rotate at the normal
   rate to this attitude for all non-engine failure takeoffs.
note: Boeing puts rotation rate technique in the Flight Crew Training Manual, Takeoff chapter. That manual is not one of the three we carry, so confirm the figure there before you brief it.

q: Normal takeoff rotation target pitch?
a: 15 degrees pitch attitude
qOrig: What is the normal takeoff rotation target pitch?
detail: Pilot monitoring calls ROTATE at VR. Pilot flying rotates smoothly toward 15 degrees of pitch, then follows the flight director after liftoff and establishes a positive rate of climb. Fifteen degrees is also the standard pitch Boeing uses for a go around.
quote: At VR, rotate toward 15° pitch attitude. At VR call “ROTATE.
note: Rotate toward 15 degrees, do not snap to it. Rate matters as much as the target, and an over rotation risks a tail strike at heavy weights.

q: Rotation target pitch after an engine failure at V1?
a: Not published in degrees; fly the flight director to V2
qOrig: What is the takeoff rotation target pitch attitude after an engine failure at/after V1 and prior to liftoff?
detail: No degrees figure for engine out rotation appears in our manuals. Fly the flight director. After liftoff with an engine failed it commands V2 if you are below V2, existing speed between V2 and V2 plus 15, or V2 plus 15 if you are faster.
quote: when an engine failure occurs, the pitch command target speed is:
note: Boeing covers engine out rotation technique in the Flight Crew Training Manual, Takeoff chapter. Get the pitch target there before the sim rather than guessing off the all engine number.

q: What are the PM callouts during an RTO?
a: SPEEDBRAKES UP, REVERSERS NORMAL, 60 KNOTS, plus omitted items
qOrig: What are the PM callouts during an RTO?
detail: The first officer verifies each captain action out loud: thrust levers closed, autothrottles disengaged, maximum brakes applied, reverse thrust applied. Then SPEEDBRAKES UP, or SPEEDBRAKES NOT UP if the lever did not come up. Then REVERSERS NORMAL, or the specific no reverser call. Then 60 knots.
quote:
Verify speedbrake lever UP and call
wheel brakes if the AUTOBRAKE             “SPEEDBRAKES UP.” If speedbrake
message is displayed or deceleration is   lever not UP call “SPEEDBRAKES
not adequate.                             NOT UP.
note: The first officer also calls out any omitted action item, and communicates the reject to the tower and cabin once stopping is assured. The captain owns the stop decision and the announcement afterward.

q: What is NADP1?
a: The close-in noise abatement profile
qOrig: What is NADP1? Describe associated procedures...
detail: NADP procedures are governed by Ops Spec C068. Specific requirements, including gradients and altitudes for configuration changes, may be defined in aircraft-specific manuals, the 10-7, or the Jeppesen Airway Manual Flight Procedures Noise Abatement Procedures.
quote: Normal takeoff procedures satisfy either close-in or distant NADP profile requirements.
note: That quote is (AS) bannered. This matters for the JCAB ramp-check question in section 1.2.3 about whether HA may perform NADP 1: the OpSpec is C068. confirm the HA-specific position and the OpSpec paperwork the JCAB inspector wants to see.

q: What is NADP2?
a: The distant noise abatement profile
qOrig: What is NADP2? Describe associated procedures...
detail: NADP2 is the distant profile. Per FOM 5.4.7, normal takeoff procedures satisfy either close-in or distant NADP profile requirements, so no separate profile is flown unless a specific published procedure requires it. Gradients and configuration-change altitudes come from the aircraft-specific manuals, the 10-7, or the Jeppesen Airway Manual.
quote: Flight Crews must comply with published noise abatement procedures when operating from noise-sensitive airports
note: The distinction between the two is where thrust reduction and acceleration occur relative to the airport. the 787 profile detail is FCTM/FCOM, not FOM.

q: How do you find max rate of climb speed?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: How do you determine max rate of climb speed?
detail: No maximum rate of climb speed in the FOM, FCOM or QRH, and the climb page has no max rate prompt. The climb page does publish a maximum angle climb speed. Do not invent a max rate number to brief.
ref: FCOM 11.41.6 FMC Takeoff and Climb - Climb Page
quote:
Displays maximum angle of climb speed.
Select – displays speed in the scratchpad for pilot selection to the speed line.
note: The climb page gives economy climb speed, the speed transition, any speed restriction, and MAX ANGLE. Nothing on that page is a rate of climb speed.

q: Severe turbulence penetration speed?
a: 290 KIAS below FL250, 310 or.84 above
qOrig: What is severe turbulence penetration speed?
detail: Severe turbulent air penetration speed in severe turbulence is 290 KIAS below 25,000 feet, and 310 KIAS or.84 Mach, whichever is lower, at and above 25,000 feet.
ref: FCOM L.10 Severe Turbulent Air Penetration Speed
quote:
290 KIAS below 25,000 feet
   • 310 KIAS/.
