note: Memory-marked limitation. Note the crossover is 25,000 ft, not FL250 by pressure altitude convention, and the upper figure is whichever is LOWER of 310 KIAS or.84 Mach. Additional guidance at FCOM SP Chapter 16 Severe Turbulence.

q: Where is max angle climb speed?
a: Control display unit climb page, MAX ANGLE prompt
qOrig: Where can you find max angle climb speed?
detail: Maximum angle of climb speed sits on the climb page of the control display unit, right side, labeled MAX ANGLE. Line select it and the speed drops into the scratchpad, then line select it up to the speed line to fly it.
ref: FCOM 11.41.6 FMC Takeoff and Climb - Climb Page
quote:
Displays maximum angle of climb speed.
Select – displays speed in the scratchpad for pilot selection to the speed line.
note: Use it when you need altitude in the shortest distance, such as a steep obstacle departure or a terrain problem. It costs you time and fuel compared with economy climb.

q: What else gets briefed on a SID beyond legs and restrictions?
a: Taxi and runway, takeoff performance, route, return plan
qOrig: Though the SID legs/restrictions get briefed from the plan view vs the CDU/FMS, what other items should...
detail: Before pushback the pilot flying briefs the plan: taxi and departure runway, takeoff performance and configuration, route with the ATC clearance compared against the programmed route, and the return plan for an emergency or takeoff alternate. Pilot monitoring calls the threats first, and considerations close it out.
quote:
Taxi, departure runway
   – Takeoff performance/configuration
   – Route (ATC clearance vs. programmed route)
note: Keep it interactive and big picture. Threats come from the pilot monitoring using the Crew Briefing Reference Card and any airport specific items on the 10-7 page.

q: Is a SID runway specific?
a: Not stated in our manuals. Read the SID plate
qOrig: Is the SID for a specific runway(s) only?
detail: SID plate items to brief beyond the FMC legs (runway applicability, obstruction climb gradients, red boxed notes, top altitude for CLIMB VIA) come from the Jeppesen chart itself plus FOM 5.5.2 Terminal Departures (IFR/VFR) and 5.5.1 Turns After Takeoff.

q: Obstruction climb gradient restrictions?
a: From runway analysis data, checked before every takeoff
qOrig: Obstruction climb gradient restrictions.
detail: Climb gradient and obstacle numbers come off the runway analysis, which has to be available and checked for every takeoff. It rides in the Flight Information Packet or on the Dispatch Release. If the data is invalid, get new takeoff data by datalink or from Dispatch.
quote: Runway analysis data must be available and checked for each takeoff.
note: If an engine fails on takeoff from a runway that has a published engine failure procedure, fly that procedure. That is what guarantees the obstacle clearance, not raw climb performance.

q: What are the red boxed notes on a SID?
a: Not defined in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Red Boxed notes e.g., speed restriction until further advised, etc.
detail: The FOM, FCOM and QRH never define what a red boxed chart note is. It comes off the chart, not out of a company manual. The FOM does send you to the chart text block for departure information, so read the box and brief whatever it says.
quote: (ODP) described in the text block of the Jeppesen chart for the airport.
note: Boxed notes are there because they change how you fly the procedure, for example a speed hold until advised. Check the Jeppesen chart legend for the convention.

q: Cleared CLIMB VIA. What is the SID top altitude?
a: Not defined in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: SID top altitude (if given “CLIMB VIA” from ATC)?
detail: No definition of a SID top altitude appears in the FOM, FCOM or QRH. What the FOM does say is that the published vertical profile and its restrictions stay in force up to a newly assigned altitude unless ATC explicitly cancels them.
ref: FOM 23.16.2 SID and STAR Altitude Restrictions
quote:
If this explicit cancellation is not provided by ATC, the pilot is expected to continue
following the published vertical profile and its associated restrictions of the SID or STAR up to the
newly assigned altitude.
note: Top altitude is printed on the departure procedure itself and changes by airport and by procedure. No single company number to memorize, so read it off the chart and brief it.

q: ATC says climb and maintain. Do SID restrictions still apply?
a: Yes, until ATC explicitly cancels them
qOrig: While on the SID, if ATC issues a “Climb and Maintain XXX” clearance, does the flight crew still need to...
detail: Published restrictions stay in force. A controller cancels them with explicit words like cancel level restriction, climb unrestricted, or disregard SID altitude restrictions. Without that phrase, keep flying the published vertical profile up to the newly assigned altitude. If the clearance is ambiguous, ask.
ref: FOM 23.16.2 SID and STAR Altitude Restrictions
quote:
European controllers explicitly cancel intermediate altitude restrictions using standardized
phraseology such as "Cancel level restriction," "Climb unrestricted to [level]," or "Climb to [level],
disregard SID/STAR altitude restrictions" when these restrictions on a SID or STAR are no longer
necessary.
note: The FOM says the same for Central America, where an altitude clearance still requires adherence to charted altitude restrictions unless you are specifically relieved.

q: Transition altitude and transition level?
a: 18,000 ft MSL in the US, charted elsewhere
qOrig: Transition Altitude/LVL?
detail: Below the transition altitude you set QNH and state altitudes in thousands and hundreds. At and above it you set 29.92 and say flight level. Outside the US the transition altitude is charted and the transition level comes from the ATIS or the approach controller.
quote:
Up to, but not including the transition altitude (18,000 ft MSL in the US and some other areas),
state the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds, (e.
note: Central America runs transition level FL200 and transition altitude 19,000 ft MSL unless charted otherwise. Europe is generally lower than the US, so read the chart every time.

q: Minimum altitude for autopilot engagement?
a: 200 ft AGL after takeoff
qOrig: Minimum Altitude for autopilot engagement?
detail: The autopilot must not be engaged below 200 ft AGL after takeoff. That is a certified limitation, not a technique. Watch it on a low acceleration height departure where the urge is to get the autopilot in early.
quote:
The autopilot must not be engaged below a minimum engage altitude of 200 feet
AGL after takeoff.
note: Coming down the numbers differ. Without LAND 2 or LAND 3 the autopilot must be off below 135 ft AGL. With LAND 2 or LAND 3 and a glideslope steeper than 3.25 degrees, off below 100 ft AGL.

q: Is the autopilot required on an RNAV SID?
a: No
qOrig: Is the autopilot required for an RNAV SID?
detail: FOM 5.1.4.1 is the only autopilot requirement tied to RNAV/RNP procedures, and it is limited to RNP AR with RNP less than 0.3 or Radius to Fix legs, where autopilot or flight director driven by the RNAV system shall be used; RNP AR departure capability must be authorized by the fleet-specific manuals (FOM 5.1.4.3).
ref: FOM 5.1.4.1 RNP Authorization Required (RNP AR) Procedures
quote:
RNP AR procedures with RNP values less than 0.3 or with Radius to Fix (RF) legs shall use autopilot
or Flight Director driven by the RNAV system.
note: Only RNP AR procedures with RNP below 0.3 or RF legs require autopilot or flight director driven by the RNAV system. Nothing in the FOM, FCOM, or QRH requires the autopilot on a standard RNAV SID.

q: Where are the ETOPS verification flight procedures?
a: Flight Operations Manual, ETOPS chapter, Verification Flight section
qOrig: Where can the ETOPS verification flight procedures be found?
detail: The Hawaiian procedure sits in the FOM ETOPS chapter under ETOPS Verification Flight, with the Alaska system verification flight section just ahead of it. Maintenance notifies you and makes a logbook entry. You report the result to Dispatch between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff.
quote:
An ETOPS Verification Flight (EVF) is a revenue or non-revenue flight during which the Flight Crew
is asked to assist Maintenance to confirm that an ETOPS Significant System is operating normally or
that an ETOPS significant problem has been resolved.
note: That report and the Dispatch acknowledgment must be complete before the ETOPS entry point. If the item is not operating normally you cannot go past it, and the Captain writes the result in the logbook.

q: Must the verification request be in the logbook before departure?
a: Yes
qOrig: Does the verification flight item request have to be in the maintenance logbook prior to departure?
detail: The Flight Crew will be notified of an open item on the MIC sheet, and Maintenance places this entry in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook: AIRCRAFT RELEASED TO ETOPS SERVICE IAW WITH HA ETOPS MAINTENANCE MANUAL FOR VERIFICATION FLIGHT DUE TO REPAIR OF ______.
quote: AIRCRAFT RELEASED TO ETOPS SERVICE IAW WITH HA ETOPS MAINTENANCE MANUAL FOR VERIFICATION FLIGHT DUE TO REPAIR OF

q: Must Maintenance talk to the crew before an EVF?
a: Yes, verbally
qOrig: Is Maintenance required to communicate with the flight crew prior to departing on an ETOPS verification...
detail: Maintenance will verbally notify the Flight Crew and place the release entry in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook. The notification is therefore threefold: the MIC sheet open item, the verbal notification, and the logbook entry.
quote: Maintenance will also verbally notify the Flight Crew

q: Must the PIC then call Dispatch?
a: Yes, a verbal acknowledgement
qOrig: Does the PIC have to communicate with dispatch after speaking with Maintenance?
detail: That closes the loop between Maintenance, the crew and Dispatch before departure.
quote: The Flight Crew must verbally acknowledge the EVF requirement with Dispatch.

q: Any Dispatch call required after takeoff, before the EEP?
a: Yes. 30 to 60 minutes after takeoff
qOrig: Is there a communication requirement to Dispatch between takeoff and prior to the EEP?
detail: Between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and prior to reaching the EEP, the Flight Crew will call or send an ACARS message to Dispatch to report the status of the affected component or system.
quote: This report and the return acknowledgment from Dispatch must be complete before reaching the EEP.
note: Two-way requirement. Your report alone is not enough; Dispatch's acknowledgment must also be received before the EEP.

q: How do you make that report?
a: Phone call or ACARS
qOrig: How can/should you make that communication of system performance?
detail: The Flight Crew will call or send an ACARS message to Dispatch to report the status of the affected component or system, between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and prior to the EEP.
quote: the Flight Crew will call or send an ACARS message to Dispatch to report the status of the affected component or system.

q: Component fails before the EEP. Can you continue?
a: No
qOrig: If the component being verified fails prior to EEP, can you continue?
detail: If the item being verified is not operating normally, the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs.
quote: the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs.
note: Unambiguous. The verification failing before the EEP removes ETOPS entry as an option.

q: Component fails after the EEP. Can you continue?
a: Yes. The restriction is on proceeding beyond the EEP
qOrig: If the component being verified fails after EEP entry, can you continue?
detail: FOM 6.5.10 states the aircraft cannot proceed BEYOND the EEP if the item is not operating normally. Once past the EEP the verification-flight restriction has already been satisfied or failed at that gate. A subsequent failure is handled as a normal in-flight system failure, using ETOPS contingency guidance at 6.4.4 and the PIC/Dispatcher judgment framework.
quote: the aircraft cannot proceed beyond the EEP and must land for repairs.
note: INFERRED from the wording of the EEP gate, not an explicit post-EEP statement. Confirm with a check airman. Treat a post-EEP failure on its own merits under 6.4.4 In-Flight System Failures and the diversion logic in 6.4.1.

q: What is the APU verification procedure?
a: Cold soak 2 hours, start within 1 hour of top of descent
qOrig: What are the APU verification flight procedures?
detail: Either stay clear of ETOPS airspace, or complete the verification before the ETOPS entry point if you can hold cruise altitude two hours or more beforehand. Cold soak the APU at least two hours shut down at cruise, then start it within one hour of top of descent.
quote: Initiate the APU start within 1 hour of top of descent.
note: The cold soak requires the APU shut down at least 2 hours at a normal ETOPS cruising altitude, ideally between FL270 and FL350. That altitude band is the point of the test: it proves a cold start at altitude.

q: How does APU verification differ from a single component EVF?
a: A scheduled cold soak and start, not a status report
qOrig: How do those procedures differ from an ETOPS Verification (single component) flight?
detail: A single-component EVF is a monitor-and-report task: confirm the system works, report to Dispatch between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and before the EEP, and land if it is not normal.
ref: FOM 6.5.10 ETOPS Verification Flight (HA) and ETOPS APU Verification Flight
quote: Allow the APU to cold soak for at least two hours.
note: If the APU verification is unsuccessful, the Dispatcher and PIC must confer to determine the best course of action, as ETOPS entry may not be possible. That is a joint decision, unlike the single-component case where the EEP rule is automatic.

q: How many APU start attempts?
a: Three attempts maximum
qOrig: How many start attempts?
detail: FOM 6.5.6 sets up the APU In-Flight Start Program: after engine start or takeoff the APU is shut down and cold soaked at least two hours at ETOPS cruise altitude, and the crew attempts a start during the 1-hour window before top of descent.
quote:
• If the APU starts within the maximum allowed three attempts, the start is deemed to be
  successful.
note: Subsequent attempts after a failed first attempt may be made at lower altitudes, minimum FL270. Do not confuse this with the ground start rules.

q: Must the APU be shut down before descent?
a: No. It may be shut down, not required
qOrig: After APU start at altitude, is it required to shut the APU down before descent?
detail: Under FOM 6.5.6 the test ends once the APU finishes its start sequence or after three failed attempts, and the APU may then be shut down; it is permissive, not required.
quote:
Once the APU finishes its start sequence or after three failed start attempts, the test is complete,
and the APU may be shut down.
note: FOM 6.5.10 ETOPS APU Verification Flight sets the same start window (within 1 hour of top of descent) and likewise imposes no shutdown requirement before descent.

q: APU shut down early, then fails to start after landing. What then?
a: Make a separate Maintenance Logbook entry
qOrig: If APU is shutdown prior to top of descent, then subsequently the APU fails to start after landing,...
detail: A post-landing APU start attempt should be made as workload permits to avoid delaying the next flight (FOM 6.5.5). If it will not start on the ground, that ground failure gets its own Maintenance Logbook entry, separate from the in-flight start or verification entry the Captain already owes per FOM 6.5.6 / 6.5.10.
quote:
an APU start
  attempt should be made after landing as workload permits. If the APU fails to start on the
  ground, a separate Maintenance Logbook entry must be made.
note: FOM 5.1.8.1 defines a failed start as three consecutive failed attempts, and 12.4.6 lists APU failure to start as a required logbook entry. The (HA) 787 in-flight start program is 6.5.6; the ETOPS APU verification flight is 6.5.10.

q: What logbook entry is required after the verification flight?
a: Verification flight completed satisfactorily or unsatisfactorily
qOrig: What maintenance logbook entry (specific verbiage) must be entered after the verification flight?
detail: The Captain must make an entry in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook detailing the results: VERIFICATION FLIGHT FOR ____ COMPLETED SATISFACTORILY or UNSATISFACTORILY. If the test was unsuccessful the Captain must list any discrepancies. For the APU specifically, a successful entry must state: VERIFICATION FLIGHT FOR APU COMPLETED, APU OPERATES NORMALLY.
quote: VERIFICATION FLIGHT FOR ____ COMPLETED “SATISFACTORILY” or “UNSATISFACTORILY”
note: Captain writes this, not the FO and not Maintenance. The APU wording is distinct from the generic component wording, so know both.

q: How do you call the cabin on the headset or handset?
a: Select CAB, dial the station; handset dials its own code
qOrig: How do you make an interphone call to the cabin using the headset? Using the flight deck handset?
detail: On the headset, select the CAB transmitter switch on the audio control panel, pick the station on the cabin interphone page of the tuning and control panel, then push the mic switch to talk. On the handset, enter the two digit code and push the dial code select switch.
quote:
Calls can also be answered or placed using the flight deck handset. The desired
call location is entered using the dial code step switches or numeric keys. The call
is then made by pushing the dial code select switch.
note: Pushing the CAB switch twice within one second places a priority call and cuts in on a station already talking. The handset push to talk is only needed for a PA announcement.

q: Review PA usage
a: No PA in critical phases except emergency announcements
qOrig: Review PA usage (see 12.1.3.16 Know FOM PA policies and Perform Effective Communication from the...
detail: FOM 7.1.18 keeps the PA out of critical air and ground phases except for emergencies, because scanning and flight deck duties come first; delay routine announcements until established in cruise. FOM 7.1.19 lists the announcements the crew is required to make, and crews may vary the wording except where the manual says verbatim.
quote:
Flight Crewmembers should not use the Public Address System during any critical air or ground
phase of flight for other than emergency announcements.
note: Required PAs are listed in FOM 7.1.19 (seat belt sign on/off, anticipated turbulence, turbulence, stopping short of the jetway). Customer service PA guidance and sample scripts are in FOM 7.1.21.

q: Where is the AIREP form in Comply365?
a: In Comply365
qOrig: Where in Comply365 can the AIREP form be found?
detail: Document location inside Comply365 changes with releases. Verify in the live app rather than trusting a written path.

q: Do you complete an AIREP every flight?
a: Not stated in our manuals. Comply365 form
qOrig: Do you need to complete the AIREP form for each flight?
detail: AIREP completion and retention, CPDLC request types, and plot saving or submission are company workflow and aircraft menu content. FOM 5.7.3.15 requires the entire cleared route be loaded for ORCN segments but does not mandate saving plots after every flight. Verify in Comply365 and on the aircraft.

q: Do you save the AIREP after each flight?
a: Not stated in our manuals. Comply365 form
qOrig: Do you need to save the AIREP form after each flight?
detail: AIREP completion and retention, CPDLC request types, and plot saving or submission are company workflow and aircraft menu content. FOM 5.7.3.15 requires the entire cleared route be loaded for ORCN segments but does not mandate saving plots after every flight. Verify in Comply365 and on the aircraft.

q: Are company position reports required?
a: Yes, and holding always requires one
qOrig: Are we required to make company position reports?
detail: FOM 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch carries the requirement set. One that is explicit: through ACARS or radio the Captain will ensure Dispatch is contacted with the holding fix, Expected Further Clearance time, and fuel on board, and diversion plans should be discussed if applicable. Abnormalities require notification under 11.1.2.
ref: FOM 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch / 5.5.15.1 Dispatch Notification of Holding
quote: the Captain will ensure that Dispatch is contacted with the holding fix, Expected Further Clearance (EFC) time, and fuel on board.
note: Three items for the holding report: fix, EFC, fuel. read 7.1.12 in full for the complete routine position-reporting requirement.

q: How do you report a discrepancy before landing?
a: ACARS or radio to Dispatch, who relays to Maintenance
qOrig: How can you report a discrepancy to Maintenance in advance, prior to landing?
detail: Report through Dispatch using ACARS or radio. FOM 11.1.2 requires contacting Dispatch for abnormalities as safety of flight permits, and if time does not permit in flight, after gate arrival. Reporting early lets Maintenance position parts and personnel at the gate rather than starting the troubleshooting clock on block-in.
quote: If time does not permit contact with Dispatch while in flight, contact shall be made after gate arrival.
note: That is also the answer to the advantages question in the maintenance logbook section: enroute notification converts ground time from diagnosis into repair.

q: What altitudes are RVSM airspace?
a: FL290 through FL410
qOrig: What altitudes define RVSM airspace?
detail: RVSM airspace is any airspace or route where aircraft are separated by 1000 ft vertically, between FL290 and FL410 inclusive.
ref: FOM 5.5.6.5 Enroute RVSM Altitude Monitoring Requirements
quote:
between FL290 and FL410, inclusive), pilots shall verify that all altimeters are set
to 29.
note: At initial level off, pilots shall verify all altimeters are set to 29.92 and crosscheck them. Use of the standby altimeter as a primary is PROHIBITED in RVSM airspace.
icao: NAT Doc 007 Chapter 11: "This is defined as any airspace between FL 290 - FL 410 inclusive" ICAO defines NAT RVSM airspace the same way as the company, FL290 through FL410 inclusive.

q: RVSM equipment requirements?
a: Both primary altimeters, one autopilot, altitude alerting
qOrig: Are there aircraft equipment requirements to operate in RVSM airspace?
detail: The following shall be operating normally prior to entry into RVSM airspace: both primary altimeters, one autopilot altitude-control system, and the Altitude Alerting System. The autopilot should be engaged during altitude capture and level cruise, except where circumstances such as the need to retrim or turbulence require disengagement. Report reaching assigned altitudes if not in radar contact.
quote:
Both primary altimeters
• One autopilot altitude-control system



                                                                                                            295
                                                                                  Chapter:            5
                             Flight Operations Manual                                Rev:        125.
note: Three items only. A common wrong answer adds transponder or TCAS to the list.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.12: "Required equipment includes two primary independent altimetry sources, one altitude alert" The sentence continues with one automatic altitude control system, so ICAO matches the company list of altimeters, autopilot and altitude alerting.

q: RVSM equipment fails in flight. What do you do?
a: Notify ATC and Dispatch
qOrig: What are you expected to do if you have a failure of required equipment while in RVSM airspace?
detail: In the event of required RVSM equipment failure prior to or within RVSM airspace, notify ATC and Dispatch to coordinate a prudent course of action.
quote: ATC may not require any action; however, a reroute or diversion may be required.
note: Both ATC and Dispatch, not one or the other. The FOM deliberately leaves the outcome open rather than mandating an immediate descent out of RVSM.
icao: NAT Doc 007 7.2.1: "The following equipment failures must be reported to ATC as soon as practicable" ICAO matches the notify ATC step; adding Dispatch is company procedure.

q: Diverting without a clearance. What altitude do you plan?
a: Below FL290
qOrig: When diverting to an alternate without a clearance, what altitude should you plan to be below when...
detail: Under the oceanic in-flight contingency procedures (FOM 5.7.4.2), if a revised clearance cannot be obtained, turn at least 30 degrees left or right to establish a same-direction parallel track offset 5 nm, and be below FL290 before diverting from the assigned clearance. Once established on the parallel route, take a 500 ft vertical offset (FOM 5.7.4.3).
quote:
The aircraft should be below FL290 prior to diverting from the assigned clearance unless a revised
ATC clearance has been obtained.
note: Same guidance is repeated in FOM 5.7.4.3. First turn at least 30 degrees off the cleared track to establish a parallel same-direction offset of 5 nm, then take a 500 ft vertical offset once established.
icao: NAT Doc 007 10.3.2: "descend below FL 290, and establish a 150 m (500 ft) vertical offset from those flight levels" ICAO matches planning below FL 290 and adds a 500 ft vertical offset from levels normally used.

q: How early do you log on to CPDLC leaving the contiguous 48?
a: About 30 minutes prior to departure
qOrig: When departing the 48 Contiguous states, to assist ATC, how many minutes prior to departure is an...
detail: CPDLC DCL becomes available roughly 30 minutes before departure at DCL airports (FOM 5.2.14), so that is the window to log on and pull the clearance. Where DCL is available and the aircraft is equipped, CPDLC DCL is expected to be used for the preflight clearance; if the logon or the DCL fails, revert to Clearance Delivery on VHF.
ref: FOM 5.2.14 CPDLC Clearances - ATC Data Link Communications
quote:
Controller Pilot Data Link Communications Departure Clearance (CPDLC DCL) is available
approximately 30 minutes prior to departure at airports with DCL operational.
note: FOM 5.2.15 gives the logon table: CONUS (Lower 48) is 'During preflight' with logon address KUSA. Contrast Hawaii, which is above 10k and 15-45 min prior to entry, logon KZAK.

q: Airborne CPDLC logon window before the FIR?
a: A time window before entry, not an altitude
qOrig: Once airborne, what is the CPDLC logon time window prior to the FIR (“Flight Information Region”)? Is it...
detail: If equipped with CPDLC, log on either on the ground during preflight or after takeoff above 10,000 ft MSL, or as required by the specific FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card.
quote: Oceanic Control Areas typically have a time window prior to entry that defines the logon window, not a specific altitude.
note: The direct answer to the second half is no, it is not the same for all FIRs. Use the FIR/OCA Pilot Reference Card. For KZAK Oakland the portal phase_flows page carries logon 45 to 15 minutes prior to entry and not below 10,000 ft.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.41: "the pilot should log on to the appropriate FIR" ICAO sets the window at 10 to 25 minutes before the boundary, matching the company time based rather than altitude based trigger.

q: How do you log on for a departure clearance? Enroute?
a: Flight Information menu for departure clearance; ATC Logon/Status page enroute
qOrig: How, specifically in your aircraft, do you logon for a departure clearance? Enroute?
detail: Departure clearance comes off the multifunction display: FLIGHT INFORMATION, then DEPARTURE CLEARANCE REQUEST. Enter flight number, the four letter facility, departure, destination, gate and the automatic terminal information service letter, then send. Enroute, use ATC LOGON/STATUS: enter the center identifier, flight number, origin and destination, then push SEND.
quote:
The ATC LOGON/STATUS page allows logon to the desired ATC facility for
establishment of a datalink connection and displays ATC datalink connection
status information.
note: Entering a new flight number on the clearance request page ends the current ATC connection. Status reads SENDING, then CONNECTING, and the page closes itself five seconds later.

q: What can you request over CPDLC?
a: In Comply365 and the FCOM
qOrig: What types of requests can be made through CPDLC?
detail: AIREP completion and retention, CPDLC request types, and plot saving or submission are company workflow and aircraft menu content. FOM 5.7.3.15 requires the entire cleared route be loaded for ORCN segments but does not mandate saving plots after every flight. Verify in Comply365 and on the aircraft.

q: Two minutes before a waypoint, what do you do?
a: Confirm the next waypoint and the one after it
qOrig: Approximately 2 minutes prior to reaching a waypoint, what crew actions are required?
detail: Approximately 2 minutes prior to reaching a waypoint, confirm that the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next plus one) agree with the Flight Plan and ATC clearance.
quote: confirm that the upcoming waypoint and the subsequent waypoint (next + 1) agrees with the Flight Plan/ATC clearance.
note: The next-plus-one check is the whole point. Verifying only the active waypoint will not catch a gross navigation error that begins one leg downstream.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.51: "Approaching an oceanic waypoint, pilots should crosscheck the coordinates of the next" ICAO ties the check to approaching the waypoint and includes the next plus one, matching the company two waypoint confirmation.

q: What gets checked after waypoint transition?
a: Time and fuel recorded, difference computed, navigation mode verified, waypoint slashed
qOrig: What items are required to be checked on the flight plan after waypoint transition?
detail: After crossing, record time and fuel from the flight management computer on the flight plan or release and compare with the estimate. Note the difference: plus is underburn, minus is overburn. Confirm the navigation mode on the flight mode annunciator, slash the waypoint, and send the position report if required.
quote:
Record the time and fuel remaining from the FMC/FMS on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release
    or the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review and compare them with the estimates. Record
    the difference (+ is ahead/underburn and - is behind/overburn).
note: Two minutes before the fix you confirm the next waypoint and the one after it against the clearance. Ten minutes after passage you run the navigation crosscheck.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.54: "Pilots should also note and record their fuel status at each oceanic waypoint." ICAO matches the fuel recording at each waypoint; 6.3.55 adds the LNAV tracking check 10 minutes after passage.

q: Where is fuel remaining recorded at waypoint transition?
a: The flight plan, the release, or the ACARS HOWGOZIT
qOrig: On which document is the fuel remaining (at waypoint transition) recorded?
detail: Time and fuel remaining from the FMC are recorded on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release, or alternatively on the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review, and compared against the estimates.
quote: Record the time and fuel remaining from the FMC/FMS on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release or the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.54: "Pilots should also note and record their fuel status at each oceanic waypoint." ICAO matches the company practice; where to write it, release or HOWGOZIT, is company guidance.

q: Ten minutes after waypoint transition, what do you do?
a: Crosscheck navigation performance and course
qOrig: Approximately 10 minutes after waypoint transition, what crew actions are required?
detail: Approximately 10 minutes after waypoint passage, crosscheck navigational performance and course compliance.
quote: Take immediate corrective action for any anomalies or deviations.
note: Cross-reference 5.7.4.11 Position Doubtful if the crosscheck does not resolve. If you are on a weather deviation, the FOM requires this process to be completed immediately rather than waiting for the 10-minute point.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.55: "pilots should confirm that proper lateral (LNAV/NAV) mode is engaged and the aircraft is tracking to the proper waypoint" ICAO matches the company crosscheck and names exactly what to verify at the 10 minute point.

q: Why track fuel score?
a: It reveals fuel leaks and burn trends early
qOrig: Why is keeping track of the actual fuel remaining vs planned fuel remaining (“FUEL SCORE”) important?
detail: Scoring fuel at every waypoint is the primary in-flight leak detector: a growing negative trend that fuel flows do not explain is the signature of a leak or fuel system malfunction (FOM 5.5.3).
ref: FOM 5.5.3 Flight Plan Time and Fuel Monitoring - Enroute
quote:
The difference between the actual and the estimated fuel remaining is an important factor in
identifying and troubleshooting fuel leaks or other fuel system malfunctions.
note: FOM 7.1.12 requires a Dispatch call when actual fuel differs from planned by 3000 lbs. Call early rather than at the gate, so Dispatch can rerun the numbers while you still have options.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.54: "Pilots should also note and record their fuel status at each oceanic waypoint. This is especially important if the cleared route and flight level differ significantly from the filed flight plan." ICAO requires the record; the leak detection rationale is the company addition.

q: Which fuel figure goes on the release, tank total or PROG?
a: Progress page fuel from the flight management computer, not tank total
qOrig: (787) Which fuel remaining is noted on the dispatch release, the EICAS fuel panel (tank total) or the PROG...
detail: The FOM says record fuel remaining from the flight management computer, so the progress page figure goes on the release, not the tank total off the fuel synoptic. Keep the same source every waypoint or the trend means nothing. Progress page 2/4 shows totalizer and calculated side by side.
quote:
Record the time and fuel remaining from the FMC/FMS on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release
    or the ACARS HOWGOZIT/Flight Plan Review and compare them with the estimates.
note: Totalizer is sensed tank fuel. Calculated is what the computer has burned down from the starting quantity. Totalizer lower than calculated is one of the fuel leak clues in the QRH.

q: OPT vs MAX vs RECOMMENDED altitude?
a: Optimum ignores winds; maximum is the ceiling; recommended uses forecast winds
qOrig: What is the difference between OPT/Max/Recommended altitudes?
detail: Optimum comes from gross weight, cost index, speed schedule and center of gravity, with no wind or temperature input. Maximum is the highest level you can hold at current weight, temperature and number of engines running. Recommended is the most economical altitude for the next 250 to 500 nm using entered forecast winds.
quote:
OPT – calculation of OPT altitude is based on gross weight, cost index, cruise
speed schedule, and cruise cg. Forecast winds and temperature deviations from
standard day are not used in the calculation.
note: Recommended reverts to your cruise altitude within 200 nm of top of descent or 500 nm of destination, so late in the flight it stops telling you anything useful.

q: Why does the tropopause level matter for cruise?
a: It sets air temperature; descending below it warms fuel
qOrig: Why is it important to consider the level of the tropopause regarding your cruise altitude?
detail: FOM 9.3.2.3 is the only place the manuals tie tropopause height to cruise altitude selection, and it does so through fuel temperature: fuel drifts toward TAT at roughly 3 degrees C per hour, up to 12 degrees C per hour in extreme conditions, so on long cold-soak sectors the tropopause level tells you where warmer air is.
quote:
For instance, a 4000 ft descent below the
  tropopause can result in approximately a 7°C increase in TAT.
note: Tropopause height per waypoint (TROP) is printed on the Navigation Log. FOM 8.3.3 also notes ozone forms primarily above the tropopause, which is why ozone converters are fitted.

q: Is there a tropopause chart in the release package?
a: No chart. TROP is a Navigation Log column per waypoint
qOrig: Do we have a chart in our dispatch release package that shows the level(s) of the tropopause with...
detail: The Navigation Log columns on the flight plan include TROP, the tropopause level at each waypoint, alongside MORA, TTK, NM, IAS, Mach, FL and TEMP (FOM 8.5.7). That per-waypoint field, not a separate chart, is the released tropopause data. FOM 8.5.1 lists the required contents of the Flight Information Packet and does not include a tropopause chart.
ref: FOM 8.5.7 Dispatch Release Sample (HA) - Navigation Log Legend
quote:
MORA                   Minimum Off Route Altitude

      TROP                   Tropopause

      TTK                    True Track to WPT

      NM                     Nautical Miles to WPT

      IAS                    Indicated Airspeed to WPT

      .
note: FOM 8.5.1 lists everything in the Flight Information Packet (release, flight plan, TAF, METAR, SIGMETs and turbulence products, NOTAMs); no tropopause chart is among them. Graphical hazard products from the weather vendor are covered in FOM 9.8.1.

q: What do you expect crossing the tropopause?
a: Temperature stops falling; an inversion may warm you climbing
qOrig: What can expect when cruising near, or crossing through, the tropopause?
detail: Near and through the tropopause the normal lapse rate breaks down: temperature stops decreasing with altitude and can invert, so a climb may actually warm TAT and help a cold fuel problem, while a 4000 ft descent below the tropopause is worth about 7 degrees C of TAT (FOM 9.3.2.3).
quote:
Occasionally, a temperature inversion at the Tropopause may occur, and, in this case, climbing
  will result in warmer temperatures and be beneficial for fuel warming.
note: The FOM only addresses the tropopause in temperature/fuel-freeze terms (9.3.2.3) and ozone terms (8.3.3). Turbulence and wind shear expectations near the tropopause are not stated in the FOM, FCOM or QRH.

q: When is an electronic plot required?
a: On all ORCN segments
qOrig: When and under what conditions are we required to do an electronic plot?
detail: An electronic plotting chart should be used on all Oceanic and Remote Continental Navigation segments. The Flight Crew should load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app, such as FD Pro X, on the EFB.
quote: An electronic plotting chart should be used on all ORCN segments.
note: Regulatory basis AC 91-70 and Ops Spec B036. Note the word is should, and the requirement is the ENTIRE cleared route, not just the oceanic portion.

q: How do you plot on the EFB?
a: Load the entire cleared route into the charting app
qOrig: How do you plot using the EFB?
detail: The Flight Crew should load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app on the EFB. FD Pro X is the app named in the FOM.
quote: load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app (such as FD Pro X) on the EFB.
note: The FD Pro X screen-by-screen plotting workflow is vendor documentation, not FOM content. Confirm with the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365.

q: Must you save or submit plots after every flight?
a: No published requirement to save or submit
qOrig: Are you required to save/submit your plots and route after every flight?
detail: FOM 5.7.3.15, written against AC 91-70 and Ops Spec B036, requires an electronic plotting chart on all ORCN segments and requires the full cleared route be loaded into the approved charting services app on the EFB. It stops there. Nothing in the section, or in the surrounding oceanic material, requires the crew to save, export or submit the plot afterward.
quote: An electronic plotting chart should be used on all ORCN segments.
note: 5.7.3.15 requires the plot be used and the entire cleared route loaded into the approved charting app such as FD Pro X, but it sets no retention, save or submission requirement. Screenshotting a plot is personal practice, not policy.

q: When is it prudent to screenshot your plotted route?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: When would it be prudent to save your plotted route (take screenshot postflight)?
detail: The FOM requires an electronic plotting chart on every oceanic and remote continental segment, with the whole cleared route loaded in FD Pro X. Nothing in the FOM, FCOM or QRH tells you to save or capture an image of it after the flight.
quote:
An electronic plotting chart should be used on all ORCN segments.
The Flight Crew should load the entire cleared route into the approved charting services app (such
as FD Pro X) on the EFB.
note: Company policy says required flight documents are captured electronically and crews need not keep flight paperwork after the flight unless told to. Saving a plot after a deviation or reroute is technique, not policy.

q: What prompts a SATCOM call to Dispatch?
a: Pilot discretion; any required report to Dispatch
qOrig: What circumstance precipitates a SATCOM call to Dispatch?
detail: FOM 7.1.7 makes satellite voice to Dispatch or MedLink purely the pilot's call, so the circumstance is judgment driven: use it when the message is too complex, too urgent, or too consequential for ACARS text. What is not discretionary is the contact itself.
quote:
Satellite voice communication with Dispatch or MedLink is at the
pilot’s discretion.
note: The mandatory triggers are in FOM 7.1.12 Reports to Dispatch: 3000 lbs fuel deviation (787), 100 nm lateral, 4000 ft altitude, 15 minute arrival delay, weather, moderate or greater turbulence, safety of flight, abnormalities, diversions, mechanical irregularities, ETOPS reroutes.

q: Who do you call on SATCOM for maintenance or a guest issue?
a: Dispatch
qOrig: When we make a SATCOM call for Maintenance or guest issue, who do we call?
detail: Inflight, the Dispatcher is the primary contact and shares operational control with the Captain (FOM 7.1.1.2). ACARS messages sent to Maintenance Control go automatically to the Dispatcher, and Maintenance does not normally communicate directly with an airborne aircraft because their diagnostic guidance differs from operational guidance for crews.
quote:
The Dispatcher is the primary contact for requests and notifications, both managing information
flow and sharing operational control with the Captain.
note: Maintenance will not normally talk directly to an airborne aircraft; the FODO provides the link to Maintenance and Engineering. For a medical event, MedLink is the SATCOM call (FOM 7.1.7).

q: How do you make a SATCOM call?
a: Select SAT, choose the number from the directory, push MAKE CALL
qOrig: How do you make a SATCOM (specifically which buttons, and in what order, must be pressed in/on which...
detail: Push SAT on the tuning and control panel to bring up the satellite phone pages. Line select a number from the directory or type one into the scratchpad. Set the priority, then push MAKE CALL. Talk with the SAT transmitter switch selected on your audio panel. MAKE CALL then reads END CALL.
quote:
The SATCOM control pages are displayed by selecting SAT on the TCP.
Directories of airline-defined numbers are line-selectable or numbers may be
manually entered if function is enabled by the operator.
note: Priorities are emergency, high, low and public. Emergency sets off an alarm at the ground station. High is for regulatory and flight safety calls, public is non safety correspondence.

q: Where are the preprogrammed phone numbers on the 787?
a: DIRECTORY key on the satellite phone page, listed by region
qOrig: In the ACARS/TCP (787) where can you find a list of telephone numbers that are preprogrammed to call?
detail: On the satellite phone main menu, the DIRECTORY key opens the airline loaded numbers sorted by geographic region. Page 2 of 2 has a directory details key listing the phone number identifiers. Line select what you want, then push MAKE CALL.
quote:
SATCOM DIRECTORY Key
Push – Displays directory of available SATCOM phone numbers by geographic
region.
note: You are not stuck with the list. Type a number into the scratchpad and the call key changes to MANUAL ENTRY, which dials what you entered.

q: Total VHF and HF failure. Any other way to reach ATC?
a: Yes. SATCOM voice, and CPDLC datalink
qOrig: If you have a total VHF/HF radio failure, is there another way to contact ATC?
detail: Satellite voice is the fallback: it is not authorized for routine ATC use, but the FOM specifically permits it when HF or CPDLC are not available (FOM 7.1.7), and all areas of the route structure have satellite voice coverage. CPDLC over SATCOM datalink is the other path, and it is the primary means in oceanic airspace when paired with ADS-C.
quote:
Routine satellite voice communication with ATC is not authorized; however, it may be used when
HF or CPDLC are not available.
note: If it is a datalink failure rather than voice, FOM 5.7.4.9 says revert to HF position reporting and tell ATC. For contingencies, FOM 5.7.4.2 also has you alert nearby aircraft on 121.5, backup 123.45, for relay.

q: Where are the current Pacific HF frequencies?
a: JetPack HF Frequencies tab, or radio.arinc.net/pacific
qOrig: Where can you find the most current (pacific) HF FREQUENCIES in use for your flight?
detail: The primary source is the HF Frequencies tab in JetPack. ARINC publishes the same list at radio.arinc.net/pacific, and Jeppesen FD Pro carries it under Pubs, North America, General Airway Manual, Enroute Data General, ARINC Services. Frequencies also print in the communications boxes on the enroute chart.
quote: (AS) The primary reference for HF frequencies is from the “HF Frequencies” tab in JetPack.
note: ARINC gives you the primary and secondary predicted for that day at check in. If neither works, try any listed frequency, and try several times on one before changing.

q: Rule of thumb for HF frequencies and the sun?
a: Operating practice, not published in the manuals
qOrig: What is the rule of thumb with HF frequencies vs the Sun?
detail: Current Pacific HF frequency sets and the position-report template come from the Jeppesen enroute pages, ARINC and the PRC, not the FOM. The day/night frequency rule of thumb is operating practice. FOM 7.1.6 covers HF policy and 5.7.3.19 the non-CPDLC report content.

q: Where is the HF position report template?
a: Jeppesen FD Pro X, Pubs, Pacific, Oceanic Position Reporting Procedures
qOrig: Where can you find a ‘template’ to make an HF Radio Position report?
detail: For the Oakland FIR the full format sits in Jeppesen FD Pro X under Pubs, Pacific, Oceanic Position Reporting Procedures. The FOM carries the same skeleton: present position, estimated next position, ensuing fix, then preplanning flight levels. Oakland also wants a meteorological report with every position report.
quote:
For operations in the Oakland FIR, oceanic position reporting procedures are clearly delineated
in the Jeppesen FD Pro X app > Pubs > Pacific > Oceanic Position Reporting Procedures Oakland
Oceanic FIR.
note: Present position is callsign, the word position, the fix, time in four digits and altitude. Ensuing fix is name only. The meteorological part is temperature, wind and any significant weather.
icao: NAT Doc 007 5.3.6: "position should be expressed in terms of latitude and longitude except when flying over named reporting points" For the NAT the report format sits in this chapter of Doc 007; the company Pacific reference covers the Oakland FIR.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: Where are the ICAO oceanic weather deviation procedures?
a: Our Flight Operations Manual oceanic chapter, reprinted from ICAO Doc 4444
qOrig: Where can you find the ICAO Weather Deviation procedures for Oceanic Controlled Airspace?
detail: The oceanic weather deviation procedure sits in the oceanic chapter of our Flight Operations Manual, taken from ICAO Doc 4444. It covers the request, what to do when a clearance cannot be obtained, and the offset table. Under 5 nm hold your level. At 5 nm or more, change level 300 ft.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace
quote:
When weather deviation is required, the pilot should initiate communications with ATC via voice or
CPDLC. A rapid response may be obtained by either:
note: Eastbound, deviating left descend 300 ft, right climb 300 ft. Westbound is the opposite. Start the offset about 5 nm off track and be back at level within 5 nm of centerline.
icao: NAT Doc 007 10.4: "The following procedures are intended for deviations around adverse meteorological conditions." Doc 007 Chapter 10.4 carries the same ICAO weather deviation procedures for the NAT that the FOM reprints.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How do you request a weather deviation?
a: State WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED by voice, or send a datalink request
qOrig: How, specifically to your aircraft, do can you make a weather deviation request?
detail: Two ways to get a quick answer. Say WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED on the frequency, which tells the controller you want priority, or send a lateral deviation request over datalink. Tell ATC how far you need. If no clearance is coming and the weather is dangerous, use PAN PAN or the urgency downlink.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.4 Weather Deviation Procedures for Oceanic Airspace
quote:
Stating “WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED” to indicate that priority is desired on the frequency
  and for ATC response; or
• Requesting a weather deviation using a CPDLC lateral downlink message.
note: Tell ATC when the deviation is over and you are back on the cleared route. On the 787 the datalink option is the controller pilot datalink lateral request.
icao: NAT Doc 007 10.4.1: "stating “WEATHER DEVIATION REQUIRED” to indicate that priority is desired on the frequency and for ATC response" ICAO matches the company procedure and adds the urgency call PAN PAN when needed.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How do you insert the offset in the CDU?
a: LATERAL OFFSET page, enter L or R and distance, execute
qOrig: Once received, how (aircraft CDU/FMS specific) can you insert the offset distance?
detail: Open the LATERAL OFFSET page with the OFST function key, the OFFSET prompt on INIT REF INDEX, the OFFSET prompt on RTE page 1, or LOAD SLOP from the SLOP TRANSITION help window (FCOM 11.42.18).
ref: FCOM 11.42.18 Route Offset and Strategic Lateral Offset Procedure (SLOP)
quote:
The LATERAL OFFSET page can be accessed by: selecting the OFST function
key, selecting the OFFSET prompt on the INIT REF INDEX page or on the RTE
page 1, or by selecting the LOAD SLOP command button on the SLOP
TRANSITION Help Window.
note: Valid DIST entries are L or R with XX.X, or XX.X then L or R, from 0.1 to 99.0 nm in 0.1 nm steps. SLOP itself is right of course only, 0.0 to 2.0 nm (FOM 5.7.4.7).
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.49: "Pilots should make sure the “TO” waypoint is correct after entering SLOP." Doc 007 leaves the CDU steps to the aircraft manuals but adds this check because some FMS sequence past a waypoint.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: How far do you stand off severe cells?
a: 20 nm laterally; clear tops by 5000 ft
qOrig: How far (in nm’s) should you avoid Severe CB’s if possible? Which direction? Vertically?
detail: FOM 9.5.5 sets 20 nm minimum lateral avoidance for any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo, and 5000 ft vertical clearance over the tops when in the clear on top; below 5000 ft of top clearance, revert to the 20 nm lateral standard.
quote:
Avoid by at least 20 miles any thunderstorm identified as severe or giving an intense radar echo.

When “in the clear” on top, cloud tops should be cleared by 5000 ft.
note: If you cannot clear the tops by 5000 ft, go back to 20 nm lateral avoidance. The FOM does not specify an upwind or downwind side for the deviation, so that preference is not manual sourced.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: No deviation clearance. What do you do?
a: Emergency authority, PAN-PAN three times, offset 300 ft beyond 5 nm
qOrig: If a weather deviation clearance cannot be attained, what is the procedure to deviate around weather?
detail: If you cannot continue per clearance due to dangerous weather and no prior clearance can be obtained, the Captain should exercise emergency authority and communicate the urgency signal PAN-PAN spoken three times, or a CPDLC urgency downlink, as early as possible.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.6 Revised ATC Clearance Cannot be Obtained
quote: If possible, deviate away from an organized track or route system.
note: Weather Deviation Table 5.7.4.6(1). Flying EAST (000 to 179 magnetic): deviating LEFT descend 300 ft, RIGHT climb 300 ft. Flying WEST (180 to 359 magnetic): LEFT climb 300 ft, RIGHT descend 300 ft.

secTitle: Analyze Weather Conditions Using Weather Radar System
group: FOM and FCTM guidance on Weather avoidance
q: What do you report to Dispatch when deviating?
a: 100 nm lateral, 4000 ft altitude, 15 minute delay, weather
qOrig: What are the four items that are required to be reported to dispatch when deviating?
detail: Dispatch wants a call for any significant deviation from the flight plan: 100 nm or more off the planned route, 4000 ft or more off planned cruise altitude, anything likely to delay arrival more than 15 minutes such as holding, and enroute changes made for weather.
quote:
Lateral deviation: 100 nm or more from the planned route.
   – Altitude deviation: deviation of 4000 ft or more from the planned cruise altitude.
note: The same section adds two you will use often. Call when actual fuel differs from planned by 3000 lb on the 787, and any time you are in moderate or greater turbulence.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: What drives normal fuel planning?
a: Weather, traffic delays, MEL penalties, turbulence and cruise altitude
qOrig: What items must you keep in mind when doing fuel planning (normal flight)?
detail: Six factors. MEL and configuration deviation list limits and penalties. Turbulence and cruise altitude. One instrument approach with a possible missed approach at destination. Anything else that could delay landing.
quote:
Wind, severe weather, and other forecast weather conditions, and
• Anticipated traffic delays, and
• MEL/CDL limitations and penalties, and
• Turbulence/cruise altitude, and
• One instrument approach and possible missed approach at destination, and
• Any other conditions that may delay landing.
note: If you and the Dispatcher disagree on extra fuel, you have the final call. Agree before fueling starts, and get changes to Dispatch at least 30 minutes before pushback.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Domestic dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Destination, alternate, plus 45 minutes
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for domestic operations?
detail: Flights must be dispatched with enough fuel to fly to the airport to which dispatched, and either fly to and land at the most distant alternate with enough fuel to fly 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate, or with no alternate required, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.
quote: With no alternate, fly for 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.
note: 14 CFR 121.639. Both reserves are at LAST CRUISE ALTITUDE consumption rate, not holding. Applicable areas at 8.1.1.1.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Flag dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Destination, 10 percent of trip time, alternate, 30 minutes holding
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for Flag operations?
detail: Flag dispatch fuel is enough to reach the destination, then 10 percent of the total time from departure to landing at destination, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, then 30 minutes at holding speed 1500 ft above the destination or that alternate.
quote:
Fly to and land at the most distant alternate airport, if one is required, then
• Fly for 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination airport or alternate if one is
  required.
note: The 10 percent here is on total flight time. That is what separates it from the B043 special reserve, where the 10 percent counts only oceanic and remote continental time.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: Supplemental dispatch fuel requirement?
a: Domestic or Flag rules, whichever applies
qOrig: What are the dispatch fuel requirements for Supplemental operations?
detail: Supplemental (non-scheduled) operations are authorized within the areas approved for enroute operations and are conducted under Domestic or Flag rules per Ops Spec A030 or Exemption 11047 (FOM 8.1.1.3). The Dispatcher must notate on the release whether the flight is being operated as Part 121 Domestic or Flag (FOM 8.5.2). Fuel then comes straight from FOM 8.3.2.1 or 8.3.2.2.
ref: FOM 8.1.1.3 Supplemental Operations / FOM 8.5.2 Dispatch Release
quote:
Supplemental (non-scheduled) flights shall be dispatched using either Domestic or Flag rules as
applicable.
note: No separate supplemental fuel rule.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: B043 special fuel requirement?
a: Destination, 10 percent of oceanic time, alternate, 45 minutes cruise
qOrig: What are the special fuel requirements for a B043 flight plan?
detail: Fuel to the destination, then 10 percent of the planned time in oceanic and remote continental airspace, then to the most distant alternate if one is required, then 45 minutes at normal cruise consumption, figured at the weight and altitude you would have at top of descent.
ref: FOM 8.3.2.3 Special Fuel Reserves in International Operations
quote:
10% of the planned time in oceanic/remote continental airspace, then
• Fly to and land at the most distant alternate airport, if one is required, then
• Fly for 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption.
note: On the 787 release these show in the fuel summary as 10% RSV and 45@CRZ. A standard flag release shows 30@1500 instead.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: What is final reserve fuel?
a: 30 minutes holding at 1500 ft, or 45 minutes under B043
qOrig: What is Final Reserve Fuel?
detail: Final reserve is the fuel that must remain untouched at the end of the planned profile. For Flag operations it is 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 ft above the destination or alternate. Under the B043 special international reserve it is 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption computed at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent.
quote: Fly for 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption.
note: Tie this to 11.2.6: if it becomes apparent you will land with less than 30 minutes of fuel, declare MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL. Final reserve is a planning number; the 30-minute emergency-fuel trigger is an in-flight number.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you ask ATC about the delay?
a: When delay plus divert could land you under 30 minutes
qOrig: When should you plan to “inquire” from ATC the current delay situation when unanticipated...
detail: FOM 11.2.5 reinforces the same posture: crews should be proactive in assessing estimated arrival fuel and, if delays are anticipated that could lead to minimum fuel, should evaluate and inquire well in advance.
quote: The PIC should request ATC delay information if it is anticipated that an airborne delay followed by a diversion could result in landing with less than a 30-minute fuel supply.
note: Inquire early. By the time you can declare minimum fuel you have already committed to an airport and given up the divert option.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you declare minimum fuel?
a: Once committed to one airport and able to accept no delay
qOrig: When should you declare Minimum Fuel?
detail: Minimum fuel means the fuel supply has reached a state where the flight can accept little or no delay. Declare it only after committing to land at a specific airport. Do not declare it at the destination while a divert to the alternate is still available. It is an advisory, not an emergency, and grants no priority.
quote: should only be made when the flight has committed to land at a specific airport
note: The FOM also directs crews to be proactive and inquire well in advance if delays could lead to minimum fuel.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
q: When do you declare MAYDAY FUEL?
a: When you will land with less than 30 minutes
qOrig: When should you declare “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL”?
detail: The PIC shall declare MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL when it becomes apparent that landing will occur with less than a 30-minute supply of fuel, to ensure priority handling. The 30-minute supply is based on holding fuel flow or higher, as required by configuration, at 1500 ft above field elevation.
quote: the PIC shall declare, “MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, FUEL” to ensure priority handling.
note: Note shall, not should. Thirty minutes is a floor, not a target. Contrast with 11.2.5 minimum fuel, which is advisory and grants no priority.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
group: Assess Diversion and Alternate Airport Weather Conditions and Minima
q: Airborne, what weather do you need at destination and alternates?
a: Crew operating minima
qOrig: Once airborne, what does the weather have to be at your destination, destination alternate, ETOPS...
detail: In flight, alternates must be at or above the crew's operating minima and remain suitable to conduct an IAP. To START the approach, do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums.
quote: Do not begin the final approach segment of an instrument approach procedure unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling (if required) is at or above the authorized minimums.
note: Three different standards get confused here: dispatch planning minima (8.2.2.1), in-flight suitability (crew operating minima, 6.3.5), and the approach-start gate (5.6.11). Keep them separate in an oral.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
group: Assess Diversion and Alternate Airport Weather Conditions and Minima
q: How do you get current METAR and TAF oceanic?
a: Ask Dispatch by datalink, satellite phone or high frequency radio
qOrig: How can you get the most current METAR/TAF when in oceanic airspace?
detail: Dispatch is your weather shop once you are off very high frequency radio range. They send updates by datalink, satellite phone or high frequency radio, and they must relay anything that would keep you out of an ETOPS alternate. Ask for the airport and the time window you care about.
quote:
Relay via ACARS, SATCOM, or HF any significant changes in airport status, forecasted weather
conditions, or any other conditions that would preclude a safe approach and landing.
note: The alternates page in the flight computer also has a weather request prompt that sends a datalink request for alternate airport weather.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
group: Assess Diversion and Alternate Airport Weather Conditions and Minima
q: Who monitors destination and alternate weather?
a: You and Dispatch, in parallel
qOrig: How often should you be checking the weather at your destination and alternates?
detail: The FOM frames this as joint PIC and Dispatcher responsibility rather than a fixed interval.
ref: FOM 6.3.5 In-Flight ETOPS Alternate Airport Weather Requirements
quote: Dispatch will update ETOPS alternates if any conditions preclude safe approach and landing at existing alternates.
note: No fixed interval is published. The practical standard is that you should never be surprised by destination or alternate weather at top of descent. Tie to the descent gouge: ATIS, Build, Bug, Brakes, Brief, RNP/Recall.

secTitle: Know Contingency Plan (i.e., Alternates, WEATHER Monitoring, Fuel, etc.)
group: Assess Diversion and Alternate Airport Weather Conditions and Minima
q: How do you get updated enroute and descent winds?
a: Push WIND DATA REQUEST on the route data page
qOrig: How (aircraft specific) can you get updated enroute/descent winds?
detail: Get to the route data page from the legs page, then select WIND DATA REQUEST. It sends a datalink request and loads winds and the descent forecast into the flight computer. You can enter up to four altitudes on any wind page first to shape what comes back.
quote:
transmits a datalink request for wind and descent forecast data.
Flight crew may enter up to four altitudes on any wind page to qualify the request.
note: Enter winds nearest the airplane first. The first entry is applied to every waypoint, so entering downtrack winds first corrupts the winds ahead of you.

secTitle: Know Engine Failure in Cruise Procedure
q: Engine failure over the western states. What do you do?
a: Driftdown on the ETCP route, land nearest suitable airport
qOrig: What are the Engine Failure and diversion procedures while flying over the western part of the 48...
detail: FOM 11.2.7 requires landing at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations, and the Captain must notify ATC and Dispatch as soon as possible and file a safety report. Suitability factors are listed in FOM 11.2.7.1; fuel sufficiency, passenger accommodation, and maintenance availability are explicitly NOT justification to fly past the nearest suitable airport with one engine out.
ref: FOM 11.2.7 Engine Shutdown in Flight / FOM 8.3.7 Enroute Terrain Clearance Program (ETCP)
quote:
If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on
time considerations, where a safe landing can be made.
note: Over the western US the driver is terrain. The Flight Plan carries the ETCP/driftdown solution with decision points and any Driftdown Alternates (FOM 8.3.7); weather for a named Driftdown Alternate must be in the Flight Information Packet.

secTitle: Know Engine Failure in Cruise Procedure
q: Engine failure in oceanic airspace. What do you do?
a: Nearest suitable airport, after getting a revised oceanic clearance
qOrig: What are the engine failure and diversion procedures while in oceanic airspace?
detail: Land at the nearest suitable airport where a safe landing can be made. Get a revised clearance before leaving the track if you can. If you cannot, turn at least 30 degrees left or right, establish a parallel track offset 5 nm, and get below FL290. Tell air traffic control what you have and ask for expeditious handling.
quote:
14 CFR 121.565 requires the Captain of a two-engine aircraft with one engine inoperative to land
at the nearest suitable airport where, in the Captain’s judgment after considering all relevant
factors, a safe landing can be made.
note: Squawk 7700, exterior lights on, and broadcast identification, condition, position and intentions on 121.5. Fuel to go farther, passenger convenience and maintenance are never reasons to pass the nearest suitable airport.
icao: NAT Doc 007 10.2.1: "a revised clearance shall be obtained, whenever possible, prior to initiating any action" ICAO matches the company procedure of getting a revised clearance before leaving the track.

secTitle: Know Engine Failure in Cruise Procedure
q: Immediate action items for engine failure in cruise?
a: None; ENG FAIL L, R has no memory items
qOrig: Review the immediate action items for engine failure in cruise (787, back of the QRC).
detail: The QRH Quick Action Index marks memory-item checklists with an asterisk; ENG FAIL L, R (QRH 7.14) is not listed, and the checklist has no dashed memory-item line.
ref: QRH Quick Action Index / QRH 7.14 ENG FAIL L, R
quote: *indicates a checklist which includes memory items.
note: ENG FAIL L, R does not appear on the QRH Quick Action Index at all, so there are no memory items to recite. Reference actions start with A/T ARM switch (affected side) confirm OFF and thrust lever (affected side) confirm idle.

secTitle: Know Engine Failure in Cruise Procedure
q: Driftdown off the route. Which way do you turn?
a: At least 30 degrees, left or right per listed factors
qOrig: When turning off the route during a drift-down, which direction will you turn? Why?
detail: FOM 5.7.4.2 has you leave the cleared track by initially turning at least 30 degrees left or right to establish a parallel, same-direction track offset 5 nm. Direction is a judgment call driven by where you sit in the track system, what is allocated on adjacent tracks, which way the alternate lies, the SLOP you are already flying, and terrain.
quote: The direction of the turn should be based on one or more of the following factors:
note: The five factors are position relative to any organized track or ATS route system, direction of flights and levels on adjacent tracks, direction to an alternate airport, any strategic lateral offset being flown, and terrain clearance.
icao: NAT Doc 007 10.2.1: "leave the cleared route or track by initially turning at least 30 degrees to the right or to the left" Same turn as the FOM, and Doc 007 lists the same direction factors, adjacent tracks, alternate, terrain.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: What is SLOP for?
a: Collision risk and wake turbulence
qOrig: What is the purpose of SLOP?
detail: The Flight Crew should use SLOP as standard operating practice in normal oceanic operations to mitigate collision risk and wake turbulence. It addresses both wake vortex encounters and the heightened collision risk when non-normal events such as operational altitude deviation errors and turbulence-induced altitude deviations occur.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.7 Strategic Lateral Offsets in Oceanic Airspace
quote: to mitigate collision risk and wake turbulence.
note: SLOP is generally accepted but disallowed in specific regions; check the AIP. Any aircraft overtaking another should offset within the procedure to create the least wake turbulence for the aircraft being overtaken.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.48: "This procedure distributes traffic between the centreline and 2 NM right of centreline and greatly reduces collision risk in the airspace by virtue of randomness" ICAO gives the same purposes and also directs SLOP when avoiding wake turbulence.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: How far can you offset with SLOP?
a: Up to 2 nm right of centerline. Never left
qOrig: Up to what distance/direction from the route is SLOP used/acceptable?
detail: SLOP is applied in relation to a route or track. The aircraft may fly zero, or up to a maximum of 2 nm right of course only, from 0.0 to 2.0 nm right of centerline in 0.1 nm increments.
ref: FOM 5.7.4.7 Strategic Lateral Offsets in Oceanic Airspace
quote: SLOP left of course is not authorized.
note: Three legal positions in practice: centerline, 1 nm right, 2 nm right, though the FOM permits any 0.1 increment. No ATC clearance is needed. Must be back on centerline by the oceanic exit point.
icao: NAT Doc 007 6.3.49: "Operators that have an automatic offset capability should fly up to 2 NM right of the centreline." ICAO matches the company limit, prohibits left offsets, and with 0.1 nm capability the 787 may fly any tenth up to 2 nm right.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: What is ITP?
a: In OpSpec A354 and NAT training
qOrig: What is “ITP”?
detail: ITP is authorized under OpSpec A354 and detailed in the oceanic/NAT training material and Jeppesen ATC pages. Confirm the request phraseology and the distance/speed criteria there before using it.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: When would you use ITP?
a: In OpSpec A354 and NAT training
qOrig: When might you consider using the ITP?
detail: ITP is authorized under OpSpec A354 and detailed in the oceanic/NAT training material and Jeppesen ATC pages. Confirm the request phraseology and the distance/speed criteria there before using it.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: How do you request an ITP climb or descent?
a: In OpSpec A354 and NAT training
qOrig: How do you (specifically) request an ITP CLB/DES clearance?
detail: ITP is authorized under OpSpec A354 and detailed in the oceanic/NAT training material and Jeppesen ATC pages. Confirm the request phraseology and the distance/speed criteria there before using it.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: How do you select a new destination?
a: Pick the airport on the alternates page, then DIVERT NOW
qOrig: How (aircraft specific) do you “Change” or “Select” a new destination?
detail: Line select the airport on the alternates page so it shows selected, then push DIVERT NOW. Review the route on the modification page and execute. Executing changes the destination, folds the diversion into the active flight plan, drops the rest of the old route, and deletes any descent constraints.
quote:
Selecting DIVERT NOW displays the route from the present position to the
selected alternate using the route displayed on the XXXX ALTN page for the
diversion airport.
note: Typing a new airport into the list does not select it. Watch for the DESCENT PATH DELETED message and rebuild the arrival for the new field.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: What is alternate navigation?
a: TCP backup navigation after losing all displays or all FMCs
qOrig: What is Alternate Navigation?
detail: Alternate navigation is a backup capability in the Tuning and Control Panel used after unrecoverable loss of all displays or all three FMCs (FCOM 11.50). Under normal power the NAV key on any of the three TCPs brings it up; on standby power only the Captain's TCP works.
quote:
In the unlikely event that an unrecoverable loss of all displays or loss of all three
FMCs occurs, a backup navigation capability is available through the Tuning and
Control Panel (TCP).
note: LNAV and VNAV are not available in alternate navigation, but autopilot and autothrottle may be. On standby power only the left (Captain's) TCP is available.

secTitle: Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
q: How do you fly alternate navigation to a point?
a: Push NAV, enter waypoint latitude and longitude, fly the displayed track
qOrig: How do you perform Alternate Navigation to a point or destination?
detail: This is the backup for losing all displays or all three flight computers. Push NAV on a tuning and control panel and enter the target latitude and longitude. The panel then shows true track to that point, ground track, groundspeed, distance and time to go. Fly the track manually or with the autopilot.
quote:
The ALTN NAV page provides a stand-alone single waypoint navigation
capability. Once the waypoint’s latitude and longitude have been entered at LSK
2 L/R, flight progress information to the waypoint is then displayed.
note: One waypoint at a time, and you update it yourself. On standby power only the Captain panel works. LNAV and VNAV are gone, but autopilot and autothrottle may still be available.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What goes into preparing for descent?
a: Review messages, check landing performance, set minimums, brief the approach
qOrig: What items are included in preparing for descent?
detail: Start it before leaving cruise altitude and finish it by 10,000 feet above field elevation. Review alerts, memos and operational notes, check landing performance and set VREF, set minimums, set the navigation radios and the autobrake. Crosscheck the flight computer against the chart, brief, then call for the descent checklist.
quote:
Start the Descent Procedure before the airplane descends below the cruise
altitude for arrival at destination.
Complete the Descent Procedure by 10,000 feet AFE.
note: Minimums depend on approach type: minimum descent altitude plus 50 for an MDA approach, the published decision altitude for a DA approach, radio for CAT II, blank for CAT III.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What do you brief off the STAR, approach and taxi charts?
a: Route and constraints, minimums, missed approach, landing runway and taxi
qOrig: What items should be briefed on the STAR/Approach/Taxi charts?
detail: The briefing runs threats, plan, then considerations. Off the charts you cover the arrival, approach and approach mode, altitude and speed constraints, minimums, fuel and route to the alternate, the missed approach, the landing runway and its assessment, the exit and taxi, autobrakes, flaps and approach speed.
quote:
Prior to beginning the descent, the PF initiates the approach briefing. The approach briefing
should be interactive, concise, and focused on the big picture.
note: The pilot monitoring calls threats first, off the Crew Briefing Reference Card and the 10-7 page. Keep it interactive and big picture, not a recital.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: How do you start the descent?
a: Set a lower altitude, then push the altitude selector or DES NOW
qOrig: How do you get the aircraft to begin the descent?
detail: Set the lower altitude in the mode control panel window. At top of descent the airplane starts down on its own in VNAV. To go early, push the altitude selector when inside 50 nm of top of descent, or page to the descent page, line select DES NOW, and execute.
quote:
During cruise, setting an altitude below the current altitude in the MCP altitude
window and pushing the altitude selector activates the DES NOW function
note: Outside 50 nm from top of descent, pushing the selector gives a cruise descent to that altitude instead of a path descent. DES NOW gives about 1250 feet per minute at economy speed.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Cleared the arrival vs cleared to descend via?
a: Not spelled out in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: What is the difference between “Cleared XX arrival” vs “Cleared to descend via XX arrival”?
detail: The only place our manuals use the phrase is the Mexico section, where a descend via clearance means fly the published lateral routing and the published altitudes. Neither the FOM nor the FCOM defines it against a plain arrival clearance. That distinction lives in the Aeronautical Information Manual, not in our books.
ref: FOM 21.3.3.5 Mexico Phraseology for Climbs and Descents
quote:
ATC expects the pilot to navigate on the lateral routing and altitudes as published on a procedure.
