Typically, the controller will issue a “Descend Via” or “Climb Via” clearance to keep the radio
transmission short and concise.
note: Central America does not use climb via or descend via at all. Charted altitude restrictions still apply there unless the controller specifically relieves you of them.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What weather do you need to begin an approach?
a: Reported RVR or visibility at or above minimums
qOrig: What must the Weather be in order to begin an approach? Ceiling and visibility?
detail: The reported weather at the destination must be at or above the visibility minimums prescribed for the approach. Do not begin the final approach segment unless the latest reported RVR, visibility, or ceiling if required, is at or above the authorized minimums.
quote: TDZ RVR reports are controlling.
note: Visibility is the controlling parameter; ceiling applies only where the procedure requires it. RVR values above 6000 are advisory only. Visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT I?
a: 1800 RVR
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT I approach?
detail: Standard CAT I is 1800 RVR. It is authorized to approved runways even without touchdown zone or centerline lights, or with those lights inoperative, provided the flight director or autopilot is used in approach mode down to decision altitude.
ref: FOM 5.6.16.1 Reduced Landing Minima - 1800 RVR and 200 ft DH
quote: Authorized precision CAT I landing minima as low as 1800 RVR to approved runways without TDZ
note: Reduced minima below standard CAT I are not available to you. Touchdown zone RVR is controlling, and the flight director or autopilot must be used in approach mode to decision altitude.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Are there high mins Captain restrictions?
a: Yes, relieved by Exemption 5549
qOrig: Are there restrictions for High Mins Captains?
detail: FOM 5.6.17 cross-references 3.16 Exemption 5549 for high minimums Captain limitations. A newly qualified Captain operates to increased minimums until the experience requirement is met, and Exemption 5549 is the FAA relief that modifies how those high-minimums restrictions apply.
quote: See 3.16 – Exemption 5549 for high minimums Captain limitations.
note: Read FOM 3.16 for the exact hour threshold and the precise relief Exemption 5549 grants. This is directly relevant to you as a new Captain and is a near-certain oral question, so get the numbers from the PDF rather than from memory.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is FAA Exemption 5549?
a: Relief allowing High Minimums Captains to fly published minima
qOrig: What is FAA Exemption 5549?
detail: Exemption 5549 lets a High Minimums Captain fly to published CAT I minima instead of the increased high-minimums values, provided the approach is flown by the Captain with an autopilot coupled to DH or missed approach (HA wording, FOM 3.16.1).
quote:
High Minimums Captains may be dispatched using Exemption 5549 and must comply with the
restrictions listed below.
note: A High Minimums Captain has under 100 hours PIC in type; without the exemption they add 100 ft and 1/2 sm to published minimums, but no less than 300-1 (FOM 3.17). OE flight hours do not count toward the 100 hours.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT II?
a: 1000 RVR
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT II approach? (C060)
detail: For CAT II the final approach segment may not begin unless the latest controlling RVR reports are at or above authorized minimums and required airborne and ground equipment is operational, including LOC and GS, an outer marker or DME defining the FAF, HIRL, and an approach light system (FOM 5.6.17.2).
ref: FOM 5.6.17.2 CAT II/SA CAT II Operating Limitations
quote:
Landings and subsequent ground operations for CAT II operations to 1000 RVR must be
  conducted in accordance with the airport’s low visibility operations plan with reference to
  the Low Visibility Taxi Charts or the Jeppesen Low Visibility AMM.
note: The controlling RVR table lives on the approach briefing cards in the PRC, not in the FOM - FOM 5.6.11 says so explicitly and FOM 5.6.14 notes CAT II/III minima are NOT tailored on the Jeppesen charts.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT II SA?
a: Not published in our manuals. It is on the approach briefing card.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT II SA approach? (C060)
detail: The FOM does not carry the number. Special Authorization CAT II visibility comes off the approach briefing card in the Pilot Reference Cards, and CAT II and III chart minimums are not tailored by the company. Read it off the card and the chart for the runway you are flying.
note: The only figure the FOM prints is CAT II operations to 1000 RVR, and that is in the context of requiring the airport low visibility plan and low visibility taxi charts.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Lowest visibility for CAT III?
a: Not published in our manuals. It is on the approach briefing card.
qOrig: What is the lowest visibility for a CAT III approach? (C060)
detail: Jeppesen minimums are tailored to our operations specifications for everything except CAT II and CAT III. For those the number comes off the approach briefing card in the Pilot Reference Cards. No CAT III visibility figure is printed in the FOM, FCOM or QRH.
quote:
CAT II/III approach minima are not tailored; see the approach briefing cards in the Pilot
Reference Cards (PRC).
note: The 787 low visibility table shows CAT III with no decision height, RVR as the controlling report, autoland and autothrottle mandatory, LAND 3 required, and the Captain flying.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Does the FOM table CAT II and III limitations?
a: No. It points to the fleet manuals, PRC and QRH
qOrig: Is there a table in the FOM categorizing CAT II/III Approach and Landing Limitations?
detail: FOM 5.6.17 directs Flight Crews to use the approach procedures in the fleet-specific manuals for all CAT II/III approaches. Missed approach criteria for CAT II/III are also in the fleet-specific manuals.
quote: The approach briefing references and required equipment tables in the PRC/QRH contain complete listings of the Flight Crew procedures and required equipment.
note: Ops Spec C060. Also: Alaska may be restricted by variant from CAT II/III at certain runway/airport combinations, see the tailored Jeppesen chart notes (5.6.17.1).

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: When can you autoland?
a: Category II or III runways only, with an autoland qualified Captain
qOrig: Under what conditions can you perform an autoland?
detail: The runway has to be a Category II or III runway, and on the 787 the Captain must be autoland qualified. At Hawaiian that means one automatic landing completed in the aircraft. Advise the tower so the ILS critical area is protected, since it is only protected automatically below 800 feet or 2 miles.
quote:
Autoland approaches and landings are permitted on CAT II/III runways only. Pilots should advise
the tower anytime Autoland operations are conducted to ensure the ILS Critical Zone is protected.
note: Before committing, check tower wind against the autoland wind limits and check the autoland maximum altitude for the field.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What qualifies a 787 Captain for autoland?
a: One automatic landing in the aircraft
qOrig: Under what conditions must you perform an autoland?
detail: For CAT II and CAT III, autoland is the approved means. The Captain must be autoland qualified and must have completed one automatic landing in the aircraft. Record every autoland attempt on the ACARS Autoland Report page.
quote: (HA) The Captain must complete one automatic landing in the aircraft to be qualified for CAT II/III (Autoland) operations.
note: This is a currency item that bites new Captains: without that one automatic landing logged in the aircraft, you are not CAT II/III qualified regardless of sim performance. Autoland reporting requirements are at FOM 7.1.14.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: How do you log an autoland?
a: Fill in every field on the datalink Autoland Report page
qOrig: What are the requirements to log/report an autoland?
detail: Every autoland attempt gets reported on the ACARS Autoland Report page, logbook page information included. If the datalink is inoperative, write a logbook entry giving airport, landing runway, category, and whether it was successful. An unsuccessful autoland also needs an Info to Maintenance entry explaining the failure.
quote:
For all Autoland attempts, the Captain is responsible for ensuring that all applicable fields on the
ACARS Autoland Report page are filled in, including the logbook page information.
note: Autoland landings are also recorded on the flight summary page. A successful autoland that maintenance did not request needs no logbook entry at all.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What drives a diversion?
a: Anything degrading a safe landing at destination
qOrig: What factors may precipitate a diversion?
detail: If an engine fails or is shut down in flight, land at the nearest suitable airport based on time considerations where a safe landing can be made. Suitability factors include aircraft configuration, weight, systems status and fuel remaining, and wind and weather conditions enroute at the diversion altitude.
ref: FOM 11.2.7 / 11.2.7.1 Engine Shutdown in Flight, Nearest Suitable Airport
quote: land the aircraft at the nearest suitable airport, based on time considerations, where a safe landing can be made.
note: Nearest Suitable Airport is FAA-approval-required text, so it is regulatory, not company preference. Nothing justifies flying past the nearest suitable airport after an engine shutdown.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: When do you start the divert?
a: Early enough to reach the alternate with 30 minutes fuel
qOrig: What factors should you consider when deciding when to start diverting to your alternate?
detail: Decide with Dispatch, and decide before you are into minimum fuel. Ask air traffic control for delay information early so you do not hold, then divert, and land at the alternate under 30 minutes. Minimum fuel is only declared once you are committed to a field, so it is not a decision tool.
quote:
The decision whether or not to divert to an alternate or other diversion airfield should be made
in coordination with Dispatch prior to the declaration of minimum fuel.
note: If it becomes clear you will land with less than 30 minutes of fuel, declare MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY FUEL. Thirty minutes is a floor, not a target.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Not using your listed alternate. What do you weigh?
a: Aircraft state and fuel, enroute weather, runways and approaches, rescue and firefighting
qOrig: If you are not diverting to your listed alternate, what factors should you consider before selecting the...
detail: Weigh configuration, weight, systems status and fuel remaining, then wind and weather at the diversion altitude, minimum enroute altitudes, and fuel burn to get there. At the field, weigh terrain, weather, wind, runways and surface condition, approach aids and lighting, and rescue and firefighting. Your familiarity with the airport counts too.
quote:
Aircraft configuration, weight, systems status, and fuel remaining
• Wind and weather conditions enroute at the diversion altitude
• Minimum altitudes enroute to the diversion airport
• Fuel burn to the diversion airport
note: With one engine out, having the fuel to go farther, passenger accommodation, and where maintenance sits are never justification for flying past the nearest suitable airport.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: Where is fuel planning in the FOM?
a: Dispatch chapter, under Planning Considerations and Requirements
qOrig: Where in the FOM is the fuel planning section?
detail: Fuel planning sits in the Dispatch chapter of the Flight Operations Manual, under Planning Considerations and Requirements. Fuel Planning covers the factors you must consider, departure fuel coordination with Dispatch, and tanker fuel. The next block, Fuel Requirements, carries the domestic, flag and international reserve numbers.
quote: When computing required fuel for a flight, the following factors must be considered:
note: Same chapter also holds departure fuel coordination. If you and Dispatch cannot agree on extra fuel, the Captain has the final say on fuel on board.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is the ETOPS critical fuel scenario?
a: Worst-case diversion fuel required from the critical point
qOrig: What is the ETOPS Critical Fuel Scenario?
detail: The critical fuel scenario is the most fuel-critical of three diversion cases from the critical point to the ETOPS alternate: immediate descent to 10,000 ft with both engines (depressurization), descent to best single-engine altitude with one engine out, and immediate descent to 10,000 ft with one engine out (simultaneous depressurization and engine failure) (FOM 6.2.5).
quote:
ETOPS (AS) FUEL REQD OVER CP (HA) CRITF is the most critical fuel scenario from the critical point
of the flight (CP/ETP to the diversion airport) chosen from the fuel scenarios outlined above.
note: It is a dispatch requirement, not an inflight limit (FOM 6.2.6 area, around FOM 6.4). If before the EEP it looks like actual FOB at the CP/ETP will be below the critical fuel requirement, coordinate with Dispatch.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is LAHSO?
a: Land and Hold Short Operations
qOrig: What is LAHSO?
detail: LAHSO involves landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, an intersecting taxiway, or some other designated point on a runway. The Available Landing Distance (ALD) is measured from the landing threshold to the hold short point, and the hold short point is marked by a painted holding position marking and red and white hold short position signs.
quote: A point on the runway beyond which a landing aircraft with a LAHSO clearance is not authorized to proceed.
note: Revisions to this section require FAA approval, which signals it is regulatory text, not company preference.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What must you check before accepting LAHSO?
a: Stopping within the ALD, using AFM distance plus 1000 ft
qOrig: What are the 4 different factors that must be considered prior to accepting a LAHSO clearance?
detail: The Captain may accept a LAHSO clearance only if every condition in 5.6.32.2 is satisfied. The HA determination is that existing conditions allow the aircraft to safely land and stop within the Available Landing Distance, where calculated landing distance equals the FAA-approved AFM distance plus 1000 ft for the actual configuration, environment and weight.
quote: The calculated landing distance will be the FAA-approved Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) distance plus 1000 ft
note: RECONCILE: Rev 125 revised LAHSO guidance to prohibit LAHSO on wet runways and require tailwind to be calm, less than 3 kts. Confirm the current four-factor list against the Rev 125.1 PDF before quoting it on the line.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What is a TLR?
a: Takeoff and Landing Report
qOrig: What is a TLR?
detail: The TLR is the performance product used for runway analysis. FOM 5.6.22.1 sets the surrounding policy: Captains shall ensure landing is allowed and executed within the appropriate performance data, and the landing data used for in-flight analysis is based on input conditions, which is what makes an accurate runway assessment critical.
quote: The landing data used for in-flight analysis is based on input conditions, this highlights the importance of an accurate runway assessment.
note: Acceptance is not weight-only: environmental conditions matter equally. Do not interchange the takeoff and landing crosswind tables, they serve different functions and the takeoff table is CG and weight sensitive while the TALPA landing table is not.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: How do you request landing performance data?
a: Fill in Landing Conditions, press SEND, read Landing Data
qOrig: How can you request landing data performance?
detail: Go to the Performance menu, open Landing Conditions, and enter airport, runway, wind, temperature, altimeter, runway condition, speed additive and reverse credit. Press SEND. When the data arrives you get a chime and a LANDING DATA READY message, and the LANDING DATA button appears.
ref: FCOM PI.19.33 ACARS Landing Performance Request
quote:
Once all required entries have been made, the SEND prompt is available
for the flight crew to select on the LANDING CONDITIONS page.
note: If the datalink request is unavailable, use the onboard performance tool on the electronic flight bag, or call Dispatch and ask for an analysis of the intended runway.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
q: What do HXX/TXX and LXX/RXX mean on the printout?
a: Headwind or tailwind knots, then crosswind from left or right
qOrig: On the landing data analysis printout, what do the designator/s “HXX/TXX” and “LXX/RXX” represent?
detail: That field is the wind broken into components for the landing runway. H means headwind and T means tailwind, in knots. L means the crosswind is from the left and R means it is from the right, also in knots. So H12/R08 is 12 knots down the runway and 8 knots from the right.
quote: 15. Headwind and crosswind (R = right, L = left)
note: The report legend spells out only R for right and L for left. Check these numbers against the reported surface wind before you accept the landing distances.

secTitle: Assess Operational and Environmental Factors for Descent and Arrival
group: Cold Temperature Altimeter Correction/VNAV Temperature Limitation
q: When do you make cold weather corrections on approach?
a: Airport temperature 0 degrees C or colder, when charted
qOrig: When/why do you make cold weather corrections while on approach?
detail: Colder than ISA means true altitude is lower than indicated, and the error grows with height above the altimeter reference source and as surface temperature approaches -30 C or colder (FCOM SP.16.10, FOM 9.3.3.1). Within the US and its territories the Jeppesen briefing strip carries a note when cold temperature corrections must be applied.
ref: FCOM SP.16.10 Cold Temperature Altitude Corrections / FOM 9.3.3.1
quote:
Extremely low temperatures create significant altimeter errors and greater
potential for reduced terrain clearance.
note: No correction is needed under ATC radar vectors, when maintaining an assigned flight level, or when reported airport temperature is above 0 C or at/above the procedure's minimum published temperature. Advise ATC of the corrections, and never correct the altimeter barometric reference setting.

q: When do you set QNH in the descent?
a: Descending below the transition level
qOrig: When, in the descent, do you change your altimeter setting to QNH (local Altimeter)?
detail: Set the local altimeter as you descend below the transition level, as part of the Approach Procedure. Above the transition level you fly on standard, 29.92 in Hg or 1013.25 hectopascals. Outside North America the transition level is usually much lower than 18,000 ft, so it comes up early.
quote: When descending below the transition level, set the altimeters.
note: Transition altitudes are charted. Transition levels normally come from the arrival information broadcast or the approach controller, so listen for it and brief it.

q: Transition level vs transition altitude?
a: Altitude is charted, flown on QNH; level is assigned, flown on standard
qOrig: What is the difference between a transition level vs transition altitude?
detail: Transition altitude is the climb boundary. At and below it you use the local altimeter setting and call the number an altitude. Transition level is the descent boundary. At and above it you use standard and call the number a flight level. The gap between them is the transition layer.
quote:
The aircraft shall be operated with the appropriate QNH value set below the Transition Altitude
and STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level.
note: Outside North America both are usually lower than the 18,000 ft you are used to, and they vary by country. Central America uses FL200 and 19,000 ft unless charted otherwise.

q: What altimeter setting defines a level?
a: Standard, 29.92 in Hg or 1013.25 hectopascals
qOrig: What (altimeter setting) defines a “level”?
detail: A flight level is a height flown on the standard setting. Set 29.92 in Hg or 1013.25 hectopascals and the number you read is a flight level, spoken as flight level three five zero. It is a pressure surface, not a true height above the ground.
quote:
The aircraft shall be operated with the appropriate QNH value set below the Transition Altitude
and STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level.
note: Two airplanes on standard stay separated from each other even when the actual pressure is far from standard, which is the whole point of using it in the upper airspace.

q: What altimeter setting defines an altitude?
a: QNH, the local altimeter setting
qOrig: What (altimeter setting) defines an “altitude”?
detail: An altitude is a height above mean sea level flown on the local setting. Set the reported QNH, in inches of mercury or hectopascals, and the number you read is an altitude. You use it at and below the transition altitude, and it is what puts your indicator near field elevation on the ground.
quote:
The aircraft shall be operated with the appropriate QNH value set below the Transition Altitude
and STD (1013.25 hPa/29.92 in Hg) above the Transition Level.
note: Outside North America most settings come in hectopascals. Confirm the unit before you set it, because 1002 hectopascals and 30.02 inches are very different worlds.

q: What is QFE?
a: Setting referenced to field elevation; altimeter reads height above the field
qOrig: What is QFE?
detail: QFE is the pressure at the airport itself. Set it and the altimeter reads zero on the runway and height above the field in the air, not height above sea level. We do not fly it. If a controller gives you QFE, ask for QNH and set that instead.
quote: Where QFE is given by ATC, the Flight Crews shall request QNH and set in the normal manner.
note: Integrated approach navigation and the automatic landing procedures are not authorized using QFE. Where charted altitudes are built on QFE, use the correction tables published on the arrival or approach chart.

q: Is the autopilot required on an RNAV1 STAR?
a: No, but recommended in high workload environments
qOrig: Is the autopilot required to be engaged on an RNAV1 STAR?
detail: FOM 2.3.9.2 makes autopilot use a recommendation, not a requirement, and FOM 2.3.9.3 encourages hand flying in lower workload terminal environments to keep proficiency. The one place the FOM mandates automation for PBN is 5.1.4.1: RNP AR procedures with RNP values less than 0.3 or with RF legs shall use autopilot or flight director driven by the RNAV system.
quote: In high workload, high traffic environments, autopilot use is strongly recommended.
note: INFERRED from absence: no autopilot requirement for an RNAV 1 STAR exists anywhere in FOM, FCOM or QRH. The only PBN autopilot mandate is FOM 5.1.4.1, and that applies to RNP AR only.

q: What is in the arrival and approach TPC briefing?
a: Threats, Plan, Considerations. The PF starts it before descent
qOrig: What items compose the Arrival and Approach TPC Briefing?
detail: Prior to beginning the descent the PF initiates the approach briefing, which should be interactive, concise and focused on the big picture. T, Threats, shared: the PM identifies relevant threats using the threat list on the Crew Briefing Reference Card and any airport-specific threats in the 10-7, and the PF briefs additional threats as needed.
quote: Pilots jointly identify any relevant threats, followed by the PF presenting the arrival plan
note: Threats is the only shared element; Plan and Considerations are PF. Management strategies are discussed as threats are identified rather than saved to the end. The departure equivalent is briefed the same way, see FOM 1.3.1 in the workbook.

q: Normal flap and gear schedule on approach?
a: Flaps 1, 5, 20 at each speed bug; gear at glideslope alive
qOrig: What is the normal flap/gear approach configuration schedule?
detail: Work the flap schedule off the speed tape: at the UP bug call flaps 1, at the 1 bug call flaps 5, at the 5 bug call flaps 20. Gear down and flaps 20 go together at glideslope alive. At glideslope capture call landing flaps, 25 or 30.
ref: FCOM NP.21.42 Landing Procedure ILS or GLS
quote:
At glideslope alive, call:
 • “GEAR DOWN”
 • “FLAPS 20”
                                          Set the landing gear lever to DN.
note: Flying an approach without a glideslope, gear and flaps 20 come about 2 nm before the final approach fix, once altitude hold or the vertical path mode is showing.

q: Where are the stabilized approach criteria?
a: Fleet-specific manuals; FOM only points you there
qOrig: Where is the Stabilized Approach Criteria parameters located?
detail: FOM 5.6.5 gives the philosophy, speed, descent rate, lateral and vertical guidance, and configuration, plus the warning not to land from an unstable approach. The gate numbers themselves live in the flight crew training manual.
quote:
Comply with the stabilized approach criteria and procedures contained in the
fleet-specific manuals. An approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met.
note: FOM 5.6.5 carries the policy and the warning but explicitly defers the numeric criteria to the fleet manual (787 FCTM/AOM). The one hard number the FOM does give is runway alignment by 500 ft AFE, with 300 ft AFE exceptions annotated on the airport 10-7.

q: What is required at each stabilized approach gate?
a: Not listed in these manuals. The 787 fleet manual holds the gates
qOrig: What are the Stabilized Approach requirements at each “gate”?
detail: The Flight Operations Manual sets the policy and sends you to the fleet manual for the actual gate numbers. What it does state: an approach is stabilized only if every criterion is met, you must normally be aligned with the runway by 500 ft above field elevation, and you do not land from an unstable approach.
quote:
An approach is stabilized only if all criteria are met. Normally, the aircraft
must be aligned with the runway by 500 ft AFE.
note: Either pilot may call the go-around under the no fault policy. Some runways carry a 300 ft alignment exception, shown on the airport 10-7 page. Get the gate numbers from the 787 flight crew training manual or your check airman.

q: Why go around if not stabilized?
a: Unstable approaches must not be landed from
qOrig: Emphasize the importance of going around if the stabilized approach criteria are not met and the no fault...
detail: FOM 5.6.5 pairs the WARNING with the no-fault go-around policy: either crewmember may call for a go-around and the professional judgment of the flight crew is used to assess the probability of meeting the criteria.
quote: Do not land from an unstable approach.
note: This is a WARNING in FOM 5.6.5, not a recommendation. Either crewmember may call the go-around under the Alaska no-fault policy, so an FO go-around call is not a challenge to your authority as PIC.

q: Demonstrate the callouts and configuration steps
a: In the FCTM
qOrig: Discuss/demonstrate the callouts and configuration steps...
detail: Handling technique: rotation rates and target pitch, bounced landing recovery, reverser use and stowing, carbon brake technique, flap and gear schedule, autothrottle policy on approach. All FCTM R9 plus FCOM NP.21. FCTM is not in the browser environment.

q: Inside the FAF. Minimum visibility?
a: Once the segment has begun, continue to DA or MDA
qOrig: What if you are inside the FAF? Minimum visibility?
detail: You may not begin the final approach segment unless the controlling RVR is at or above the authorized minimums and both the airborne and ground equipment are operational. Ground equipment means localizer and glide slope plus the required lighting. Once the segment has begun, you may continue to decision altitude.
ref: FOM 5.6.17.2 CAT II/SA CAT II Operating Limitations
quote: The Final Approach Segment (FAS) of an IAP may not begin unless the latest controlling RVR reports for the landing runway are at or above the minimums authorized
note: Note visibility below 1/2 sm is not authorized and shall not be used for approach minimums (5.6.11).

q: What shows on the FMA with the approach armed?
a: Localizer and glideslope in small white letters below the active green modes
qOrig: Discuss what is shown on FMA when the approach is armed...
detail: Push the approach switch and the armed roll and pitch modes appear at the bottom of the roll and pitch boxes, small and white on the primary flight display, green on the head up display. On an instrument landing system approach that is LOC and G/S. Flying integrated approach navigation you get FAC and G/P instead.
quote:
Armed modes (except for TO/GA in the air) display in
smaller letters (white on the PFD) at the bottom of the flight mode annunciation
boxes.
note: Armed modes move up into large green letters as each one captures. Glideslope or glidepath capture is blocked until the localizer or course captures first.

q: Which modes are eligible for a non-precision approach?
a: IAN or VNAV
qOrig: What different approach modes(s) are eligible to perform a non-precision approach?
detail: IAN drives the APP mode with an ILS-look-alike FAC and G/P presentation, so it is armed with the APP switch; VNAV flies the FMC path with LNAV or LOC as the roll mode. FCOM NP.21.45 adds that IAN is not recommended when the approach has a visual maneuver segment not in the FMC database.
ref: FCOM SP.4 Instrument Approach - RNAV (RNP) AR (note); NP.21.45 and NP.21.48
quote:
Note: For RNAV (GPS) and RNAV (GNSS) procedures use the
      Landing Procedure - Instrument Approach using IAN or Landing
      Procedure - Instrument Approach using VNAV in Normal
      Procedures.
note: FCOM NP.21.45 (IAN) and NP.21.48 (VNAV) are the two non-precision landing procedures. Both require a published GP angle on the LEGS page, an RWxx waypoint at the approach end, or a missed approach waypoint before the runway end. Neither is authorized using QFE.

q: Which approaches are flown managed or selected?
a: Vertical is always the FMS glide path; lateral is FMS or localizer
qOrig: What approaches would be flown in Managed/Selected?
detail: Integrated approach navigation flies every non precision approach like an instrument landing system approach, and vertical guidance is always the computed glide path. Lateral guidance comes from the final approach course mode on area navigation, satellite, omnidirectional range and beacon approaches. It comes from the localizer mode on localizer, directional aid and simplified directional facility approaches.
quote:
Approaches flown with IAN procedures always use FMC computed glidepath
(G/P) for vertical path guidance. Depending on the type of approach flown, lateral
guidance can come from the FMC or localizer.
note: Arm both modes with the approach switch. Integrated approach navigation does not support an automatic landing, so disconnect the autopilot and land manually or you get a NO AUTOLAND alert at 100 ft.

q: Can you fly a visual approach at night?
a: Yes, unless that airport restricts night visuals
qOrig: Can we fly a visual approach at night?
detail: FOM 5.6.6.1 permits visual approaches with 1000 ft ceiling and 3 sm visibility or better, VFR cloud clearance, within 35 nm of the destination, under ATC control, with the airport or preceding aircraft in sight.
ref: FOM 5.6.6.1 Visual Approach or RNAV Visual Flight Procedure (without CVFP)
quote:
Airports that restrict night visual approaches require that an instrument approach procedure be
  flown to guarantee adequate terrain clearance.
note: Night restrictions are published in the airport 10-7 (see FOM 5.6.6.3 note). FOM 5.6.6.1 also tells you to consider terrain a threat any time a night visual is planned or even possible.

q: Is the autothrottle required on approach and landing?
a: Not a published requirement. FCTM technique
qOrig: Is the auto-thrust/auto-throttle system required during approach and/or landing?
detail: Handling technique: rotation rates and target pitch, bounced landing recovery, reverser use and stowing, carbon brake technique, flap and gear schedule, autothrottle policy on approach. All FCTM R9 plus FCOM NP.21. FCTM is not in the browser environment.

q: What would make you turn the autothrottle off?
a: Approach category, wind and gust protection, plus the speed additive you lose
qOrig: What factors should be considered if deciding to turn off the auto-thrust/auto-throttle system for the...
detail: Think about three things. Approach category: the autothrottle is mandatory for CAT III and recommended for CAT II. Wind and gusts: with it active, VREF plus 5 already gives you gust protection, and you give that up when you turn it off. Windshear risk: if you plan to fly manual thrust, add a speed correction up to 15 knots.
ref: FCOM 4.20.19 Automatic Flight, Approach and Landing
quote:
With a command speed of VREF+5 knots and landing flaps, there is sufficient
wind and gust protection available with the autothrottle active.
note: Manual thrust also raises workload right when you need capacity for the runway and the go-around decision. Brief it and tell the First Officer what you want called.

q: Where is crosswind landing guidance?
a: FCOM Limitations crosswind tables; FOM Wind Limits
qOrig: Where can you find guidance on landing the aircraft in a crosswind?
detail: Crosswind limits come off the FCOM table by runway condition code: 40 kt at code 6 and 5, 35 kt at 4, 25 kt at 3, 17 kt at 2, 15 kt at 1, no landing at 0. Subtract 5 kt on a wet or contaminated runway when using asymmetric reverse.
ref: FCOM L.10.7 Landing Crosswind Limitations - TALPA
quote:
*** Sideslip only (zero crab) landings are not recommended with crosswind
components in excess of 25 knots.
note: FCOM L.10.7 carries both the TALPA table (keyed to Runway Condition Code / braking action) and the Non-TALPA table. Landing technique itself (crab, decrab, sideslip) is in the 787 FCTM Landing chapter, which is not one of these three manuals.

q: Is max reverse required on landing?
a: Not a published requirement. FCTM technique
qOrig: Is max thrust reverser required upon landing?
detail: Handling technique: rotation rates and target pitch, bounced landing recovery, reverser use and stowing, carbon brake technique, flap and gear schedule, autothrottle policy on approach. All FCTM R9 plus FCOM NP.21. FCTM is not in the browser environment.

q: When do you stow the thrust reversers?
a: Start at 60 knots, reverse idle before taxi speed
qOrig: When should the thrust reversers be stowed?
detail: By 60 knots indicated, start moving the reverse thrust levers so they reach the reverse idle detent before taxi speed. Once the engines are at reverse idle, move the levers full down to stow. If you used maximum reverse and performance allows, begin reducing at 80 knots.
quote:
reverse thrust levers to reach the reverse
idle detent before taxi speed.
note: Reducing early cuts engine wear from debris ingestion. Once the reverse levers are raised you are committed to a full stop landing.

q: Braking technique with carbon brakes?
a: Fewer, steady applications with the pedals fully released between them
qOrig: What braking technique is used with carbon brakes?
detail: Carbon brake wear tracks the number of applications, not how hard you press. So brake in fewer, firmer, steady applications and let the airplane roll between them rather than riding the pedals. Below 30 knots the airplane applies half the brakes on each main gear and alternates wheel pairs, but only if you fully release the pedal.
quote:
The system sequences through alternating wheel pairs at each brake application,
reducing the number of brake applications by each brake. The brake pedal must
be fully released to transition to the other two brakes on a main landing gear.
note: Dragging the brakes defeats the alternating logic and costs brake life. The full braking technique writeup is in the 787 flight crew training manual, not the operating manual.

q: Factored vs unfactored landing data?
a: Factored adds margin. The 787 adds 15 percent
qOrig: What is the difference between factored vs unfactored landing data?
detail: Unfactored landing distance is the raw computed distance. Factored distance applies a safety margin on top. Rev 125 moved the 787 to a TALPA landing model using a 7-second air/flare distance and a 15 percent margin on TOTAL landing distance including air distance, calculated to a computed rather than fixed touchdown point.
quote: this distance includes air-run to touchdown plus ground roll and a 15% safety factor for degraded braking action requests
note: Read 5.6.22.3 in full for the landing distance wording. The model adds a 7 second air and flare distance and a 15 percent margin on the total landing distance, calculated rather than assuming a fixed touchdown point.

q: Key to bounced landing recovery without a tail strike?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: What is a key component during a bounced landing recovery to avoid a tail strike?
detail: The FCOM sends you to the Flight Crew Training Manual for bounced landing recovery. What our books do say is that a high bounce ends in a go around, and that once you have touched down you must push the thrust levers up by hand.
ref: FCOM Bulletin HWI-31 R1 Descent and Go-around Procedure Changes
quote: high bounced landings, all result in performing a go-around.
note: The 787 cuts elevator deflection when it computes a tail strike is coming, but steady back pressure on the column overrides that protection.

q: What are the FCOM procedures after landing?
a: After Landing, Shutdown, then Secure Procedure
qOrig: What are the FCOM procedures after landing?
detail: After Landing (NP.21.53): speedbrake down verified by the Captain, APU as needed, engine anti-ice as needed, exterior lights, weather radar off, autobrake OFF, flaps UP, transponder to XPDR, and the COMPANY ARRIVAL REPORT page ON/IN times and landing pilot.
quote: Start the After Landing Procedure when clear of the active runway.
note: After Landing starts when clear of the runway (FCOM NP.21.53), Shutdown starts after taxi is complete (NP.21.54), Secure is run any time the flight deck will be left unattended (NP.21.56).

q: Where are the single engine taxi procedures?
a: Fleet-specific manuals; FOM states the policy only
qOrig: Where can you find the single engine taxi procedures? Review any differences in SOP.
detail: FOM 5.3.3 makes single-engine taxi the standard procedure when operationally feasible and points to fleet-specific manuals for the procedure. The identical green-policy sentence is repeated at FOM 5.6.22.1 for the taxi-in case.
quote:
When operationally feasible, a single-engine taxi is the standard procedure to optimize fuel
efficiency.
See fleet-specific manuals for further guidance.
note: No single-engine taxi procedure anywhere in the FOM, FCOM or QRH. FOM 5.3.3 and FOM 5.6.22.1 both state the green policy and then defer to the fleet manual (787 FCTM/AOM). Pull the actual procedure from there before OE.

q: Engine cool requirement before shutdown?
a: At least 3 minutes at taxi thrust
qOrig: What is the engine cool requirements before shutting down an engine?
detail: FCOM NP.21.53 sets the cooldown at a minimum of 3 minutes at no more than normal all-engine taxi thrust, and this is the clock that governs a single-engine taxi-in shutdown as well as arrival at a short-taxi gate.
quote:
Engine cooldown recommendations:
 • Run the engines for at least 3 minutes
 • Use a thrust setting no higher than that normally used for all engine
   taxi operations
                Pilot Flying                         Pilot Monitoring
The captain positions or verifies that the SPEEDBRAKE lever is DOWN.
note: It is worded as a recommendation, not a limitation, but it drives the taxi-in plan.

q: What do you weigh before a single engine taxi?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: What factors should you consider before conducting a single engine taxi?
detail: The FOM makes single engine taxi standard when it is operationally feasible, then sends you to fleet manuals for the rest. Neither the FCOM nor the QRH carries a single engine taxi procedure or a list of factors. Get the items your check airman expects before you brief it.
quote:
When operationally feasible, a single-engine taxi is the standard procedure to optimize fuel
efficiency.
note: FOM taxi guidance still applies: no more than 30 knots on straight smooth taxiways and about 10 knots in congested areas.

q: Gate arrival procedures
a: Marshaller or VDGS, two wing walkers, parking brake set
qOrig: Gate Arrival Procedures...
detail: FOM 5.6.33 requires two wing walkers and one marshaller/VDGS operator for the 787. With manual marshalling the signals must be clearly visible to the Captain at all times (hand signals are in FOM 5.3.12).
quote: • Two Wing Walkers and One Marshaller/VDGS Operator
note: The 787 requires more people than the narrowbodies: two wing walkers plus one marshaller/VDGS operator. Station exceptions to the two wing walker requirement are published in the airport 10-7.

q: What do you check before taxiing into the gate area?
a: Correct aircraft type displayed on the VDGS
qOrig: What should be checked prior to taxiing into the gate area?
detail: FOM 5.6.33 gives the VDGS sequence: correct aircraft type displayed before entering the gate area, guidance screen with centerline indicator displayed before the nose passes the jet bridge, and stop on WAIT or STOP. If lead-in line visibility is poor at night or in weather, the crew may request manual marshalling from Station Ops.
quote: Ensure the correct aircraft type is displayed prior to entering the gate area.
note: Also confirm required personnel are in place (two wing walkers plus marshaller/VDGS operator for the 787), that the Circle of Safety is clear, and that the engine cool-down will be satisfied.

q: No marshaller. Where do you stop?
a: Stop; marshalling signals must be visible throughout
qOrig: If there is no marshaller or if they are not marshalling you in, where should you stop the aircraft?
detail: FOM 5.6.33 lists one marshaller/VDGS operator and two wing walkers as required personnel for the 787, and requires marshalling signals be clearly visible to the Captain at all times under manual procedures.
quote:
Manual – for standard manual procedures, the marshalling signals shall be clearly visible to the
  Captain at all times (see 5.3.12 – Hand Signals).
note: The FOM does not name a specific stop point for a missing marshaller.

q: Perform the securing procedure
a: Run it whenever the flight deck is unattended
qOrig: Perform Securing Procedure (Optional/If not performed, discuss)
detail: FCOM NP.21.56 flow: IRS selectors OFF, BATTERY switch off, FD POWER switch OFF, EMERGENCY LIGHTS switch OFF, PACK switches OFF, EFB PWR switch off (both), HUD combiner stowed with the caution to ensure it is fully raised and securely latched, then the Captain calls for and the FO does the SECURE checklist.
quote: Run the Secure Procedure any time the flight deck will be left unattended.
note: Trigger is an unattended flight deck, not end of day. Watch the PECS caution: up to 22 minutes of cool-down may be required before removing power (FCOM SP.6 Electrical Power Down).

q: ACARS post-flight report pages?
a: All Autoland attempts and all RNP AR procedures
qOrig: ACARS Post-Flight Report (Autoland and RNP-AR Report pages)
detail: FOM 5.6.21.2 makes the Captain responsible for completing the ACARS Autoland Report page for every Autoland attempt, including the logbook page information; if ACARS/ATSU is inoperative the Captain makes a logbook entry stating Autoland successful or unsuccessful with airport, runway and category, and the reason for any failure.
ref: FOM 5.6.21.2 Autoland Reporting - ACARS; FOM 7.1.13.1 RNP AR Required Reporting
quote:
For all Autoland attempts, the Captain is responsible for ensuring that all applicable fields on the
ACARS Autoland Report page are filled in, including the logbook page information.
note: Autoland reporting is every attempt, satisfactory or not. RNP AR reporting covers results of all RNP AR procedures plus any RNP degradation, and excludes visual approaches even if an RNP AR approach was displayed as reference (FOM 7.1.13.1 note).

q: Debrief
a: PF initiates it and asks PM for feedback
qOrig: Debrief...
detail: FOM 5.6.39 says the postflight debriefing should be interactive, concise and focused on relevant items in order to learn from experiences and facilitate mentoring, and that the PF initiates it by asking the PM for positive and/or constructive feedback, referencing the Crew Briefing Reference Card.
quote:
After the completion of each flight, as workload allows, the PF should initiate the postflight
debriefing.
note: The PF initiates regardless of seat, so as Captain you may be debriefed by your FO after their leg. Use the Crew Briefing Reference Card. Separate from FOM 11.1.12 Postflight Debriefing/Flight Irregularities, which is the irregularity reporting path.

q: Where are the logbook review procedures?
a: Maintenance Logbook Preflight Review, in the FOM maintenance chapter.
qOrig: Where in the FOM can you find the maintenance logbook review/checking procedures?
detail: Hawaiian procedures sit under Maintenance Logbook Procedures, Preflight Review. Every pilot reviews at least the last 10 pilot entered discrepancies, not counting No Items or Info to Maintenance entries. Alaska has its own preflight review paragraph a few pages earlier in the same chapter.
quote:
Prior to the first flight on a particular aircraft, all Flight Crew shall review the Aircraft Maintenance
Logbook.
note: Deferred items get a second look. Check the MEL, CDL or SDL for restrictions, operational procedures and performance penalties, and confirm every one is on the release.

q: How long is the PDSC good for?
a: Four hours from the Airworthiness Release signature.
qOrig: How long is the PDSC good for?
detail: The clock starts when the Airworthiness Release block is signed in the M258 logbook, not at scheduled departure. If four hours pass and boarding has not started, the check is invalid and Maintenance must redo it. If boarding started in time you may continue, but tell Maintenance Control.
ref: FOM 6.5.4 ETOPS Pre-Departure Service Check, PDSC Policy
quote:
An ETOPS PDSC Airworthiness Release will be valid for four (4) hours from the time the
Airworthiness Release block was signed in the M258 Aircraft Maintenance Logbook.
note: An aircraft swap always needs a new check. The check belongs to that tail and that flight number and cannot follow the airplane to another flight.

q: White vs yellow MEL placard?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: What is the difference between a white (HAL 46-1333) vs yellow (HAL 46-1333b) MEL placard?
detail: Our FOM describes only the white form, HAL 46-1333, the Project Operation and Maintenance Information Form. It rides in the logbook to tell you about special installations or engineering changes, and it is how an APU in flight start request reaches the crew. The yellow version is not described.
ref: FOM 12.4.12.7 HAL Project Operation and Maintenance Information Form
quote:
When required, a Project Operation and Maintenance Information Form (HAL 46-1333) will
be placed in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (HAL M258) to notify Flight Crew of special
installations or engineering modifications that have been accomplished on an aircraft.
note: Look in the MEL introduction and ask Maintenance Control about the yellow card. It does not appear in the FOM or the FCOM.

q: What are the four repair intervals?
a: Categories A, B, C, and D.
qOrig: What are the 4 different repair intervals...
detail: Repair categories run A through D. Category A carries its own limit written into the MEL item itself, while B, C and D are fixed day limits published in the MEL general pages. All four are dispatch limits, not limits on the flight once it is under way.
ref: FOM 8.5.4.1 Dispatch Release Sample and Description
quote:
The repair categories of A, B, C, or D in
             an MEL are dispatch time limits not flight operational time limits.
note: Dispatch happens at pushback or engine start, whichever comes first. Start inside the limit and you may finish that flight, but you may not continue past the next termination point.

q: What is an (O) procedure in the MEL?
a: A crew operational procedure required with that item inoperative.
qOrig: What is an “(O)” procedure listed in an MEL?
detail: An (O) means the flight crew has something to do to operate with that item deferred, such as a limit, a workaround or an extra check. Read it during the logbook review, before you accept the airplane. An (M) is the maintenance side, done by mechanics.
quote:
all Flight Crew shall review the aircraft
MEL/CDL/SDL for applicability, restrictions, MEL Operational Procedures (O), and performance
decrements.
note: The full wording lives in the MEL introduction. The FOM requires you to review deferred items for applicability, restrictions, operational procedures and performance decrements.

q: Where is the crew placarding procedure?
a: Maintenance chapter of the FOM, and Crew Placarding in the MEL.
qOrig: Where can you find the Crew Placarding Procedure?
detail: The FOM paragraph sets the conditions: a discrepancy after pushback but before takeoff, with Dispatch and Maintenance Control both concurring, and no return to the gate needed. The step by step placarding text is in the MEL under Crew Placarding. Remote placarding follows right after it.
quote:
If the item is Crew Placardable in the MEL/CDL/SDL, follow the appropriate procedures as
described in the MEL/CDL/SDL under Crew Placarding and a return to gate (BTB) is not required.
note: Maintenance Control normally sends the whole item by ACARS. Print it, check the blocks, do the placarding and any procedures, and note the item on the release.

q: EVF communication requirements with Maintenance?
a: Call or ACARS Dispatch 30-60 minutes after takeoff, before EEP
qOrig: What are the ETOPS verification flight communication requirements regarding contacting Maintenance...
detail: FOM 6.5.10 (HA): the crew is notified of an open item on the MIC sheet, Maintenance also verbally notifies the crew and enters AIRCRAFT RELEASED TO ETOPS SERVICE IAW WITH HA ETOPS MAINTENANCE MANUAL FOR VERIFICATION FLIGHT DUE TO REPAIR OF ___ in the logbook, and the crew must verbally acknowledge the EVF requirement with Dispatch.
quote:
Between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and prior to reaching the EEP, the Flight Crew will call or
send an ACARS message to Dispatch to report the status of the affected component or system.
note: Gotcha: the in-flight report goes to Dispatch, not to Maintenance. Maintenance's role is the up-front verbal notification plus the logbook entry, and the crew verbally acknowledges the EVF requirement with Dispatch. The report AND Dispatch's acknowledgment must both be complete before the EEP.

q: Why tell Maintenance enroute rather than at the gate?
a: The arrival station can have Maintenance ready before you block in.
qOrig: What are the advantages of notifying MX of a discrepancy enroute (time permitting) vs after blocking in?
detail: Airborne, put the discrepancy in the logbook and pass it to Maintenance and Dispatch by the ACARS maintenance report page or company radio. Telling them early is what lets the inbound station plan for the airplane. Waiting until block in gives them no lead time.
quote:
Communicate defects via
ACARS MAINT REPORT page (primary) or Company radio. Ensure the inbound station is aware of
the defect.
note: MEL and crew placarding procedures are not used in flight. Enroute you report and coordinate. The deferral or repair happens on the ground.

q: Where in FD Pro are the ICAO country procedures?
a: In the FD Pro guide in Comply365
qOrig: Where in FD Pro can you find the ICAO (country) procedures for destinations that we serve?
detail: This is a Jeppesen FD Pro X or EFB workflow step, not FOM/FCOM content. Verify against the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365 and demonstrate on the actual device during OE. FOM 5.7.3.15 does require the ENTIRE cleared route be loaded into the approved charting app for ORCN segments.

q: Where in FD Pro are the ICAO emergency procedures?
a: In the FD Pro guide in Comply365
qOrig: Where in FD Pro can you find the ICAO (country) emergency procedures for destinations that we serve?
detail: This is a Jeppesen FD Pro X or EFB workflow step, not FOM/FCOM content. Verify against the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365 and demonstrate on the actual device during OE. FOM 5.7.3.15 does require the ENTIRE cleared route be loaded into the approved charting app for ORCN segments.

q: Review the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide
a: In the FD Pro guide in Comply365
qOrig: Review FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365...
detail: This is a Jeppesen FD Pro X or EFB workflow step, not FOM/FCOM content. Verify against the FD Pro Pubs Quick Reference guide in Comply365 and demonstrate on the actual device during OE. FOM 5.7.3.15 does require the ENTIRE cleared route be loaded into the approved charting app for ORCN segments.

q: When is an HF position report required?
a: Only when you are not on CPDLC
qOrig: When is an HF position report required?
detail: When using CPDLC you must contact ARINC after a successful CPDLC logon but prior to the initial Gateway Fix to obtain a SELCAL check on HF, establishing a backup if CPDLC fails. No other HF reports need be made while using CPDLC. Non-CPDLC position reporting varies by area and is specified on the enroute chart.
quote: Flight Crews should not make HF position reports when using CPDLC procedures.
note: REV 125.1 ADDED: if SELCAL is not functioning, one member of the crew must listen to HF continuously. That is the new sentence in this revision and a likely oral question.
icao: NAT Doc 007 5.1.17: "flight crews of flights using ADS-C should not additionally submit position reports via voice unless requested by aeronautical radio operator" ICAO matches the company rule and separately requires the SELCAL check before oceanic entry.

q: Can you enter oceanic airspace with both HF radios out?
a: No. At least one HF radio is required
qOrig: Can you enter Oceanic airspace with both HF radios not working?
detail: FOM 20.4.1 sets dispatch minimums of two HF radios or a single HF plus SATVOICE, and after pushback prior to entering oceanic airspace requires dual LRNS plus two HF radios, or a single HF with SATCOM data link, or a single HF with SATVOICE.
ref: FOM 20.4.1 Required Equipment for OAK, ANC, and FUK FIRs
quote:
After pushback, prior to entering oceanic airspace:

• Dual Long Range Navigation Systems (to include 2 MCDUs)
• Two HF radios, or

   – A single HF radio and SATCOM data link, or
   – A single HF radio and SATVOICE
note: Every authorized combination for OAK/ANC/FUK includes at least one working HF. Same story in the NAT: FOM 22.4.3 requires two independent LRCS, one of which must be HF. FOM 20.4.4.1 covers what to do if both HF fail after you are already established oceanic.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 5.1.1: "Operations in the NAT outside VHF coverage require the carriage of two long range
         communication systems, one of which must be HF." ICAO matches the company requirement and allows SATVOICE or CPDLC over SATCOM as the second system.

secTitle: Analyze and Assess Terrain Critical Routes
q: Western US depressurization strategy?
a: Fly the charted decompression polygon escape procedure
qOrig: Western U.S. Depressurization Strategy...
detail: FOM 11.2.9 covers the western high-terrain depressurization strategy: polygons show where a direct descent to 10,000 ft is not possible before passenger oxygen depletes.
quote:
Decompression polygon procedures provide a calculated safe method for descending to 10,000 ft
before passenger oxygen supplies are depleted following a rapid decompression over high terrain.
note: Polygons live on the Jeppesen FD Pro IFR High/Low charts; click the polygon label to open the detail drawer. The three escape types are Exit Any Dir, Exit Twd <fix>, and To Fix then Route.

group: APU In-Flight Start Program (APU component currency)
q: What release items matter for the APU in-flight start program?
a: The APU Administrative Control Item and any conflicting MEL items
qOrig: What items on the dispatch release must you take note of when planning an APU In-Flight Start Program...
detail: Per FOM 12.4.12.5, a Maintenance request for an APU in-flight start is issued as an Administrative Control Item (ACI) found in Section 05 of the fleet MEL, and that ACI is reflected on the Dispatch Release.
ref: FOM 12.4.12.5 Maintenance Requests / FOM 6.5.6 APU In-Flight Start Program (HA)
quote:
These requests will be in the form of an Administrative Control Item (ACI) as found in Section 05
of the fleet MEL. The associated ACI will be applied to the aircraft and will be reflected on the
Dispatch Release.
note: The ACI comes from Section 05 of the fleet MEL. Crew is also notified by an open item on the MIC sheet and a placard card (form HAL-46-1333) in the AML per FOM 6.5.6.

group: APU In-Flight Start Program (APU component currency)
q: How does that differ from the APU in-flight start program?
a: EVF confirms a specific repair; the start program is routine currency
qOrig: How does this differ from the APU In-Flight Start Program?
detail: FOM 6.5.10 defines an EVF as a flight where the crew assists Maintenance in confirming an ETOPS Significant System works normally or that an ETOPS significant problem has been fixed, and Maintenance makes an AML release entry the crew must verbally acknowledge with Dispatch.
ref: FOM 6.5.10 ETOPS Verification Flight (HA) vs FOM 6.5.6 APU In-Flight Start Program (HA)
quote:
An ETOPS Verification Flight (EVF) is a revenue or non-revenue flight during which the Flight Crew
is asked to assist Maintenance to confirm that an ETOPS Significant System is operating normally or
that an ETOPS significant problem has been resolved.
note: EVF adds a required report to Dispatch between 30 and 60 minutes after takeoff and before the EEP; if the item is not operating normally the flight may not proceed past the EEP. The APU In-Flight Start Program has no such Dispatch report requirement.

group: Verification flight vs APU in-flight start program
q: What do you log during the APU start?
a: Flight level, outside air temperature, attempts, result, seconds to available.
qOrig: What items must be logged/noted during the APU start?
detail: The Captain writes the result in the logbook in a set format: flight level and outside air temperature at the attempt, the number of attempts, the word successful or unsuccessful, and the seconds from start sequence to APU available. Successful means it started within three attempts. List any discrepancies if it failed.
quote:
APU IN-FLIGHT START
     FL ___ (flight level during start attempt)
     OAT ___°C (Outside Air Temperature)
note: Shut the APU down after start or takeoff, let it cold soak at least two hours at cruise, then attempt the start in the hour before top of descent.

group: Verification flight vs APU in-flight start program
q: What goes in the logbook after the flight?
a: No Items, Info to Maintenance, or a discrepancy, plus signature.
qOrig: What items must be entered into the maintenance logbook after flight completion?
detail: If you are done with the airplane, the Captain closes out the logbook. Record No Items, Info to Maintenance, or the mechanical discrepancy, then sign and add your employee number on the proper lines. Info to Maintenance is information only, so never use it to preface a real discrepancy.
quote:
This can be accomplished by recording “No Items,” “Info to Maintenance,” or a mechanical
discrepancy as appropriate and entering their signature and employee number on the appropriate
lines.
note: Date entries by current GMT wherever you are, one discrepancy per block, and leave the Action Taken column alone.

group: Verification flight vs APU in-flight start program
q: What aircraft currency items are the ACIs?
a: Max thrust takeoff, autoland, and APU in-flight start.
qOrig: What A/C Currency Items are listed in the “Administrative Control Items” (ACI’s)?
detail: Maintenance asks for these through an Administrative Control Item in Section 05 of the MEL, and it shows up on the release. Typical requests are a max thrust takeoff, an autoland, or an APU in flight start.
note: A completed item can still appear on a later release that was built before you finished it. That is normal, not a second request.

group: Verification flight vs APU in-flight start program
q: How many start attempts are allowed?
a: Three
qOrig: How many start attempts can be made?
detail: FOM 6.5.6 allows a maximum of three start attempts; a start within three attempts is successful. The first attempt is made during the 1-hour period prior to top of descent after at least a two-hour cold soak at ETOPS cruise altitude, and follow-on attempts may be flown at lower altitude but no lower than FL270.
quote:
• If the APU starts within the maximum allowed three attempts, the start is deemed to be
  successful.
note: If the first attempt fails, subsequent attempts may be made at lower altitudes, minimum FL270. FOM 5.1.8.1 uses the same three-attempt rule to define an APU start failure.

group: Flight crew actions prior to the EEP
q: What steps are required?
a: ETOPS alternate forecast at crew minima; complete ETOPS verification checks
qOrig: What steps are required?
detail: FOM 6.3.2 lists what is required before crossing the EEP. For the 787 the two that apply are forecast weather at the ETOPS alternate at or above the operating crew's minima (accounting for crew minima and any MEL), and completion of any ETOPS verification flight checks.
ref: FOM 6.3.2 Flight Crew Duties, Prior to Crossing ETOPS Entry Point (EEP)
quote:
• Forecast weather at the ETOPS alternate must be at or above crew’s operating minima (this is
  the weather required for the operating crew to conduct the approach, given the crew’s minima
  and any applicable MEL).
note: Applicable items are CAT II and CAT III, RNAV, GPS, RNP and RNP AR currency, plus autoland and APU in flight start when Maintenance asks. Check the release for the request before you plan the leg.

group: Flight crew actions prior to the EEP
q: How is the EEP determined and shown to the crew?
a: 60 minutes from an adequate airport, 410 nm; listed on the release
qOrig: How is the EEP determined and depicted to the flight crew?
detail: Per FOM 6.3.3 the EEP is the point 60 minutes from an adequate airport at the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in still air under standard conditions; for the 787 that is 410 nm (FOM 6.2.3 ETOPS Area of Operations table). The EXP is the same fixed distance on the way out.
ref: FOM 6.3.3 ETOPS Entry/Exit Point/Equal Time Point
quote:
When approaching the ETOPS area of operation, the aircraft reaches the ETOPS Entry Point (EEP)
when it is 60 minutes from the adequate airport.
note: 787 60-minute distance is 410 nm at.84M/290 KIAS per the FOM 6.2.3 table. Adequate airports defining EEP/EXP must be listed on the Dispatch Release, and crew and Dispatch must use the same ones.

group: Flight crew actions prior to the EEP
q: Max diversion distance for ETOPS 120 and 180?
a: 806 nm at 120 minutes, 1207 nm at 180 minutes
qOrig: What is the maximum diversion distance, ETOPS 120? ETOPS 180?
detail: Table 6.2.3(1) in FOM 6.2.3 lists the 787 at.84M/290 KIAS single engine speed, giving 410 nm for 60 minutes, 806 nm for 120 minutes, and 1207 nm for 180 minutes.
ref: FOM 6.2.3 ETOPS Area of Operation, Table 6.2.3(1)
note: Same table gives the 60-minute EEP/EXP distance of 410 nm. These are Maximum Diversion Distances derived from the approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed (FOM 6.2.9).

group: Flight crew actions prior to the EEP
q: ETOPS diversion speed?
a: .84M/290 KIAS, the one-engine-inoperative cruise speed
qOrig: ETOPS Diversion speed?
detail: FOM 6.4.5 ties the ETOPS diversion speed to the approved One-Engine-Inoperative Cruise Speed in FOM 6.2.3, which for the 787 is.84M/290 KIAS. That speed is what the critical fuel scenario, the EEP/EXP distance, and the Maximum Diversion Distance are all built on, so flying materially off it invalidates the fuel plan.
ref: FOM 6.4.5 Diversion Speed Strategy / FOM 6.2.3 ETOPS Area of Operation
quote:
Engine inoperative ETOPS fuel requirements are based upon the approved One-Engine-Inoperative
Cruise Speed (see 6.2.3 – ETOPS Area of Operation), which should be followed in case of a
diversion following an actual engine failure.
note: The Captain may deviate from the planned speed profile after assessing the emergency and fuel remaining. For a two-engine decompression diversion the flight plan one-engine diversion speed or LRC is used when level (FOM 6.4.3).

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: Where is the dangerous goods policy in the FOM?
a: The HAZMAT chapter, under Dangerous Goods
qOrig: Where can the dangerous goods policy be found in the FOM?
detail: Dangerous goods policy lives in FOM Chapter 14, HAZMAT, section 14.1 Dangerous Goods, starting with 14.1.1 Regulatory Compliance (Ops Spec A055, 49 CFR Parts 171-175, IATA DGR). Key subsections for a 787 Captain: 14.1.4 eNOTOC (HA), 14.1.6 Captain Responsibilities (HA), 14.1.8 NOTOC acceptable versions (HA), 14.1.17 rejected shipments (HA), 14.1.20 ICAO ERG drill codes, and 14.1.26 damaged or leaking DG.
quote:
• The Company accepts Dangerous Goods (DG) in accordance with International Air Transport
  Association (IATA) Dangerous Goods Regulations and the domestic Code of Federal Regulations
  (CFR) Title 49.
note: FOM Chapter 14 is titled HAZMAT and section 14.1 is Dangerous Goods, running 14.1.1 through 14.1.28. eNOTOC and HA Captain responsibilities are 14.1.4 and 14.1.6.

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: What is an eNOTOC?
a: The electronic Notice to Captain of dangerous goods, sent by ACARS
qOrig: What is an eNOTOC?
detail: Per FOM 14.1.4 the eNOTOC is the Hawaiian electronic Notice to Captain for dangerous goods, uplinked at departure minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific and international flights and departure minus 15 minutes for inter-island, and it prints automatically.
quote:
The eNOTOC will be sent to the Flight Crew at departure time minus 30 minutes for trans-Pacific
and international flights and at departure time minus 15 minutes for inter-island flights.
note: It prints automatically on all aircraft. Versions per FOM 14.1.8: eNOTOC (primary), hard-copy eNOTOC from the Load Master if ACARS/printer is inop but FM Amadeus works, and HAL Form 902 (freighter DG COMAT only).

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: How do you acknowledge an eNOTOC?
a: Select ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC on the Comm page
qOrig: How do you acknowledge an eNOTOC?
detail: FOM 14.1.6 requires the HA Captain to acknowledge the eNOTOC by selecting ACCEPT* on the MCDU or ACKNOWLEDGE NOTOC on the Comm page, depending on fleet type, which on the 787 means the MFD COMPANY/communications page.
quote:
• Acknowledging the eNOTOC by selecting either “ACCEPT*” on the MCDU or “ACKNOWLEDGE
  NOTOC” on the Comm page (depending on fleet type).
note: Acknowledge the NOTOC on the Comm page. If digital acknowledgment is impossible, acknowledge by voice to Dispatch and note it, because the acknowledgment is the record that you saw the load.

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: How do you fight a lithium battery fire?
a: HALON, then water. Never ice
qOrig: How do you fight a lithium battery fire?
detail: FIGHT THE FIRE with a HALON extinguisher. Water may be used to fight a lithium ION battery fire but should NOT be used on a lithium METAL battery fire. It is very important to prevent the fire spreading to adjacent flammable materials.
ref: FOM 11.1.10.2 PED Fire Containment Bag (Yellow Bag)
quote: AVOID USING ICE to cool the device. Ice will act as an insulator.
note: It may take 15 or more minutes to completely cool the device. REV 125.1: this is the YELLOW bag section, renumbered from 11.1.10.

secTitle: Demonstrate Dangerous Goods Policies and Procedures
q: Where are the cabin lithium battery limits?
a: The Alaska Airlines onboard PED and prohibited-items web pages
qOrig: Where can you find lithium battery type/size limitations to be carried in the cabin?
detail: FOM 13.4 sends you to the alaskaair.com onboard-policies portable electronic devices page and the prohibited-items page for the list of permitted and restricted devices and battery types/sizes.
ref: FOM 13.4 Portable Electronic Devices / FOM 13.4.1 Lithium Batteries in PEDs
quote:
See the list of portable electronic devices that are permitted and restricted on board at:
https://
www.alaskaair.com/content/travel-info/policies/onboard-policies-portable-electronic-devices
and
https://www.
note: The FOM itself does not publish watt-hour numbers; it points to the alaskaair.com PED policy and prohibited-items pages. FOM 13.4.1 gives the carry-on vs checked rules, and 11.1.10 covers the containment bags.

q: Review the ACARS menus and functions
a: Six top level menus reached by the COMM display switch.
qOrig: Review ACARS menus and quiz them on where to find specific functions to demonstrate proficiency.
detail: Push COMM and the main menu gives six picks: ATC, Flight Information, Company, Review, Manager, and New Messages. Flight Information holds clearance, weather and taxi requests. Company holds the airline messages. Review and New Messages gray out when there is nothing to show.
ref: FCOM 5.40.3 MFD Communications Functions, Communications Menus
quote:
Selecting ATC, FLIGHT INFORMATION, COMPANY, REVIEW, MANAGER,
or NEW MESSAGES selection:
note: White text on gray means selectable, cyan on black means inhibited, and three dots after an item mean another menu sits below it.

q: Where is the directory of ACARS functions?
a: The FCOM Communications chapter, MFD Communications Functions
qOrig: Where can you find a list/directory of ACARS FUNCTIONS?
detail: The datalink and ACARS function set is documented in the FCOM communications chapter, under MFD Communications Functions. Its table of contents lists each function by page: communications menus, command key functions, message list, air traffic control datalink and the downlink pages.
ref: FCOM 5.40 Communications - MFD Communications Functions (see 5.TOC table of contents)
quote:
The MFD communications functions are used to control datalink features.
Datalink messages not processed by the FMC are received, accepted, rejected,
reviewed, composed, sent, and printed using communications functions on the
MFD.
note: The Communications chapter table of contents (5.TOC.2 through 5.TOC.4) is the closest thing to a directory: it indexes every menu and page from Communications Menus through Manager Functions and New Messages.

q: Where is the spare ACARS paper?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Where is the spare ACARS paper located on the flight deck?
detail: Neither the FOM nor the FCOM gives a stowage location for spare printer paper. The FOM does make it a flight deck consumable you may replace yourself, with no tools. After you change a roll, make an Info to Maintenance entry so the spare gets restocked.
quote:
Consumable items such as light bulbs, ACARS printer paper, tissue boxes, and trash bags are
provided to the Flight Crew and may be replaced by the Flight Crew when they are expended
during normal operations.

q: Where are the instructions to change ACARS paper?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Where are the instructions on how to change the ACARS paper?
detail: No paper loading steps appear in the FOM or the FCOM. The FCOM gives you the hardware only: a cover release lever that opens the printer cover, a paper door lever, and a slew switch that advances paper. The PAPER light means out of paper or the loading door open.
quote:
(HA) If ACARS printer paper is replaced, the Flight Crew should enter an “Info to Maintenance”
logbook entry to ensure spare printer paper is restocked.

secTitle: [PM] Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
group: Procedure selection, waypoint coding, navigation performance
q: Diversion. How do you select a new destination?
a: Select the airport on the FMS alternates page, then DIVERT NOW
qOrig: Diversion Procedures/Select New Destination...
detail: Go to the alternates page on the control display unit, put the airport in the selected slot, then push DIVERT NOW. That builds a route from present position to that airport. Look it over and change what you need, then execute. Executing changes the destination and drops the rest of the old route.
ref: FCOM 11.43.27 FMC Descent and Approach, Alternates Page
quote:
Selecting DIVERT NOW displays the route from the present position to the
selected alternate using the route displayed on the XXXX ALTN page for the
diversion airport.
note: The divert also deletes any existing descent constraints. Read the modified route before you execute, because everything from the old route that is not part of the diversion goes away.

secTitle: [PM] Demonstrate Ability to Correctly Program Aircraft Guidance Systems Including Approach
group: Procedure selection, waypoint coding, navigation performance
q: What is the alternate navigation system?
a: TCP backup navigation after loss of all displays or all FMCs
qOrig: Alternate Navigation System...
detail: FCOM 11.50 describes the alternate navigation system as a backup capability hosted in the Tuning and Control Panels, reached by pushing the NAV key on any TCP; on standby power only the left (Captain's) TCP works. It runs two pages, ALTN NAV and ALTN NAV RADIO.
ref: FCOM 11.50.1 Flight Management, Navigation - Alternate Navigation System Description
quote:
In the unlikely event that an unrecoverable loss of all displays or loss of all three
FMCs occurs, a backup navigation capability is available through the Tuning and
Control Panel (TCP).
note: Push NAV on any of the three TCPs under normal power; on standby power only the Captain's left TCP is available. LNAV and VNAV are lost, but autopilot and autothrottles may still be available.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are fuel conservation considerations?
a: Green Policy; green-symbol fuel efficiency items appear throughout
qOrig: Where can you find the Fuel Conservation considerations in the FOM?
detail: FOM 1.6.3 Green Policy establishes that green-symbol guidance supports Alaska Air Group's fuel efficiency commitment, with the explicit safety is always first and fuel saving measures must never compromise safety.
quote: operational decisions that align with Alaska Air Group’s commitment to fuel efficiency.
note: No section titled Fuel Conservation exists in the FOM. The guidance is marked by a green symbol wherever it applies: single engine taxi in the taxi guidance, cruise and optimum altitude, and route deviation and optimization.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Flight deck door procedure with no flight attendants?
a: Yes. Captain covers cabin duties; door closed, critical phases
qOrig: Are there special Flight Deck Door Procedure on Flights with No Flight Attendants?
detail: FOM 16.1.11 states that when Flight Attendants are not on board a Company-operated flight, the Captain must ensure the cabin duties normally done by F/As are accomplished, and refers to fleet-specific manuals for procedures. The WARNING requires galley carts to be properly secured and the Flight Deck Door closed during critical phases of flight.
ref: FOM 16.1.11 Pilot Duties With No Flight Attendants
quote: properly secured and the Flight Deck Door is closed during critical phases of flight.
note: FOM 15.2.6.2 sends you to Pilot Duties With No Flight Attendants at 16.1.11, which then refers to the fleet manuals for the actual procedure.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are the US holding speeds?
a: 200 knots below 6000 ft, 230 to 14,000, 265 above
qOrig: Where can you find the holding speeds (FAR) in USA?
detail: At or below 6000 ft hold at 200 knots or less. Above 6000 ft through 14,000 ft the limit is 230 knots. Above 14,000 ft it is 265 knots. Inbound leg is one minute at or below 14,000 ft and one and a half minutes above.
quote:
Altitude                    Maximum Airspeed                    Time (Inbound Leg)

       6000 ft or below                       200 KIAS

         Above 6000 ft                        230 KIAS                           1 minute

       Through 14,000 ft                     (210 KIAS)*

        Above 14,000 ft                       265 KIAS                         1 1/2 minutes
note: Charts marked 210K in Alaska or New York hold you to 210 knots above 6000 through 14,000 ft, except the Anchorage and Fairbanks approach control areas. Pattern protection assumes 280 knots or Mach 0.8, whichever is lower.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are international holding speeds?
a: ICAO Doc 8168 and the theater chapters
qOrig: Where can you find international country-specific holding speeds?
detail: FOM 5.5.15 cites AIM 5-3-8 and ICAO Doc 8168. Country-specific holding speeds and procedures appear in the theater chapters 19 through 24 and in the Jeppesen country pages, for example the Heathrow holding restriction in the Europe chapter.
quote:
ICAO DOC 8168

Flights anticipating holding at an enroute fix or flights that have not received clearance beyond a
fix should begin a speed reduction no earlier than three minutes prior to reaching such fix.
note: Rev 125.1 renumbering: the United Kingdom chapter is 23.17 with LHR subsections under 23.17.1, and Italy is 23.18.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are TCAS procedures in the FOM?
a: TCAS Policy, in the Operating - General chapter
qOrig: Where can you find TCAS procedures in the FOM?
