detail: FOM 2.3.17 TCAS Policy is the FOM home for TCAS. It requires compliance with an RA unless the pilot considers it unsafe, prohibits maneuvering opposite an RA unless visually determined to be the only means of safe separation, and reminds crews the aircraft in sight may not be the intruder.
quote:
Compliance with a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) is required, unless the pilot considers it unsafe
to do so.
note: The FOM carries policy only. The actual maneuver is the QRH recall item Traffic Avoidance (QRH MAN.1.5), and the system description is FCOM 15.20.17. Oceanic TCAS guidance is at FOM 5.7 (TA/RA mode whenever possible).

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What is a TA?
a: Traffic advisory: traffic predicted to conflict in 20-48 seconds
qOrig: What is an “TA”?
detail: Per FCOM 15.20.18, a Traffic Advisory predicts another airplane entering the conflict airspace in 20 to 48 seconds, and exists to help the crew get visual contact. Indications are the amber ND message TRAFFIC plus a single 'TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC' voice annunciation; No PFD/HUD vertical guidance for a TA.
quote:
A TA is a prediction that another airplane will enter the conflict airspace in 20 to
48 seconds.
note: A TA gets an amber TRAFFIC message on the ND and one 'TRAFFIC, TRAFFIC' aural, no vertical guidance. TA symbol is a filled amber circle (amber circle with black chevron for ADS-B traffic).

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What is an RA?
a: Resolution advisory: conflict predicted in about 15-35 seconds
qOrig: What is an “RA”?
detail: FCOM 15.20.18 defines an RA as a prediction that another airplane will enter the TCAS conflict airspace within approximately 15 to 35 seconds; without altitude data from the intruder, no RA can be generated.
quote:
An RA is a prediction that another airplane will enter the TCAS conflict airspace
within approximately 15 to 35 seconds.
note: No RA is possible if the intruder is not reporting altitude. RA gives a red ND TRAFFIC message, a voice annunciation, and PFD/HUD vertical guidance; the symbol is a filled red square.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What is a phantom TA?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: What is Phantom TA?
detail: The term phantom traffic advisory appears nowhere in the FOM, FCOM or QRH, so No company definition to recite. What the FOM does warn about is the related trap: the airplane you can see out the window may not be the one the system is alerting on. Do not brief a definition you cannot source.
quote:
Flight Crews are cautioned that the aircraft in visual contact may
not necessarily be the intruder aircraft causing the TCAS RA.
note: The traffic surveillance description in the FCOM covers how targets are built from transponder and ADS-B data, but it never uses that phrase either.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are the TCAS symbology definitions?
a: FCOM Warning Systems chapter, TCAS traffic display pages
qOrig: Where can you find TCAS symbology definitions?
detail: Symbol definitions are in FCOM Chapter 15 Warning Systems: the annotated display legend at 15.10.16-15.10.17 and the same set described in prose at 15.20.17-15.20.19. TCAS-only traffic uses a filled red square for an RA, a filled amber circle for a TA, a filled white diamond for proximate traffic, and an unfilled white diamond for other traffic.
ref: FCOM 15.10.16 TCAS Traffic and Alert Message TRAFFIC Display
quote: filled red square indicates a resolution advisory (RA)
note: Controls and Indicators at 15.10.13-15.10.20 has the annotated ND picture and symbol legend; the narrative repeat is in System Description at 15.20.17-15.20.19. ADS-B (In) symbology is separate, at FCOM 10.40.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What is MedLink?
a: Contract ER physicians giving 24-hour inflight medical advice
qOrig: What is MedLink?
detail: FOM 11.1.9.1 describes MedLink as emergency room physicians available 24 hours a day with aviation-specific experience, providing recommendations on onboard medical issues, and notes contact with MedLink removes Company liability for passenger health.
quote:
MedLink utilizes emergency room physicians 24 hours a day to provide crewmembers with
informed recommendations regarding on-board medical issues.
note: Company policy is to follow MedLink's recommendation, but the Captain keeps final authority on operational requests. The one-way exception: if MedLink says a passenger is not fit to fly, the Captain will not override MedLink.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: When do you contact MedLink?
a: Any medical support need, aircraft oxygen use, fitness-to-fly doubt
qOrig: When should you contact MedLink?
detail: FOM 11.1.9.2 makes MedLink contact mandatory, except during critical phases of flight, for any medical situation where the crew requires support or advice, any passenger or crew use of aircraft oxygen, and any uncertainty about whether a passenger is contagious or physically fit to fly (see 11.1.8.2 Communicable Diseases).
quote: MedLink shall be contacted for the following, except during critical phases of flight:
note: Note the carve-out: not during critical phases of flight (sterile flight deck per 2.3.12). Passenger or crew use of aircraft oxygen is a mandatory trigger even if the person seems fine.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Who contacts MedLink on the ground?
a: CSA at the gate; after door close, F/As or crew
qOrig: Who is responsible for contacting MedLink while on the ground?
detail: FOM 11.1.9.3 On Ground has the Flight Crew, F/As, station personnel, and MedLink work together to decide fitness to fly, and requires MedLink contact to clear a passenger even if paramedics already responded. At the gate or prior to door closure the CSA should initiate contact, and may deplane the passenger for privacy while assessing fitness to fly.
ref: FOM 11.1.9.3 Responsibility for Contacting MedLink - On Ground
quote: The CSA should initiate contact with MedLink.
note: After door closure and after landing the split is by equipment: with operational broadband or a SATCOM cabin device the F/As initiate; without it the Flight Crew initiates. Advise Operations if medical assistance is expected at the gate.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Who contacts MedLink in flight?
a: F/As if cabin SATCOM works; otherwise the Flight Crew
qOrig: Who is responsible for contacting MedLink while in flight?
detail: Per FOM 11.1.9.3 In Flight, on HA aircraft with available and operational cabin SATCOM handsets the F/As advise the Flight Crew and then call MedLink directly; if the cabin device is unavailable, the Flight Crew initiates.
ref: FOM 11.1.9.3 Responsibility for Contacting MedLink - In Flight
quote: On aircraft with operational SATCOM handsets in the cabin, the F/As call MedLink directly.
note: MedLink is reached directly, with Dispatch conferenced in when a diversion looks possible. Get the flight attendants gathering vitals while you set up the call, so the doctor has data on first contact.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Do you call MedLink direct or Dispatch first?
a: Directly. Dispatch is conferenced in if diversion possible
qOrig: Do we as flight crew contact MedLink directly, or do we call dispatch first?
detail: FOM 11.1.9.3 has you go to MedLink first, not Dispatch. With operational cabin SATCOM the F/As call MedLink directly; with SATCOM but no cabin handset the 787 Flight Crew calls MedLink directly at (602) 282-4910 and conferences the F/As on the cabin headset.
ref: FOM 11.1.9.3 Responsibility for Contacting MedLink - In Flight
quote:
The Flight Crew will call MedLink. MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance may be reached at
     (602) 282-4910.
note: Only with no operational SATCOM does the call route through a relay: ARINC patch, or Dispatch if ARINC fails. Dispatch always gets notified for a potential diversion, either by MedLink conferencing them in or by you calling after.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: How do you make a MedLink call from the aircraft?
a: SATCOM to (602) 282-4910, or ARINC phone patch
qOrig: How do you make a MedLink call from the aircraft?
detail: Per FOM 11.1.9.3, the 787 primary method is a SATCOM call to MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance at (602) 282-4910, with the Flight Crew conferencing in the F/As using the cabin headset.
ref: FOM 11.1.9.3 Responsibility for Contacting MedLink - In Flight
quote: The Flight Crew will contact ARINC for a patch to MedLink Inflight Medical Assistance at (602)
note: On the 787 conference the F/As in on the cabin headset so the physician talks to the person with eyes on the patient. Ground Medical Assistance is (602) 282-6613 or (800) 961-4847; the (AS) number listed elsewhere in Ch 11 is (602) 282-4967.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Medical event on an international flight. Any special notifications?
a: Yes. General Declaration entry; Australia notified 30 minutes before landing
qOrig: If on an international flight, are there special procedures/notifications that must be made by the flight...
detail: FOM 18.1.15 uses the US Public Health Service 'ill person' definition: temperature of 100F (38C) or greater persisting more than 48 hours; fever with rash, swollen glands, jaundice, persistent cough, vomiting, difficulty breathing, muscle pain, headache with stiff neck, decreased consciousness, or unexplained bleeding; or persistent diarrhea.
ref: FOM 18.1.15 Death or Illness Reporting - International
quote:
For Flights to Australia: The Captain must report to the Australian authorities the presence on
board the aircraft of any apparent death or any ill person among passengers or crew at least 30
minutes before landing.
note: The General Declaration requirement applies to countries other than the US and Canada. For a suspected communicable disease inbound to the US, 11.1.8.2 adds the CDC/public health authority path, usually conferenced in by MedLink or set up through Dispatch.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What are icing conditions?
a: OAT or TAT 10C or below with visible moisture/contamination
qOrig: What is definition of icing conditions?
detail: FCOM SP.16.1 defines icing conditions as OAT on the ground or TAT in flight of 10C or below, plus either visible moisture (clouds, fog with visibility of one statute mile / 1600 m or less, rain, snow, sleet, ice crystals) or ice, snow, slush, or standing water on the ramps, taxiways, or runways.
quote: Icing conditions exist when OAT (on the ground) or TAT (in-flight) is 10°C
note: Two-part test: temperature AND either visible moisture (including fog with visibility 1 SM / 1600 m or less) or ice, snow, slush, or standing water on ramps, taxiways, or runways. Note the ground/air split: OAT on the ground, TAT in flight.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are the aircraft de-ice and anti-ice procedures?
a: FCOM Supplementary Procedures, Adverse Weather; company deicing in FODM
qOrig: Where do you find the aircraft de/anti-Ice procedures?
detail: FCOM SP.16 Cold Weather Operations carries the airplane procedures: Preliminary Preflight, Exterior Inspection, Engine Start, Engine Anti-ice Operation On the Ground (SP.16.4), De-icing / Anti-icing (SP.16.6), Fan Ice Removal (SP.16.8), Wing Anti-ice Operation In-flight (SP.16.8), Cold Temperature Altitude Corrections (SP.16.10), and the cold weather Secure Procedure.
ref: FCOM SP.3.1 Anti-Ice Operation, referring to SP.16 Cold Weather Operations
quote:
Note: (Refer to Cold Weather Operations in Chapter SP, Section 16, for
      additional information.
note: Split the question: airplane anti-ice system operation is FCOM SP.16 (SP.3 covers only windshield washer/wiper). Ground deicing/anti-icing fluid, holdover times, and the contamination check are FODM and the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual, per FOM 9.3.1 and 16.2.9.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are airport specific deice procedures?
a: FODM and the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual
qOrig: Where do you find specific airport deice procedures?
detail: FOM 16.2.9 states plainly that all deice procedures are found in the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual and the FODM, with the Deicing Procedures Manual available through Maintenance Control.
quote: All deice procedures are found in the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual and the FODM .
note: Verified only to this level: the FOM contains no airport-specific deice pages, and states all deice procedures live in the FODM (on the EFB) and the ASA Deicing Procedures Manual, which is obtained or reviewed through Maintenance Control.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: When must engine anti-ice be on?
a: Whenever icing conditions exist or are anticipated, above -40C
qOrig: When are you required to turn the engine anti-ice on?
detail: FCOM SP.16.7 requires engine anti-ice AUTO or ON during all flight operations when icing conditions exist or are anticipated, except below -40C SAT. SP.16.4 requires it selected ON and left on for all ground operations in the same conditions, except below -40C OAT, and confirms EAI shows on the primary engine display for both engines.
ref: FCOM SP.16.7 Engine Anti-ice Operation - In-flight (and SP.16.4, On the Ground)
quote:
Engine anti-ice must be AUTO or ON during all flight operations when
 icing conditions exist or are anticipated, except when the temperature is
 below -40°C SAT.
note: Ground and air differ: on the ground it must be selected ON (manual) and remain on, in flight AUTO or ON satisfies the requirement. Cutoff is -40C OAT on the ground, -40C SAT in flight; do not use above 10C OAT/TAT.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: When must wing anti-ice be on?
a: AUTO normally; select ON manually when wing icing possible
qOrig: When are you required to turn on the wing de/anti-ice...
detail: FCOM SP.16.8 says the wing anti-ice system is mainly used to prevent icing in flight, with the primary method being the automatic ice detection system controlling it throughout the flight envelope for the cleanest airfoil, least runback ice, and least thrust and fuel penalty.
ref: FCOM SP.16.8 Wing Anti-ice Operation - In-flight
quote:
The secondary method is to select the WING ANTI-ICE selector ON
 when wing icing is possible and use for anti-icing.
note: Wing anti-ice is primarily an in-flight system and is inhibited on the ground below 75 knots (FCOM 30.20). Do not use it above 10C displayed TAT. Ice on window frames, windshield center post, wiper arm, or side windows is the cue for structural icing.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Discuss the SureWx app
a: In the SureWx guide and the FOM
qOrig: Discuss SureWx app...
detail: SureWx holdover-time workflow is vendor material. The governing policy is the pretakeoff contamination check requirement. Verify the app steps in the SureWx guide and the de-icing policy in FOM Chapter 9 and the fleet cold weather supplement.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Where are cold weather procedures?
a: Weather chapter, the fleet manuals, and the FODM deicing manual
qOrig: Where can you find the cold weather procedures in the FOM? Any other manual?
detail: The FOM does not list cold weather steps. It sends you to the fleet books and to the FODM, which carries the deicing procedures, holdover times and the post-deicing check. For the 787 the procedure itself is in FCOM Supplementary Procedures, Cold Weather Operations.
quote: Comply with the cold weather procedures in the fleet-specific manuals and FODM.
note: The Weather chapter still owns the policy side: icing intensity definitions, adverse weather restrictions and liquid water equivalent holdover times. Cold weather approach restrictions and altitude corrections point back to the fleet manuals.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Review QRH procedures without moving switches
a: Open the electronic checklist, then select CHKL OVRD
qOrig: Review QRH procedures without moving any switch positions (when time permits). This reviews the...
detail: Opening a non-normal checklist to read it makes that checklist active. When you finish reading, press CHKL OVRD at the bottom of the page before you close the electronic checklist or move to another one. That forces it back to inactive. No switch has to move to do this.
ref: QRH CI.2.2 Checklist Instructions, Using CHKL OVRD
quote:
If the flight crew decides not to do the checklist, select the CHKL OVRD key on
the bottom of the checklist page before closing ECL and before selecting another
checklist.
note: Do not use CHKL OVRD if you only want to pause and finish later. Close the page or go to another checklist and it stays active in the queue. Override also wipes collected notes, checklist inhibits and deferred items.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Terrain polygons with no own-ship position on the EFB?
a: Not published in our manuals. Ask the check airman.
qOrig: Consider techniques for terrain polygons without own-ship position on the EFB...
detail: The FOM tells you the polygons live on the Jeppesen high and low charts and what each escape type means, but it gives no technique for using them when the chart will not show your own position. Sort out a method with your check airman before you need it.
quote:
Polygons are located in the IFR High and IFR Low charts in Jeppesen FD Pro and denote areas
of high terrain where a descent directly to 10,000 ft may not be possible.
note: The one workaround of this kind the FOM does publish is for the area of magnetic unreliability: drop a waypoint on the charted border, then display those coordinates on the navigation display through FIX INFO.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Terrain polygon vs ETP considerations?
a: ETPs are calculated at 10,000 ft, the polygon descent target
qOrig: Terrain polygon procedure vs ETP considerations (example: ETP is usually west of Greenland and BIKF is...
detail: The polygon answers how to get down safely over high terrain. The equal time point answers which airport is shortest in time. They meet at 10,000 ft, since that is the altitude the equal time points are built on. Terrain drives the descent path first, then you settle the airport with Dispatch.
quote: ETPs are calculated using flight performance and winds at 10,000 ft.
note: Equal time points come from planning-time winds, so treat them as a start point. The FOM expects you to weigh weather, visibility, ATC and grid minimum off-route altitudes, and it lets you pick a closer airport that is not a designated ETOPS alternate.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: When do you use the HDG REF switch?
a: When assigned a heading where true north is used
qOrig: AMU, when do you use the HDG REF switch?
detail: FCOM SP.10.1 is blunt: use TRUE when assigned a heading in a region where true north is used, and NORM in all other regions.
ref: FCOM SP.10.1 Supplementary Procedures - Flight Instruments, Displays (Heading Reference Switch Operation)
quote:
Use TRUE when assigned a heading in a region where true north is used.
Use NORM in all other regions.
note: The 787 switches to true automatically in the polar regions with HEADING REF in NORM (FCOM 11.31, FMC Polar Operations), so TRUE is a manual selection you make for an ATC-assigned true heading, e.g. inside the AMU (FOM 22.2.3).

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: How do you identify the OEP?
a: Named waypoint on or near the FIR boundary entering the OCA
qOrig: How do you identify the OEP?
detail: FOM 22.2.2 defines the OEP as the waypoint from which RCL time estimates are calculated, generally a named waypoint on or near the FIR boundary where the aircraft enters an OCA.
quote:
The OEP is the waypoint from which Request for Clearance (RCL) time estimates are typically
calculated (e.g., “X” minutes prior to OEP via data link). It is generally a named waypoint located
on or near the FIR boundary where an aircraft enters an OCA.
note: If the route has no waypoint sitting on the OCA boundary, the OEP backs up to the last named waypoint before it; on random routing it is the last named waypoint before the first LAT/LONG inside the OCA.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Entering the GOTA eastbound. Is an RCL required?
a: Yes, to Gander Oceanic
qOrig: When entering the GOTA eastbound, are you required to send an RCL?
detail: FOM 22.2.1 states that transition areas (GOTA, NOTA, SOTA, BOTA) are buffers between domestic and oceanic airspace, are not part of the OCAs, and leave aircraft under domestic ATC control - GOTA under Gander or Montreal, NOTA and SOTA under Shannon Domestic, BOTA under Brest Domestic.
quote:
transition area. Also, eastbound flights through the GOTA are to send an RCL message to Gander
Oceanic. For specific transition area rules and exceptions, see the FIR card and Operational Notes
in Jeppesen FD Pro by selecting the airspace.
note: This is a named exception. The GOTA is not part of the Gander OCA and stays under Gander or Montreal Center control, yet you still send the RCL to Gander Oceanic.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: NUUK FIR. Who controls what, and what do you do?
a: Nuuk owns it; fly Reykjavik OCA north, Gander OCA south
qOrig: NUUK FIR: Owned by Nuuk but controlled by Gander South of N6330 and Reykjavik to the North. What are...
detail: FOM 22.4 makes the ownership-versus-control distinction operational: in North Atlantic operations CPDLC and ADS coverage is based on Oceanic Control Areas, not FIRs, and the logon must be directed to the controlling authority for the relevant OCA regardless of which FIRs you transit.
quote:
For example, the north section of the Nuuk FIR is in the Reykjavik OCA, but the south section of the
Nuuk FIR is in the Gander OCA. CPDLC should sequence and a new SELCAL check is required.
note: The practical action is the SELCAL check: CPDLC coverage in the NAT follows OCAs, not FIRs, so crossing inside one FIR you still change controlling OCA, CPDLC re-sequences, and a new SELCAL check is required on the new HF frequencies.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 6.3.41: "the pilot should log on to the appropriate FIR 10
        to 25 minutes prior to the boundary" ICAO gives the generic logon timing; the company chapter names the controlling OCA for the Nuuk FIR.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Can you cross the NAT-HLA without HF?
a: No. At least one HF radio is required
qOrig: Can you Fly across the NAT-HLA without HF radios? If so, how?
detail: FOM 22.4.3 requires two independent LRCS outside VHF coverage in the NAT, one of which must be HF. FOM 22.1.10 lists the NAT HLA equipment as dual IRS, dual long range nav with two MCDUs, dual NDs, one GPS receiver, ADS-C, CPDLC, SATCOM data link, and two HF radios or a single HF radio and SATVOICE.
quote:
Operations in the NAT outside of VHF coverage require aircraft to be equipped with two
independent Long Range Communications Systems (LRCS), one of which must be HF.
note: Cross-check FOM 7.1.8, which lists the only two NAT HLA ETOPS dispatch options: 2 HF radios plus SATDATA/CPDLC, or 1 HF plus SATDATA/CPDLC plus SATVOICE. Both contain HF. FOM 22.1.10's note softens it only after departure: a single HF radio and SATCOM data link.
icao: NAT Doc 007 4.2.12: "When operating outside of VHF coverage the carriage of fully functioning HF is mandatory" ICAO matches the company rule that HF is required to cross the NAT outside VHF coverage.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: GPS jamming reporting requirements?
a: Report to ATC; file a safety report
qOrig: GPS Jamming reporting requirements.
detail: FOM 5.1.21.3 says GPS/GNSS disruptions cluster around conflict zones, military operations areas and counter-UAS protection areas, and directs the crew to report any GPS/GNSS malfunction to ATC and submit a safety report for the listed discrepancies.
quote:
Report any GPS/GNSS malfunction to ATC. Submit a safety report for any of the following
discrepancies or anomalies:
note: The safety report is required for any of five listed anomalies: inability to use GPS for navigation, loss of RNAV/RNP capability, unreliable EGPWS triggering, inaccurate position on the ND, and loss of or erroneous ADS-B outputs (FOM 5.1.21.3). Background on the threat is in 5.1.21.2.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 9.1.10: "Flight crews should inform ATC of any GNSS
      malfunction. ATC aircraft separation minimums may be affected by the GNSS malfunction." ICAO matches the report to ATC; the safety report is a company addition.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: How and when do you request an RCL?
a: ACARS data link; Gander 60-90 min, Shanwick 30-90 min prior OEP
qOrig: How do you request an RCL and when?
detail: FOM 22.6.1 is the reason the RCL still exists: except for Shanwick, oceanic clearances are no longer issued in North Atlantic OCAs, but the RCL message is still required for every other OCA except New York East.
quote:
• Gander: 60-90 minutes. Flights departing from airports less than 45 minutes flying time from
  the OEP should send the RCL 10 minutes prior to start-up.
• Shanwick: 30-90 minutes.
note: Santa Maria is at least 40 minutes, Bodo at least 20 (FOM 22.6.4). Go to voice only if ACARS is inop, you get RCL REJECTED, or nothing comes back within 15 minutes (FOM 22.6.3). Shanwick telephone fallback is 01294-655100.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What is your oceanic exit point?
a: Flight specific; the point re-entering domestic airspace
qOrig: What is your oceanic Exit point?
detail: FOM 22.1.6 identifies the Oceanic Exit Point (OXP) as the point of re-entry into domestic airspace, and directs crews to request Normal Speed via CPDLC or voice after it when ATC has assigned a fixed Mach.
ref: FOM 22.1.6 Mach Number Technique and Cost Index (ECON)
quote:
When ATC assigns a fixed Mach number in Oceanic Airspace, crews should request Normal Speed
(via CPDLC or voice) after the Oceanic Exit Point (OXP) upon re-entry into domestic airspace.
note: The OXP is taken off your flight plan, not defined in the FOM.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 6.3.61: "If ATC assigns a fixed Mach number in oceanic airspace, request NORMAL SPEED (via
        CPDLC or voice) after the OXP in Domestic airspace." ICAO matches the company procedure for resuming ECON after the OXP.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Initial call to Gander or Shanwick. Exact words?
a: Callsign, SELCAL check, and the next OCA
qOrig: What does your initial call to Gander or Shanwick on VHF or HF require? (Exact verbiage (not RCL call))
detail: FOM 22.4 publishes the model call for an eastbound flight entering the Gander OCA: Gander Radio, Alaska 123, SELCAL Check, Shanwick Next. The response format shown is Alaska 123, Gander Radio, HF Primary and Secondary, at 30W contact Shanwick Radio HF Primary and Secondary.
quote:
Example (Initial contact from an eastbound flight entering GANDER OCA):
“Gander Radio, Alaska 123, SELCAL Check, Shanwick Next.
note: Expect the reply to hand you HF primary and secondary frequencies plus the next transfer point, e.g. at 30W contact Shanwick Radio. A new SELCAL check is required before entering each individual OCA, not each FIR (FOM 22.4).
icao: NAT Doc 007 5.1.13: "after the radio operator responds, request a SELCAL check and state the next OCA" ICAO matches the company model call word for word, including the Gander Radio example.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What transponder setting monitors traffic?
a: XPDR or above; that enables ADS-B (In)
qOrig: What should you set your transponder to in order to monitor traffic?
detail: FCOM 11.10 lists the Transponder/TCAS Mode Selector positions. STBY leaves the transponder inactive. ALT RPTG OFF enables modes A and S, disables altitude reporting, enables ADS-B out but disables ADS-B (In).
ref: FCOM 11.10 Flight Management, Navigation - Controls and Indicators (Transponder/TCAS Mode Selector)
quote:
• altitude reporting disabled
  • ADS-B out enabled
  • ADS-B (In) disabled
XPDR (transponder) –
  • transponder enabled in modes A, C, and S
note: ADS-B (In) is disabled in STBY and in ALT RPTG OFF, so anything below XPDR blinds you to traffic.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: When do you request a SELCAL check?
a: After CPDLC logon, before the initial gateway fix
qOrig: When do you request a SELCAL check?
detail: When using CPDLC, contact ARINC after a successful CPDLC logon but prior to the initial Gateway Fix in order to obtain a SELCAL check on HF. This establishes a backup means of communication if CPDLC fails.
quote: Flight Crews must contact ARINC after a successful CPDLC logon, but prior to the initial Gateway Fix in order to obtain a SELCAL check on HF.
note: REV 125.1: if SELCAL is not functioning, one crew member must listen to HF continuously, which is a real workload consideration on a long Pacific crossing.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 5.1.22: "check the operation of the SELCAL equipment, at or prior to entry into oceanic airspace, with
                  the appropriate radio station." The company timing, after CPDLC logon and before the gateway fix, satisfies this ICAO deadline.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Is your ETOPS distance 120 or 180?
a: 180 minutes MDT; as dispatched on the Release
qOrig: What is your ETOPS distance set to? (120 or 180)
detail: FOM 6.2.3 sets the Alaska Airlines authorized Maximum Diversion Time at 180 minutes, computed at one-engine-inoperative cruise speed under standard conditions in still air, and requires the MDT the flight was planned on to be listed in the Dispatch Release.
quote: The Alaska Airlines’ authorized MDT is 180 minutes.
note: MEL-deferred items can knock Hawaiian down to 120 minutes (FOM 6.2.3), so read the Release rather than assuming 180. Table 6.2.3(1) gives the 787 flying distances at.84M/290 KIAS: 410 nm at 60 min, 806 nm at 120 min, 1207 nm at 180 min.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: What are your common ETOPS airports?
a: Those listed on your Flight Plan/Dispatch Release
qOrig: What are your common ETOPS airports?
detail: FOM 6.2.2 defines an ETOPS alternate as an adequate airport listed in FOM 8.1.3 and designated on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release for use in the event of an ETOPS diversion, and it explicitly says this is a flight-planning definition that does not limit PIC authority in flight.
quote:
An ETOPS alternate airport is an adequate airport that is listed in 8.1.3 – Authorized Airports
and is designated on the Flight Plan/Dispatch Release for use in the event of a diversion during
ETOPS.
note: The master list is FOM 8.1.3 - Authorized Airports, where an E in the fleet column means the field may be listed as an ETOPS alternate. Anything coded A, F, R, P or E may also be planned as an adequate airport to define EEP/EXP.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Transition level by ATC. When do you set QNH?
a: Descending through the level the controller or ATIS assigns
qOrig: When do you set QNH when transition level states “by ATC”?
detail: When the chart says the transition level is by air traffic control, the number comes off the ATIS or from the approach controller. Get it early and put it in the descent brief. Set QNH descending through that level. Standard stays set above it, QNH below the transition altitude.
quote:
Transition altitudes are normally charted, while transition levels normally are on either the ATIS or
provided by the approach controller.
note: European transition altitudes and levels are lower than in the United States and vary by country. Settings are normally hectopascals. If a controller gives you QFE, ask for QNH and set it in the normal manner.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Review the airspace around eastbound oceanic entry
a: GOTA transition area, then the Gander OCA
qOrig: Review airspace surrounding Eastbound oceanic entry...
detail: FOM 22.2.1 describes the transition areas adjacent to the major OCAs - GOTA, NOTA, SOTA and BOTA - as buffers that are not part of the OCAs, with aircraft in them remaining under domestic ATC: GOTA under Gander or Montreal Centers, NOTA and SOTA under Shannon Domestic, BOTA under Brest Domestic.
quote:
Transition areas such as the Gander Oceanic Transition Area (GOTA), Northern Oceanic Transition
Area (NOTA), Shannon Oceanic Transition Area (SOTA), and Brest Oceanic Transition Area (BOTA)
note: Two GOTA traps for eastbound entry: OEPs sit in the middle of the airspace so SLOP starts halfway through, and you send the RCL to Gander Oceanic while still talking to a domestic center (FOM 22.2.1).
icao: NAT Doc 007 3.3.12: "Air Traffic service is provided by the Gander ACC, call sign GANDER CENTRE." ICAO confirms GOTA traffic stays with domestic Gander Centre, matching the company description.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Westbound into BIRD at RATSU. Oceanic clearance needed?
a: No. Only Shanwick still issues oceanic clearances
qOrig: Do westbound routes that enter BIRD from Scottish at RATSU need an oceanic clearance?
detail: FOM 22.6.1 states that except for the Shanwick OCA, oceanic clearances are no longer issued in North Atlantic OCAs, and that for all other OCAs the pre-departure clearance serves as the oceanic clearance while the crew still transmits an RCL message as a notification.
ref: FOM 22.6.1 Request for Clearance (RCL) and Oceanic Clearances
quote: Except for the Shanwick OCA, oceanic clearances are no longer issued in North Atlantic OCAs.
note: You still send an RCL message as a notification into Reykjavik; the pre-departure clearance serves as the oceanic clearance.
icao:
NAT Doc 007 6.3.35: "Enroute aircraft shall enter the oceanic airspace in accordance with their existing ATC
        clearance. No oceanic clearance is required." ICAO matches the company answer; a separate note keeps Shanwick issuing clearances until further notice.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Arrival and departure considerations on the Jepps
a: Transition altitude charted; transition level from ATIS or ATC
qOrig: Arrival/Departure considerations – Jepps...
detail: FOM 23.4 lists the ICAO chart and weather differences that bite on arrival and departure: visibility in meters or kilometers, QNH in hectopascals with some fields defaulting to QFE, and transition altitude/level typically low and country-dependent, with STAR charts that may just say TRANS LEVEL: BY ATC.
quote:
• Transition Altitude/Level: Typically, low in Europe and can vary by country. Vigilance is required
  for correct altimeter settings on arrival and departure. STAR charts in Europe may indicate
  "TRANS LEVEL: BY ATC.
note: European transition altitudes run lower than US values and vary by country (FOM 22.1.7, 23.10). Altimeter settings come in hectopascals, visibility in meters or kilometers, and wind speed can be in meters per second. Jeppesen FD Pro search term for this is TRANSITION LEVEL.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: FCO and LHR departures. Who do you call?
a: Clearance delivery; they give your start-up and takeoff slot times
qOrig: Departure considerations – FCO/LHR. Who are you going to call and what are they giving you?
detail: Target Off-Block Time is when the airline says you will be ready to push. Target Start-Up Approval Time comes back from air traffic control and is when to expect pushback and start clearance. Calculated Takeoff Time is your slot, a window from 5 minutes early to 15 minutes late.
quote:
TOBTs and TSATs are communicated through various methods, including docking guidance systems,
clearance delivery, data link, or Operations.
note: Be ready at the off-block time. At Rome you report ready no later than 5 minutes past it or you have to request a new slot. If you cannot make the takeoff time, tell air traffic control as early as you can.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: The ground frequency dance: clearance, ramp, clearance, ground
a: ATC on #1/L VHF, ramp control on #2/R
qOrig: Frequency dance on the ground = Clearance-ramp-clearance-ground...
detail: FOM 7.1.5 assigns #1/L VHF to primary communications including ATC, Tower, Ground, CTAF and Ramp Control; #2/R to monitoring 121.5 or Company in flight and Company on the ground; and #3/C to ACARS. The solves the ground shuffle reads that #2/R VHF may be used for ramp control when transitioning to and from the movement area.
quote: #2/R VHF may be used for ramp control when transitioning to/from the movement area.
note: The base rule puts ATC/Tower/Ground/CTAF/Ramp Control on #1/L, 121.5 or Company on #2/R, and ACARS on #3/C. The note lets you park ramp on #2/R so you can hold clearance or ground on #1/L through the handoffs instead of retuning one radio repeatedly.

secTitle: Know Airplane Shutdown and Securing Procedures
q: Diversion airport considerations. Benefits and pitfalls?
a: Planned ETOPS alternates unless a better one exists
qOrig: Diversion airport considerations - Benefits/pitfalls of which ones are used.
detail: FOM 6.4.1 says the ETOPS alternates picked during flight planning are in some cases the optimum diversion airports, but the Flight Crew in concert with Dispatch may select another if it is more suitable for prevailing operational conditions.
quote:
The Flight Crew, in concert with Dispatch, may select another diversion airport if they determine it
is more suitable based the prevailing operational conditions.
note: The pitfall is in FOM 6.2.1's caution: an adequate airport may not be appropriate for an ETOPS diversion because it may lack rescue and firefighting support or be in bad weather.
